narrative.markdown: Text inputs enable the user to interact with and input content and data, let users enter and edit text. This component can be used for form entries. ### Design > **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site. Text fields are used to allow users to input and edit text. There may be data validation (ex. confirming proper email format), but otherwise, users are free to type any combination of letters, numbers, & symbols. ![Input anatomy: label, placeholder text, input area, hint text](/assets/input/anatomy.png) 1. **Label:** Should show what sort of information the field requires and is left-aligned directly above the input area. 2. **Placeholder text:** Let people know how they should use the field, for example, “Start typing to see names.” 3. **Input area:** This is where people enter text. 4. **Hint text:** Gives context about a field's input. ### Variants #### Text The text variant is a single-line text field for generic text. ![Text input variation](/assets/input/variation-text.png) #### Number Input field designed to accept numerical input. Launches the numerical keyboard on mobile devices. ![Number input variation](/assets/input/variation-number.png) #### Max Text inputs can be set with a maximum character limit. Inline validation can also be set to alert the user and clarify the request. **Recommendations** Give subtle feedback when the user has got enough characters and let users know that they have written too much, by using a chip with the number of characters inserted and the maximum character limit. ![Max character limit input with counter chip](/assets/input/variation-max.png) #### Password The password input is a single-line text field whose value is obscured, used when you need to protect the user's content from being read. **Recommendations** * Show the password requirements and make sure the user can see them before interacting, to reduce friction when creating a password. * Allow the user to see the password they are typing by adding the eye icon as a toggle to display or hide the password. By default, keep the password hidden. * Passwords that don’t meet the criteria should use error messages to help the user correct their input. ![Input example — Variants Password](/assets/input/variants-password.png) #### Search ![Search input variation](/assets/input/variation-search.png) For the search field's full guidance, see [SearchInput](/components/core/search-input/). #### Email Email input is a text input that allows a user to specifically enter an email address. ![Email input variation](/assets/input/variation-email.png) #### InputGroup Icons can be added before the text field to clarify an action and call attention to a button. ![Input group with leading icons](/assets/input/variation-inputgroup.png) ##### Currency When an input has an associated currency it should be used with the `InputGroup` component. ![Currency input using InputGroup](/assets/input/variation-currency.png) #### With supporting content An input label should make it clear what the user should enter into the field. For legibility, keep the label short and limit it to a few words. * The input label needs to help the user understand what is expected of them, but it doesn't need to be instructive * Labels are placed above the input text field * Labels are to be written in sentence case and should only be 1-3 words long ##### Label with description ![Input with label and description](/assets/input/supporting-label-description.png) ##### Hint text Hint text can be added below an input field in order to better clarify how the user should answer. ![Password input with show/hide toggle](/assets/input/variation-password.png) ##### Placeholder Placeholder text is shown inside the text input to help users know what information they can enter. * Field placeholder text is used for supplementary information * The text should be written as examples instead of instructions * Placeholder text disappears after the user begins entering data into the input and should not contain crucial information. **Do:** ![Do example](/assets/input/variation-email.png) **Don't:** ![Don't example](/assets/input/supporting-placeholder.png) Putting instructions on how to complete an input, requirements, or any other essential information into placeholder text is not accessible. Once a value is entered, this text is no longer viewable; if someone is using an automatic form filler, they will never get the information in the placeholder text. #### Right-aligned numeric fields Left-aligned text input should be your default choice, however, is also available right-aligned text input to use in specific circumstances: * Right-aligned text input could be used for numeric inputs. * Right-aligned text input should be used when multiple numeric fields need to be compare. ![Right-aligned numeric fields in a list](/assets/input/right-aligned-numeric.png) #### Sizes > **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site. #### States An input’s state depends on the interaction itself or a submission error. ##### Default The default form of a text field. ![Default state](/assets/input/state-default.png) ##### Placeholder and active-placeholder Placeholder text (if used) remains until user types ![Placeholder state](/assets/input/state-placeholder.png) *Input placeholder* ![Input example — States Placeholder and Active-placeholder: Input Active-placeholder](/assets/input/active-placeholder-input-active-placeholder.png) *Input Active-placeholder* ##### Active typing ![Active typing state](/assets/input/state-active.png) ##### Disabled A disabled text input shows that the user cannot interact with the text field. This can maintain layout continuity and communicate that a field may become available later. ![Disabled state](/assets/input/state-disabled.png) ##### Read-only Text inputs have a read-only option for when the content in the disabled state still needs to be shown. This allows for content to be copied, but not interacted with or changed. ![Read-only state](/assets/input/state-readonly.png) ##### Required or optional Text fields can be marked as optional or required, depending on the situation. Required shows that the user must specify a value for the input before the form can be submitted. Optional text inputs have no sign at all. ![Required state](/assets/input/state-required.png) *Input Required* ##### Focused The focused variation is used to highlight an element that has focus applied. This provide more visibility when an input gets focus. ![Focused state](/assets/input/state-focused.png) #### On dark ![Input example — On dark](/assets/input/on-dark.png) ### Behavior #### Validation ##### States Text Inputs use inline validation. The error displays under the field and the expected behavior in most cases is to avoid showing the error until the user has finished with the field and moved to the next field. ![Input example — Validation States: Input error placeholder](/assets/input/states-input-error-placeholder.png) *Input error placeholder* ![Input with inline error validation](/assets/input/validation-error.png) *Input error - inline validation* Inline errors should be presented with copy explaining the issue and how to fix it. ![Input with warning validation](/assets/input/validation-warning.png) *Input warning* ![Input example — Validation States: Input warning placeholder](/assets/input/states-input-warning-placeholder.png) *Input warning placeholder* ##### Wait to validate Only show error validation messages, or styling after a user has interacted with a particular field. **Do:** ![Do example](/assets/input/validation-wait-to-validate-do.png) **Don't:** ![Don't example](/assets/input/validation-wait-to-validate-dont.png) #### Previous search When the user searches and accesses a detail page and then comes back, it should go back to the immediately previous action/page that the user was on and not reset by the initial state to maintain a consistent experience regardless of context and based on the user journey. ![Input example — Behavior Previous search](/assets/input/behavior-previous-search.png) If the user goes to a different page with the search results, it also should go to the previous search performed. #### Length of the input The length of the text input provides a hint to users how much text to write. Do not require users to write paragraphs of text into a single-line input box; use a text area instead. **Do:** ![Do example](/assets/input/behavior-length-of-the-input-do.png) **Don't:** ![Don't example](/assets/input/behavior-length-of-the-input-dont.png) ### Resources Find this component under: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Form Elements > Input` * [Input component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Cobalt-Core-Components?node-id=260%3A25717) — Core component library * [Input](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COB/pages/1835860207/Input) — Cobalt documentation * [V1](https://talkdesk.github.io/cobalt-react-components/?path=/story/form-elements-form-field--default) — Cobalt ### Code ### Props ### Examples ### Content * Use a combination of a concise label and supportive helper text for clarification of the field input. Don’t rely solely on placeholder text as it is not visible at all times. * Use a concise label to indicate what information goes in the text area input. For example, if the text area appears in a modal called *Create component*, the label for a description text area should only say *Description* and not repeat the modal’s title. * Place helper text above the text input (below the area label) if it is necessary to understand the field. * If appropriate, you can have pre-filled information in the text input. (see image 1). **Do:** Label and helper text clarify what the user needs to do/know. The pre-filled information in the text area expedites the user's work. ![Do example](/assets/input/do.png) **Don't:** Don't rely solely on placeholders. ![Don't example](/assets/input/dont.png) #### Include a label Labels must be must be meaningful and always visible when possible. * Provide a label that describes the purpose of each field **Do:** ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-do.png) **Don't:** ![Don't example](/assets/input/include-a-label-dont.png) * Provide a label that explicitly describes the information expected in the field **Do:** ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-do-2.png) **Don't:** ![Don't example](/assets/input/include-a-label-dont-2.png) #### Placeholder text In general, placeholder text should only be used if it adds value. In recurrent tasks, it’s particularly important to have this in mind to prevent cognitive overload. Help text can show hints and requirements. The help text’s message should not simply restate the same information in the label in order to prompt someone to interact with it. **Note:** Do not use a placeholder as the label of the field. **Do:** When appropriate, help users to know what is expected of them, by giving examples. ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-placeholder-text-do.png) **Don't:** Do not add extra text just to fill space. ![Don't example](/assets/input/include-a-label-placeholder-text-dont.png) **Do:** ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-placeholder-text-do-2.png) **Don't:** ![Don't example](/assets/input/include-a-label-placeholder-text-dont-2.png) ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-placeholder-text-do-3.png) *Do* Leave it blank if the label is self-explanatory. #### Search fields Placeholder copy in search fields should not include ellipsis (exception: *Jump to...*) or other ending punctuation and it should help users to know **everything** they can search for whenever there is enough space. Do not truncate text. **Do:** Be specific. ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-search-fields-do.png) **Don't:** Don't use ellipsis. ![Don't example](/assets/input/include-a-label-search-fields-dont.png) **Do:** “Search” (If there is no space for more information or if it's absolutely obvious what the user can search for). ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-search-fields-do-2.png) **Don't:** “Search…” ![Don't example](/assets/input/include-a-label-search-fields-dont-2.png) **Do:** When possible we should make it clear what user the can search for. ![Do example](/assets/input/include-a-label-search-fields-do-3.png) **Don't:** The word “search” without a preposition means we are searching a specific area for something in particular. E.g., “I searched the office (for my laptop)”. ![Don't example](/assets/input/include-a-label-search-fields-dont-3.png) ### Accessibility ### Considerations #### Design * [1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose AA](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/identify-input-purpose) * [1.3.1 Info and Relationships](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/info-and-relationships.html) * [3.3.2 Labels or Instructions A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/labels-or-instructions) * [2.4.6 Headings and Labels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/headings-and-labels.html) * [4.1.2 Name, Role, Value A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/name-role-value) #### Development In order for users to know how to fill out a form, the form has to be accessible. Users may not be able to fill out form fields correctly if the visible label is not programmatically associated with its field. For assistive technologies like screen readers to interact with and render messages to users, messages need to be composed using programmatically determinable text: either actual text or text available through alternatives such as `alt`, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, and `aria-describedby`. Key concepts include: * Labels for form inputs * Instructions and hints, where necessary * Error prevention * Form validation * Keyboard support ##### Provide a valid label All form inputs and controls need to have a label — a label that is understandable by all users whether the user can see the page or not. * Labels must be in proximity to their control. * Ensure form field constraints and errors are associated with their corresponding field **Labels must be programmatically associated with their control** There is a hierarchy of methods for providing an accessible name for an input: **\

narrative.markdown:
InputGroups are useful for giving context to input field values.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

InputGroup allows form controls to be extended by grouping inputs, buttons, and other elements into an adjacent visual unit.

### Anatomy

![InputGroup anatomy: label, icon, hint, item, value, dropdown, extra input](/assets/input-group/anatomy.png)

1. **Label**
2. **Icon**
3. **Hint**
4. **Item**
5. **Value**
6. **Dropdown**
7. **Extra input**

### Variants

#### Sizes

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### States

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Modifiers

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Orientation

You can use the gray BG variation to highlight and improve more meaning of what the user needs to add in the input (white BG variation). Also, this gray variation is only interactive when associated with an expandable arrow (Dropdown).

![Last item in a group](/assets/input-group/spacing-last.png)
*Last*

![First item in a group](/assets/input-group/spacing-first.png)
*First*

![Middle item in a group](/assets/input-group/spacing-middle.png)
*Middle*

#### Quantity

In Figma, our component supports a maximum of 3 items combined.

![2 items grouped](/assets/input-group/quantity-2-items.png)
*2 items*

  ![3 items grouped](/assets/input-group/quantity-3-items.png)
*3 items*

On the implementation side, there is no limitation for the max of inputs grouped. For now, we recommend a max of 5 inputs together.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/11bf86-inputgroup) — Design tab, image 32.*

Quality Manager reference with 5 items applied.

### Guidelines

#### Placement

This component should be used inside form pages and associated with form elements.

#### Best practices

![Do example](/assets/input-group/dodont-do-1.png)
*Do*
Use it to add on at either end of a field related to a question, like an amount with a numerical value or a time frame value.

![Do example](/assets/input-group/dodont-do-3.png)
*Do*
Use it when there’s an association between one attribute and another, as it adds a clear affordance for what type of data is required to be entered in the field. e.g. $ or %.

![Do example](/assets/input-group/dodont-do-2.png)
*Do*
Combine it with icons to improve the meaning of the InputGroup need.

![Caution example](/assets/input-group/dodont-caution-1.png)
*Caution*
Caution with complex groupings that will be constricted by horizontal space, prefer to use individual inputs instead.

### Behavior

#### Responsiveness

The small size should be used for small viewports and the medium size only for medium and large viewports.

#### Text truncation

When the entered text is too long for the available horizontal space in the field, the text truncates.

![Text truncated inside a grouped input value](/assets/input-group/text-truncation.png)

#### Spacing

![0px spacing between grouped items, 16px spacing between separate InputGroups](/assets/input-group/spacing-annotation.png)

### Resources

Access this Cobalt component from: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > FormElements > InputGroup`

* [InputGroup Component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?type=design\&node-id=841%3A59275\&t=zwIBY1J1BrxidX75-1) — Core components library
* [InputGroup Handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?type=design\&node-id=189%3A132879\&t=n6rlp69VxUxeh39Q-1) — Specs

### Code

### Installation

> **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Examples

### Props

### Content

### Writing guidelines

This component has no component-specific copy rules yet. For copy rules that apply
everywhere, see [Grammar and mechanics](/foundations/content/content-grammar-and-mechanics/).

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Development

* Keep the grouped input's own associated label.
* Label any add-on (icon/button), or hide it from assistive tech if purely decorative.

For accessibility guidance that applies to every component, see
[Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

narrative.markdown:
Labels give context to the information that a user needs to input.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

Labels are usually 1–2 words that are commonly used in forms like inputs, dropdowns, checkboxes, etc. Text is used to **tell the user what to do** and should be simple.

### Anatomy

![Label anatomy diagram with 8 numbered callouts](/assets/label/anatomy.png)

1. **Label** - Text that informs the user what to expect in the input
2. **Required** - Used to specify that the input element must be filled out before submitting the form
3. **Info** - Interactive icon that shows a tooltip with more information about the topic
4. **Secondary label** - Additional text to give more context if necessary
5. **Tertiary label** - Additional text to give more context if necessary
6. **Link** - Add a link if necessary
7. **Tag** - Add a tag if necessary
8. **Description** - Gives more context about the label

### Variants

#### Modifiers

![Label using the default text color](/assets/label/modifier-label.png)
*Standalone*

  ![Label with description](/assets/label/modifier-description.png)
*Description*

![Required label with asterisk](/assets/label/modifier-required.png)
*Required*

  ![Label with info icon and tooltip](/assets/label/modifier-info.png)
*Info*

![Label with secondary label](/assets/label/modifier-secondary-label.png)
*Secondary label*

  ![Label with tertiary label](/assets/label/modifier-tertiary-label.png)
*Tertiary label*

![Label with a link](/assets/label/modifier-link.png)
*Link*

  ![Label with a character-count tag](/assets/label/modifier-tag.png)
*Tag*

#### Arrangement

Label width is always dependent on the associated component width. For example, if the input width=`320px`, label width=`320px`.

![Label example — Variants Arrangement: Full-width](/assets/label/arrangement-full-width-2.png)
*Full-width*

#### Position

A label should be placed only on top of an input. This position is the default because they work better with long copy, localization, and responsive layouts. Also, they could be oriented on the left/right regarding the priority of the label.

![Full-width label matching the width of its input](/assets/label/arrangement-full-width.png)
*Top Left*

  ![Label example — Variants Position: Top Right](/assets/label/position-top-right.png)
*Top Right*

### Guidelines

#### Placement

Use labels inside form elements.

#### Best practices

##### Label color

Label color should never be changed.

**Do:** 
![Do example](/assets/label/do-s-don-ts-label-color.png)

**Don't:** 
![Don't example](/assets/label/label-color-dont.png)

##### Requirement or optional

Label inputs could be required or optional, depending on the situation, using a necessity indicator.

By default, the required indicator is shown with an asterisk icon. Required inputs are marked with this at the end of the label and be sure to include hint text to explain what it means.

**Do:** Always add a hint to explain why the input is required.
![Do example](/assets/label/requirement-do.png)

**Don't:** You submitted and don't know the problem.
![Don't example](/assets/label/requirement-dont.png)

You can also use the secondary label to say that the input is “optional”. Optional inputs do not need to add an icon.

**Do:** Label with optional information
![Do example](/assets/label/optional-do.png)

**Don't:** Don't use any icon to inform the input is optional.
![Don't example](/assets/label/optional-dont.png)

### Behavior

#### Interaction

When a user clicks or touches/taps a label, the browser passes the focus to its associated input (the resulting event is also raised for the input).

To explicitly associate a `<label>` element with an `<input>` element, you first need to add the `id` attribute to the `<input>` element. Next, you add the `for` attribute to the `<label>` element, where the value of `for` is the same as the `id` in the `<input>` element.

* [Playroom example](https://prd-cdn-talkdesk.talkdesk.com/cobalt/playroom/index.html#?code=N4Igxg9gJgpiBcIA8AhCAPABACxgSwHNsAXAXgB0QBGABhoDdtLMAHAQyijwDsDTgAHAF8AfOW6ZMSAMIRuxGOmJiJkzMAAUwHBAgBrAM6YhASkykR68WrWRuB4pgDaeA9Nxg9MKABpMBmGIASTcPLygAXXNMACUYNjBiADoAVwCAZWI2BQ0AMzYAGwCTAG5xaxtMACdAlKqJDQrKqQAxAsVMLhrEvDkKcAgClIBbbmYCNhZ%2BgGZKFWabJAAVRUdIAogq-pqoOYB1PGJsCBTHFiqIFgN4JAB6FaV5hckkNo7Cwm4ATX6wGHkYFVxpN%2BgAmOZNZ5SAAybAARjACiJYQiCncUYinlCpEFuCxTphiABPFgwX5hOEYZi3LELO5vdAqSHNZarTDrTb9Ag1f77Q7YVgXK43e6rWkshmYD4Eb6-f4KIEgTATKaUcEgcV0jEFTC5TmUArwxEAWioc216KNSOZdNx%2BOINueYDC3n4rncME83iEjoWcncbF4ZM0Zgs-kCIQ9XqgGgAhO6XVATD7VNjJHgoP1DajTZRfc1iaTyZ69JT0HnU1CafmpLcGZqXnX2oybaVIUIU43ZADHuI7mgW9wQD4QEcYMMYAYEE4QAVCCQQBERwB3DNHKfwJwANgALDQIkIgA) — A label with and without props

#### Overflow

When the field label is too long for the available horizontal space, it wraps to the line above.

![An extremely large and unnecessary label wraps to the line above](/assets/label/overflow.png)

#### Internationalization

For RTL (right-to-left) languages, the layout of the label is mirrored and the label is right-aligned. However, some types of content (e.g., email addresses) are not translated.

![RTL email label and input, right-aligned and mirrored](/assets/label/internationalization.png)

### Resources

Access this Cobalt component from: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Label`

* [Label component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?node-id=1104%3A298755) — Core Components library
* [Label handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?node-id=119-119830) — Handoff guidelines

### Code

### Props

### Examples

### Content

### Introduction

The label component is used to provide a clear and concise description of the input field, allowing the user to easily understand the information being requested.

### Tone and voice

The tone and voice used for the Label component should be informal and positive, using clear and concise language that is easy to understand.

### Word choice

* Field labels should be short and in noun form, providing clear context for the input field.
* For text fields that are placed individually on a page, the label should be written as a call to action to avoid confusion.
* Labels can include instruction and formatting, such as "Full name" or date format "MMM D, YYYY".
* Words like **"Optional"** and **"Required"** should be used as a Secondary Label.

### Concise and clear writing

Label text should be short and concise. Users should be able to quickly understand what information is being requested without having to read a long or complex label.

Although in some cases it may be necessary to give more context, in general, a label with 1 or 2 words is best.

### Variants

For text fields that are not part of a form and are placed individually on a page, the label can be written as a call to action.

### Examples

Dos and don'ts.

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Development

* Renders a native `<label>`; requires `htmlFor` matching the control's `id` to give it an accessible name.
* Keep label text concise and descriptive.

For accessibility guidance that applies to every component, see
[Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

narrative.markdown:
A link is an interactive component that could be used preceding or following a text to navigate or redirects to external sources

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Anatomy

![Link anatomy: label text and underline](/assets/link/anatomy.png)

1. **Label text**
2. **Underline**

### Variants

#### Sizes

Link size should match the associated text size.

![Medium size link](/assets/link/size-medium.png)
*Size - Medium*

  ![Small size link](/assets/link/size-small.png)
*Size - Small*

#### Types

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### States

![Default state](/assets/link/state-default.png)
*State - Default*

  ![Hover state](/assets/link/state-hover.png)
*State - Hover*

  ![Disabled state](/assets/link/state-disabled.png)
*State - Disabled*

![Focused state](/assets/link/state-focused.png)
*State - Focused*

  ![Visited state](/assets/link/state-visited.png)
*State - Visited*

  ![Pressed state](/assets/link/state-pressed.png)
*State - Pressed*

### Guidelines

#### Group

![A link used inline within a sentence of body text](/assets/link/group-link-with-text.png)
*Link with text*

![A message with a title, description and a link](/assets/link/group-link-on-message.png)
*Link on message*
The link can only be used in default messages, with or without block property. The link type must match the message type.

![A message banner with a title, description and a link](/assets/link/group-link-on-message-banner.png)
*Link on message banner*
The link can only be used in default messages, with or without block property. The link type must match the message type.

#### Link vs button vs LabeledIcon

A link should never be used with an icon.

To use an interactive component with an icon and label it should use the button component.

To use a non-interactive component with an icon and label it should use the labeledicon component.

![Link](/assets/link/comparison-link.png)
*Link*

  ![Transparent button with icon](/assets/link/comparison-button.png)
*Transparent button with icon*

| **Component** | **Interactive** | **Icon**                 | **Size**                               | **Font size**                                                                         | **Label weight**             |
| ------------- | --------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Labeledicon   | False           | True                     | Micro XSmall Small Medium Large XLarge | Micro: Small XSmall: Medium Small: Medium Medium: Medium Large: Medium XLarge: Medium | Optional (Regular or Medium) |
| Button        | True            | Optional (True or False) | Medium Small XSmall                    | Medium: Medium Small: Small XSmall: N/A                                               | Medium                       |
| Link          | True            | False                    | Medium Small                           | Medium: Medium Small: Small                                                           | Regular                      |

### Resources

Find this component under: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Link`

* [Link component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?node-id=579%3A32310) — Core component library
* [Link handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?node-id=200%3A131810) — Handoff guidelines

### Code

### Installation

> **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Examples

### Props

### Content

Links should be as descriptive and specific as possible and make sense in isolation.

* Links should be sincere and predictable, they should always tell the user what will happen or what they'll find when they click on it.
* Start with the most important terms.
* Avoid one-word links. Users with poor motor skills might have trouble selecting them.
* Don't write Click here, Read this or Learn more, as they're not clear, specific, or accessible. Ask about what the link does, where it takes the user or what it shows to them: answer these questions before, then start writing.
* For links that lead to information, the link should be the text about that information (e.g., Visit our support page for more information).
* For links that lead to a page where the user can perform a task, always start with a verb (e.g., Create article).
* Use sentence case.
* Don't include ending punctuation. Exception: when the link is a question, it should include the question mark.
* Don't include articles in the link (e.g., Read our Terms of Service, not Read our Terms of Service).
* If you have to refer to a link, say click the link and not follow the link.
* For links with icons, place the icon to the left side of the link. Exception: for RTL (Right-to-Left) languages, such as Arabic and Hebrew, icons should appear to the right of links.

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Development

* Renders a native `<a>` and adds `rel="noreferrer noopener"` for external targets.
* Write link text that's descriptive on its own.
* A "disabled" link still needs an accessible treatment (anchors can't be natively disabled like buttons).

For accessibility guidance that applies to every component, see
[Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

narrative.markdown:
Lists are continuous, vertical indexes of content. They are highly legible, intuitive, and simple.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

Lists are compiled of an ordered set of items. They can be used stand-alone but usually, they’re mixed with other components like dropdowns or popup menus.

### Anatomy

![List anatomy: asset, main label, secondary label, secondary icon, tag, action, divider, description, avatar](/assets/list/anatomy.png)
*List Anatomy*

1. **Asset** - Element that can indicate an icon, flag, checkbox, radio, and more.
2. **Main label** - Mandatory text that informs what to expect on that list item.
3. **Secondary label** - Optional value to indicate a microcopy aligned on the right.
4. **Secondary icon** - Optional visual representation of the item displayed in a simplified way.
5. **Tag** - Optional visual reference to indicate a type of list item.
6. **Action** - Optional button to allow an interactive list item.
7. **Divider** - A line to create a separation between the list of items.
8. **Description** - Optional content to give more context about the item.
9. **Avatar** - Optional modifier that indicates a person/user reference.

### Variants

#### Sizes

Lists don’t have a defined width or height. They adjust to its container. However, they have different spacing values for each viewport.

![Large list item size](/assets/list/size-large.png)
*Large*

  ![Medium list item size](/assets/list/size-medium.png)
*Medium*

  ![Small list item size](/assets/list/size-small.png)
*Small*

#### States

![Default state list item](/assets/list/state-default.png)
*Default*

  ![Hover state list item](/assets/list/state-hover.png)
*Hover*

![Focused state list item](/assets/list/state-focused.png)
*Focused*

  ![Active state list item](/assets/list/state-active.png)
*Active*

![Error state list item](/assets/list/state-error.png)
*Error*

  ![Disabled state list item](/assets/list/state-disabled.png)
*Disabled*

#### Modifiers

Some variations may be:

![List with text-only items](/assets/list/modifier-text-only.png)
*With Text only*

  ![List items with an action](/assets/list/modifier-action.png)
*With Action*

![List items with an asset (icon, flag, checkbox, radio)](/assets/list/modifier-asset.png)
*With Asset*

  ![List items with an avatar](/assets/list/modifier-avatar.png)
*With Avatar*
Use when showing an image or initial of an user

![List items with a description](/assets/list/modifier-description.png)
*With Description*
Use to add supporting text content to list items.

  ![List items with a secondary icon](/assets/list/modifier-icon.png)
*With Icon*

![List items with a secondary label](/assets/list/modifier-secondary-label.png)
*With Secondary label*

  ![List items with a tag](/assets/list/modifier-tag.png)
*With Tag*

### Guidelines

#### When to use

Use lists to highlight benefits, provide links to other screens, and much more.

* To create simple and easily scannable lists.
* To break up chunks of related content to make the information easier to scan.
* To display name/value pairs such as terms and definitions.
* To display a glossary list.

#### When not to use

* To show tabular or multi-column data. Instead, use a [Table](/components/core/table/).
* For list items with multi-actions.

#### Group

Use a divider to create logical groups of information inside a list.

![List with a divider creating logical groups of items](/assets/list/group-divider.png)

#### Placement

This component does not have a specific placement rule.

### Behavior

#### Stacking

Lists can be only stacked vertically.

#### Actionable content

If it has an action, the whole list item is clickable. During user interaction, the button action state should be always Default.

![Clickable list item with a hover state on the whole row](/assets/list/actionable-content.png)

#### Responsiveness

The component is ready to adapt to any screen like mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports.

#### Text truncation

Text truncation is supported, however, we recommend you to try to be concise whenever possible.

If the text is too long for one line, add an ellipsis `(…)` for overflow content, and accompany a tooltip to show the full string of text.

![List item with truncated text shown as an ellipsis with a tooltip](/assets/list/text-truncation.png)

#### Internationalization

For RTL (right-to-left) languages, the layout of the list should be mirrored. All texts are right-aligned while icons are left-aligned.

### Resources

Access this Cobalt component from: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > List`

* [List component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?node-id=470%3A11284) — Core Components library

* [List Handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?node-id=314%3A177509) — Specs

* [Marketplace component](https://prd-cdn-talkdesk.talkdesk.com/cobalt/docs/index.html?path=/docs/marketplace_marketplace-components-list-stories--basic)

### Code

### Installation

> **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Examples

### Props

### Content

### Writing guidelines

This component has no component-specific copy rules yet. For copy rules that apply
everywhere, see [Grammar and mechanics](/foundations/content/content-grammar-and-mechanics/).

### Accessibility

### Interactions

#### Keyboard

No keyboard interaction is needed.

* [Listbox](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/listbox/) — W3C guidelines

### Considerations

#### Development

Components must be accessible to allow interaction regardless of the user's context. Lists are announced as expected in all screen readers including VoiceOver.

* List outputs a description list that has a semantic meaning in HTML. For this reason, the list component should never be used for displaying e.g. tabular data.
* By default, list items are conveyed as a group of related elements to assistive technology users.

props.name: placement
props.description:
Where the menu's popover opens relative to its trigger. Accepts
react-aria `Placement` values (e.g. `"bottom start"`, `"top end"`);
`start`/`end` are RTL-aware. Defaults to react-aria's own placement for
the surrounding trigger (`"bottom start"` for `MenuTrigger`, `"end top"`
for `SubmenuTrigger`) unless overridden here. The popover still flips
automatically when there isn't room on the chosen side.

props.name: header
props.description:
Non-interactive content shown above the menu's items, outside the
selectable/keyboard-navigable collection entirely.

props.name: onSelectionChange
props.description:
Called when the selection changes. Receives a `Set<Key>`, or the string
`"all"` when the user selects every item (e.g. via Ctrl/Cmd+A) — check
for `"all"` before treating the argument as an iterable of keys.

props.name: selectedKeys
props.description:
Currently selected keys. A `Set<Key>`, or the string `"all"` when every
item is selected — `"all"` is a sticky sentinel (it keeps future items
selected too) rather than an enumerated set, so handle it explicitly.

props.name: defaultSelectedKeys
props.description: Initially selected keys for an uncontrolled menu. See `selectedKeys`.

props.name: escapeKeyBehavior
props.description:
Whether pressing the escape key should clear selection in the menu or not.

Most experiences should not modify this option as it eliminates a keyboard user's ability to
easily clear selection. Only use if the escape key is being handled externally or should not
trigger selection clearing contextually. @default 'clearSelection'

props.name: shouldFocusWrap
props.description: Whether keyboard navigation is circular.

props.name: onAction
props.description: Handler that is called when an item is selected.

props.name: onClose
props.description: Handler that is called when the menu should close after selecting an item.

props.name: items
props.description: Item objects in the collection.

props.name: disabledKeys
props.description:
The item keys that are disabled. These items cannot be selected, focused, or otherwise
interacted with.

props.name: disallowEmptySelection
props.description: Whether the collection allows empty selection.

props.name: className
props.description:
The CSS [className](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/className) for the
element. A function may be provided to compute the class based on component state. @default 'react-aria-Menu'

narrative.markdown:
Messages can be used to display critical messages about the loss of data or important information that affects the normal use of the product. Use them as many times as needed all over the screen. Find below the documentation to know exactly how to use this component.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

![Message styles: Primary/Feature, Info, Success, Warning, Error, and Secondary](/assets/message/message-styles-overview.png)

### Variants

There are two types of messages: **Default** and **Banner**

For the Default type could be activated the property **Block**

![Default, Default Blocked, and Banner message variations](/assets/message/message-variations.png)

#### Styles

Each message can be displayed in these variations:

* **Info**: Use it to update users about a change or to give them advice.
* **Success**: Use it to inform when the task is completed.
* **Warning**: Use it to display information that needs attention or users need to take any action on. Seeing these kinds of messages can be stressful for users so be cautious when using them.
* **Danger**: Use to communicate a problem that needs to be solved as soon as possible. Seeing these kinds of messages can be stressful for users so be cautious when using them.
* **Primary/Feature**: Friendly advice to communicate a new feature is available.
* **Secondary:** To be used when any other variant isn’t valid.

#### Sizes

Messages don’t have a maximum or a minimum width, they’ll adjust to the width of the container they are placed in.

It should be easily adapted to every screen size. Mobile, Tablet and Desktop.

#### Types

##### Basic

Basic messages are single-lined. They are composed of a Title and/or Description. You can use both or just one of them with or without a link. Please mind that the description comes after the title in **horizontal** order.

![Basic message content combinations: dismissible with title/description/link, with title and description, with title only, with description only](/assets/message/message-types-basic-content.png)

![Basic message styles: Primary/Feature, Info, Success, Warning, Error](/assets/message/message-types-basic-styles.png)

##### Block

A block Message is a variation of the Default message but uses more vertical space. The description is placed under the title and because it can grow vertically, we can also add CTA’s at the bottom. You can use any combinations of it (with or without title, descriptions and/or actions).

![Block message combinations: dismissible with title, description and actions; with title and description; with title and actions; with description and actions](/assets/message/message-types-block.png)

##### Banner

Used exclusively for **global system messages, or cross-application communications**. Banners are placed at the top of the content areas (this is, over the primary and secondary areas of Workspace) and they should occupy the entire width of the page.

Colors have been boosted to call more effectively for attention. This way, they can inform effectively about system status and can be easily noticed wherever they are used.

Find the full banners documentation on [Banners | Design](https://zeroheight.com/51aaf6147/p/3335b0/b/35e7dd).

![Banner styles with boosted colors: Primary/Feature, Info, Success, Warning, Error](/assets/message/message-types-banner-styles.png)

![Banner content combinations: dismissible with title and description, with title and description, with title, with description](/assets/message/message-types-banner-content.png)

#### Alignment

All Message elements (Icon, Text elements and Close button) should be vertically aligned on top for all Message types and in all viewports

![Icon, text, and close button aligned to the top of a multi-line message](/assets/message/message-alignment.png)

### Guidelines

#### Use cases

##### Dismissing a message

* The close button is optional. When used it allows users to dismiss the message. Without this, the message will persist on the screen.

##### Positioning

* **Default message**
  * Can be shown anywhere on the screen
* **Banner message**
  * Banners are used for system messages and they are placed at the top of the page or section they apply

##### Status icons

* Each message type comes with a corresponding icon. **These are not changeable** as we want to be consistent when displaying these messages to the user. The only exception is for Primary/Feature Messages. As an example, to use a Loader icon instead of the message icon for cases where we want to show a loading message.

##### Highlighting a description

You can highlight a portion of a sentence in the description of the Message. On the implementation side, it's possible to have bold text with the `Text` component and its `weight` prop.

#### Placement

Banner Message is positioned on top, below the title bar without any spacing between them.

Banner Message span the full width.

![Banner message placed below the title bar, spanning the full width above the page content](/assets/message/message-placement.png)

### Behavior

#### Responsiveness

There are no differences between screen sizes except for the lateral paddings of **Banner** messages (to match the page paddings).

![Large, Medium, and Small message size examples](/assets/message/message-responsiveness-sizes.png)

Message left and right paddings follow the general rules for each viewport, **L:24px / M:16px / S:12px**

![Message example — Behavior Responsiveness: Small](/assets/message/responsiveness-small.png)
*Small*

![Message example — Behavior Responsiveness: Medium](/assets/message/responsiveness-medium.png)
*Medium*

![Message side padding reference across Large, Medium, and Small viewports](/assets/message/message-responsiveness-padding.png)
*Large*

When necessary Default and Banner Messages text elements could be multiline, however, this should be avoided so use clear and concise copy as our content guidelines suggest.

#### Dimensions

##### Message maximum width

Messages have `width=100%`. Additionally, an optional maximum width of **620px** can be set.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/04b4cd-message) — Design tab, image 9.*

### Toast (floating type)

The toast component is a non-disruptive message that appears at the bottom of the interface to provide quick, at-a-glance feedback on the outcome of an action.

In Cobalt, Toast is `<Message type="floating">`.

#### Overview

Toasts inform users of a process that a system has performed or will perform. They shouldn’t interrupt the user from performing a task.

#### Anatomy

![Toast anatomy: icon, title, description, actions, dismissible button, and timer](/assets/message/toast-anatomy.png)

1. **Icon.** Customizable only for Primary and White types.
2. **Title**
3. **Description** (optional)
4. **Actions** (optional)
5. **Dismissible button**
6. **Timer** (optional)

#### Variants

##### Sizes

Toast notifications use a fixed width and their height depends on the length of the notification message.

![Large toast](/assets/message/toast-size-large.png)
*Large*

![Medium toast](/assets/message/toast-size-medium.png)
*Medium*

![Small toast](/assets/message/toast-size-small.png)
*Small*

##### Types

![Primary toast](/assets/message/toast-type-primary.png)
*Primary*

  ![Info toast](/assets/message/toast-type-info.png)
*Info*

  ![Error toast](/assets/message/toast-type-error.png)
*Error*

![Success toast](/assets/message/toast-type-success.png)
*Success*

  ![Warning toast](/assets/message/toast-type-warning.png)
*Warning*

  ![White toast](/assets/message/toast-type-white.png)
*White*

##### Modifiers

![Dismissible toast](/assets/message/toast-modifier-dismissible.png)
*Dismissible Toast*
Toasts with actions and toast with a message that suggests action should never use the timer.

![Primary toast](/assets/message/toast-type-primary.png)
*Auto-dismissible Toast*

**What is the default timer duration?**

Auto-dismissible Toasts must be a minimum of 5 seconds on screen. This is the default value for the toasts timer, however, if the Toast content has more than 50 characters the timer should increase by applying the formula, 1 second per 10 characters.

**Hovering an auto-dismissible Toast?**

Hovering the cursor over a toast prevents it from disappearing. When the cursor leaves the toast, the toast's timeout restarts.

#### Guidelines

##### Group

Could be displayed a maximum of 2 toasts.

The spacing between toasts on the page should follow the global rules of **L:24px / M:16px / S:12px**.

![Two toasts stacked in a group above the bottom-right corner of the screen](/assets/message/toast-group.png)

##### Use cases

###### When to use the timer (auto-dismissible toast)?

The timer is optional and should not be used if,

* it is critical for a user to read or interact with the toast.
* if the toast has actions.
* if the toast message suggests an action (e.g. Please try again).

![Decision flowchart for when to use an alert modal vs. a toast, and when to use the auto-dismiss timer](/assets/message/toast-timer-decision.png)

The previous information suggests that a Toast with actions shouldn't use the timer, however, there are two expectations when a Toast can combine actions with times:

* Toasts that will be shown multiple times in a short period of time can combine actions with a timer.
* If the actions available in the Toast are also available on the same screen after the Toast disappears, the Toast can combine actions with the timer.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/09132a-toast) — Design tab, image 15.*

###### Merge two toasts in a single one

When an app generates two toasts with the same specs and contents, they should be combined by deleting the last generated toast.

###### Remove a toast from the queue

When the user performs actions that make a specific toast useless, it should be removed from the queue.

##### Placement

Toasts should be placed on the bottom right corner of the screen at **L:24px / M:16px / S:12px** from the right and bottom, in front of the content. Avoid placing a toast in front of frequently used touch targets or navigation.

Inside Workspace, an app asks Workspace to show the toast, and Workspace places it in the bottom-right corner of the whole window, not of the app. See [Messages](/workspace/messages/#toasts) for how that works and which settings an app controls.

##### When to use

* Should be used for unexpected errors. When something doesn’t work, we send an error message.
* It is used immediately after a specific event, such as a user action that does not relate to an object on the page. For example, confirmation of deleted items.

##### When not to use

* When you are speaking directly to a piece of content, use Inline Notifications which can be positioned closer to it.
* When an action is user-triggered and you need to inform the user, use a Confirmation Modal.
* When the control the user acted on can show the result itself. For example, Marketplace [CopyToClipboard](/components/marketplace/copy-to-clipboard/) briefly turns its icon into a green check when it copies.

##### Toast vs modal

When showing toasts while a modal is open, the toasts should appear on top of the overlay.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/09132a-toast) — Design tab, image 16.*

### Resources

Find this component under: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Message`

* [Message](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/Cobalt-Core-Components?node-id=596%3A28983) — Cobalt Core Component

[Banners | Design](https://zeroheight.com/51aaf6147/p/3335b0/b/35e7dd)

* [V1](https://talkdesk.github.io/cobalt-react-components/?path=/story/message-basic-messages--color-status) — Cobalt

**Toast**

Find this component under: `Cobalt Design System > Core Components > Toast`

* [Toast](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2)-%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Cobalt-Core-Components?node-id=734%3A41946) — Cobalt core component

* [V1](https://talkdesk.github.io/cobalt-react-components/?path=/story/toaster--basic) — Cobalt

### Code

### Props

### Examples

### Content

### Message

#### Banner

Every banner should:

* be clear and concise.
* start with the most important information.
* help the user solve the issue (when possible) by following up with a solution and making the text actionable with a link (see image 1)
* use ellipsis when there’s a process going on: this helps indicate that it will be brief.
* use sentence case.
* have at least 40% of space available for wordier languages.

**Do:** Our voice is colloquial, so it's better to use "we" instead of "Talkdesk", and "turn on" instead of "enable".
![Do example](/assets/message/message-content-do-banner.png)

**Don't:** Avoid punctuation. In this case, the sentence should not have a fullstop.
![Don't example](/assets/message/message-content-dont-banner.png)

#### Block message

* Titles should clearly describe the issue or reason for the message.
* Description text should be clear, concise, empathetic, and informative.
* Use active verbs in the CTAs to guide the user on any actions they need to take.

#### Default message

* Titles should clearly describe the issue or reason for the message.
* Description text should be clear, concise, empathetic, and informative.
* Use active verbs to guide the user on any actions they need to take.
* If there is both message title and message description, use punctuation in both.

**Do:** Use active voice to explain to the user what they can or must do.
![Do example](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

**Don't:** We’re using an abbreviation that we’ve never explained before and we’re using the passive voice.
![Don't example](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/04b4cd-message) — Content tab, image 3, image 4.*

#### Error message

An error message occurs after the users has taken an action. Besides focusing on being clear, you should explain what has happen, what are the consequences of this action, and what the user can to do move forward.

##### An error message is different from a warning message

A warning message alerts users to an exception condition that may cause a problem in the future. An error message alerts users of a problem that has already occurred (caused by the users or the system).

##### How to write an error message

**Title**

* Titles are optional depending on the component you’ve chosen.
* Write an informative title, usually explaining what has happened.
* Avoid giving a solution in the title.
* Keep the title short, using three to four words if possible.

**Body**

* Avoid repeating content that is already in the title.
* Explain the reason for the error, how the user should act and what can happen if they don’t act.
* Keep it to 2 sentences max.
* Don’t use technical words and unnecessary information in the message. If needed, use a link with the support contact (or any other that makes sense in the case you’re dealing with).

**Call to action (CTA)**

* In case you’re using a CTA, use imperative verbs to describe what action the user will be making. **Example:** Save contact
* Write a CTA with only 1 or 2 words. **Example:** Remove contact

**Voice and tone**

As errors can be frustrating, it’s important to give the user the feeling of support and reassurance. Writing these messages with the same [voice and tone](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/359359-voice-and-tone) as the whole product is important to build the user’s trust and confidence.

* Be empathic: maybe it’s their first time using Talkdesk (or any similar technology).
* Error messages are important to help the user understand how our products work and avoid similar issues in the future.
* The use of *we* and *you* is important to give a more conversational feeling.
* Avoid messages that focus on the problem without offering a solution.
* Provide quick instructions so the problem can be solved fast.
* [The use of “please”](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/48e27a-grammar-and-mechanics/t/05c815).
* [Avoid saying “sorry”](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/48e27a-grammar-and-mechanics/t/33f884).

#### Success message

A success message should appear after the user has taken an action or completed a task successfully.

##### How to write a success message

**Title**

* Titles are optional depending on the component you’ve chosen.
* Write an informative title, usually explaining what has happened.
* Keep the title short, using three to four words if possible.
* Avoid using the words “success” or “successfully”.
* Avoid exclamation points, as we don’t need to be overly excited about everything!

**Body**

* Avoid repeating content that is already in the title
* Confirm what was the action taken or what was the task that has been completed.
* Keep it to 2 sentences max.
* Don’t use technical words and unnecessary information in the message. If needed, use a link with the support contact (or any other that makes sense in the case you’re dealing with).

**Call to action (CTA)**

* If the user has created or changed something, let them have access to it and view it.
* In case you’re using a CTA, use imperative verbs to describe what action the user will be making. **Example:** Save contact
* Write a CTA with only 1 or 2 words. **Example:** Remove contact

**Voice and tone**

Success messages should give users the feeling of motivation and satisfaction towards their actions. Writing these messages with the same [voice and tone](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/359359-voice-and-tone) as the whole product is important to build the user’s trust and confidence.

* Do not over celebrate the user’s actions.
* Success messages that are repetitive and shown more frequently should be simpler and concise.
* If the user has done a bigger task, write a more optimistic message, that can build trust and confidence.
* Success messages are also a good timing to be a little playful and conversional.

### Toast

#### Toasts

Toasts are temporary, usually lasting from 3 to 5 seconds. This means we have a limited amount of time to pass on information to our users, so:

* Keep toasts as short as possible. In most cases you can omit articles, pronouns and other non-essential words to convey meaning.
* Adjust the duration of the toast so that the reading speed does not exceed 150 words per minute.
* Use sentence case.
* Avoid punctuation. **Exceptions:** more than one sentence requires periods and loading toasts require ellipsis.
* The body should not repeat the information that’s in the title.
* Text in the body is optional.

##### Success toasts

Use them to reaffirm the outcome and then get out of the user's way. If they have just created something, you can provide a link to its location (another page or Atlas app, for example).

Messages that appear more frequently should have less personality and go straight to the point.

**Do:** Short message that contains the necessary information that the user can read in those 3 to 5 seconds.
![Do example](/assets/message/toast-content-do-success-1.png)

**Don't:** The word “successful(ly)” can be omitted because the checkmark and the green color we use in our toasts already signify success. Avoid punctuation.
![Don't example](/assets/message/toast-content-dont-success-1.png)

Messages that appear after a bigger or more infrequent action can congratulate the user and have a more human touch, but should remain concise.

**Do:** Success message in the title and reaffirmation of the outcome.
![Do example](/assets/message/toast-content-do-success-2.png)

**Don't:** This isn’t appropriate for a toast due to its temporality. This tone is better used in an empty state, for example.
![Don't example](/assets/message/toast-content-dont-success-2.png)

##### Error toasts

Using a conversational tone, you should let the user know what’s causing the error and explain how to fix it/how to proceed. Avoid ambiguity.

**Do:** Error message in the title and explanation in the body.
![Do example](/assets/message/toast-content-do-error.png)

**Don't:** The body should not repeat the same information that's in the title.
![Don't example](/assets/message/toast-content-dont-error.png)

##### Loading toasts

* In general, keep them clear and short. If the loading is consistently slow, longer text is suitable or a random sequence of messages can be shown as time passes.
* Be specific: when possible, communicate exactly what’s happening in the background. E.g., *Loading your flow\...* instead of just *Loading…*
* Be informative only and don’t ask any additional action from the user.
* If loading times are usually long, inform the user about the time left to complete the process (E.g., *Uploading your files… This can take up to 1 minute*). You can also remind users that they shouldn't refresh the page.
* Reading speed should not exceed 150 words per minute.
* Use sentence case.
* Use ellipsis to help indicate that the process will be brief.
* You can be playful if appropriate.

**Do:** The flow takes a few seconds to load, so we can be a bit more specific.
![Do example](/assets/message/toast-content-do-loading.png)

**Don't:** The ellipsis is missing.
![Don't example](/assets/message/toast-content-dont-loading.png)

### Accessibility

### Message

#### Interactions

##### Keyboard

Users should be able to navigate to the dismiss and action buttons of the message using normal keyboard navigation (tab key).

#### Considerations

##### Development

Depending on the message type we can have two ARIA roles that should be used. These should be applied to the title of the message. In the absence of the title, it should be added to the description.

For **info, success, feature,** and **warning** messages, which usually have advisory information for the user that is not important enough to justify an alert, we should use the status role ([documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/ARIA_Techniques/Using_the_status_role)).

However, for **error/danger** messages which are often used to communicate an important and usually time-sensitive message to the user, we should use the alert role ([documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/ARIA_Techniques/Using_the_alert_role)).

### Toast

#### Considerations

##### Design

Toast messages are a great way to report transient statuses and messages that are not critical. However, for a small visual element, there are many accessibility considerations.

* [2.2.1: Timing Adjustable](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/timing-adjustable.html)
* [2.2.3 No timing](https://www.w3.org/TR/UNDERSTANDING-WCAG20/time-limits-no-exceptions.html)
* [2.2.4 Interruptions](https://www.w3.org/TR/UNDERSTANDING-WCAG20/time-limits-postponed.html)
* [3.2.4 Consistent Identification](https://www.w3.org/TR/UNDERSTANDING-WCAG20/consistent-behavior-consistent-functionality.html)

##### Development

Users need to know what is going on, and get appropriate feedback during interaction. Without taking extra steps, toasts can have numerous accessibility issues that can impact both people with and without disabilities.

###### How it works

The content of the toast component is implemented as an ARIA live region using `aria-live`. When the toast appears, screen readers should announce the toast text after any other more pressing announcements.

The close button contains an ARIA label of `aria-label="close"`, and the icon has `aria-hidden="true"` so it is ignored by assistive technologies.

The `Tab` key is used to move focus to the close button within the notification and the `Space` key or `Enter` key activate the button to close the notification.

###### Considerations

Avoid using toast for critical information that users need to act on immediately. Toast might be difficult for users with low vision or low dexterity to access because it:

* Disappears automatically
* Can’t be easily accessed with the keyboard
* Might appear outside the proximity of the merchant’s current focus

###### Resources

* [W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Alert Design Pattern](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-practices-1.1/#alert) covers the usage of ARIA names, state and roles.
* [W3C Web Accessibility Tutorial - User Notifications](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/) provides a tutorial on notification accessibility.
* [Notifications - Inclusive components](https://inclusive-components.design/notifications/)
