narrative.markdown:
A non-interactive preview of the UI structure which visually communicates that content is in the process of loading.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

A **Skeleton** loading provides a low-fidelity representation of the user interface (UI) before content appears on the page improving the load time perceived by users.

Give people an idea of what’s about to come and that the content is currently loading when a page full of content/data takes more than 300ms to load.

### Anatomy

![Skeleton example — Anatomy](/assets/skeleton/anatomy.png)

1. **Skeleton**: The visual representation of the page structure is loading.

### Variants

#### Sizes

Note: The size specified is only for design prototyping reference in Figma. The expected behavior for the implementation is that the Skeleton is made to be responsive depending on the size of the content.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Types

Could have different shapes accordingly to the content. For example, *Circular*, *Rectangular*, etc.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Theming

The Skeleton loading always follows the shape and form of what will be loaded – the width, height, colors, and text line heights aligned with the built components. This behavior should be applied regardless of the theme.

### Guidelines

Use a skeleton to compose a loading structure of a page where the page content is dynamic.

![Skeleton example — Guidelines](/assets/skeleton/guidelines.gif)

Example of a skeleton loading content in a page.

#### When to use

* Used to represent blocks of different contents being loaded.
* Used to load a specific part of a page (eg. a page composed of a card with lists and tables).
* Be used for pages where all content loads at the same time.
* Give users an indication of what the page layout structure will be once loaded. This means that the layout will be similar to the state that will be loaded and filled with the skeleton appearance.
* Show the minimum number of items as a skeleton before loading however many content items in a list, for example.
* Use when data takes more than 300ms to load on an average connection.

![Skeleton example — Guidelines When to use](/assets/skeleton/guidelines-when-to-use.gif)

Loading a specific part of a page.

#### When not to use

* Don't use it for loading small components.
* Don't use it for loading multiple components.
* Don't use it for a long-running loading process.

#### Group

The Skeleton is expected to be used in a group. This means that you should use it when there’s more than 1 element loading at the same time that requires an indicator.

![Skeleton example — Guidelines Group](/assets/skeleton/guidelines-group.gif)

Loading lots of elements at once inside a page structure.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Placement

They need to be placed in the same position on the screen as the live elements following the expected UI structure, to avoid the feeling of things jumping around on the page.

#### Comparison between components

##### Skeleton vs ProgressBar

For a long-running process or background process, e.g. importing data or exporting reports, use a [ProgressBar](/components/core/progress-bar/) instead.

##### Skeleton vs 3Dots

3Dots is the loader Workspace shows while a whole app loads; apps can't use it (see
[App loading](/workspace/app-loading/)). For fast processes that take less than 300ms, consider no loading
state at all.

##### Skeleton vs spinner

For a tiny, inline action or feedback, e.g. clicking a button and the action will take time, consider using a [Spinner](/components/core/spinner/) instead.

##### Skeleton vs EmptyState

If a page refresh is required, use an [EmptyState](/patterns/empty-states-and-loading/) with a CTA to refresh.

narrative.markdown:
A Spinner is an animated element that indicates loading is in process and where it will appear when loading data is slow.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

Spinners loadings indicate that a system process is going on that will end with the content being displayed to the user. They animate as soon as user action is initiated and disappear once the content appears.

### Anatomy

![Spinner anatomy: track, fill, label](/assets/spinner/anatomy.png)

1. **Track**: The path of the loader.
2. **Fill**: The visual representation of what is being loaded.
3. **Label**: Text that informs the user what to expect when loading the content.

### Variants

#### Sizes

Note: Engineering has the variation Xsmall named Tiny (in review to change)

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Styles

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Modifiers

![Spinner with label stacked vertically](/assets/spinner/modifier-with-label-vertical.png)
*With Label*

![Large spinner size](/assets/spinner/size-large.png)
*Isolated*

#### Orientation

![Spinner with label stacked vertically](/assets/spinner/modifier-with-label-vertical.png)
*Vertical*

![Spinner with label arranged horizontally](/assets/spinner/modifier-with-label-horizontal.png)
*Horizontal*

#### Theming

A spinner will respect the current theme. You can use the variations MonoDark or MonoLight depending on the color background. This is useful when you are displaying a spinner on a background that is not in the same mode as the body.

### Guidelines

The **Spinner loader** should be used when a single component is processing. For example, when the user clicks on a button, an inline loading component indicates the system is processing the request.

#### When to use

* Used to notify users that their requested action is being processed.
* For a tiny, inline action or feedback, e.g. clicking a button and the action will take some time.
* Only show a spinner if the expected wait time is more than a second.
* Should only be used for content that can’t be represented with skeleton loading components, like for data charts and inline loading.
* If only a portion of a page is displaying new content or being updated, place the spinner in that part of the page.
* When data takes less than 10s to load on an average connection.

##### Inside a button / small component

![Spinner example — When to use Inside a button / small component](/assets/spinner/when-to-use-inside-a-button.gif)

Example of an inline loading inside a single component

##### Inside a portion of a page

When a portion of a page is displaying new content or being updated, place the spinner in that part of the page.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/207230-spinner) — Design tab, image 12.*

An error ocurrer for a transfer and the user needs to try again.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/207230-spinner) — Design tab, image 13.*

The Spinner loading is applied and positioned inside the content that is being processed.

#### When not to use

* Not be used to give feedback for an entire page load.
* Avoid showing multiple loading spinners on a single page.
* For a long-running process or background process, e.g. importing data or exporting reports, use a [ProgressBar](/components/core/progress-bar/) instead.

#### Group

There should only be one component being loaded at one time. If you need to load multiple components consider using a progressive loading with a [Skeleton](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/243842-skeleton) content structure.

For example, in a list, you might show one loading spinner for the entire group of items instead of showing one for each item in the list.

![Spinner example — Guidelines Group](/assets/spinner/guidelines-group.png)

  ![Spinner example — Guidelines Group](/assets/spinner/guidelines-group-2.png)

#### Placement

It should be placed centered inline in the middle of the component.

![Spinner centered inline in the middle of a component](/assets/spinner/placement.png)

#### Comparison between components

##### Spinner vs 3Dots

3Dots is the loader Workspace shows while a whole app loads; apps can't use it (see
[App loading](/workspace/app-loading/)). When a whole page inside your app is loading, use a
[Skeleton](/components/core/skeleton/).

##### Spinner vs ProgressBar

Use a [ProgressBar](/components/core/progress-bar/) for more detailed journeys when you need to determine the percentage of a completed task.

##### Spinner vs skeleton

If you want a more specific loading experience focused on the page structure you should use a [Skeleton](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/243842-skeleton) to better represent loading content. The simplest view of the page loads first, followed by progressively more detailed batches until the entire viewport has loaded.

### Behavior

#### Over content

When using a Spinner directly over content, apply an `opacity token` to de-emphasize the content and allow the spinner to be seen.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)
Light token (0.16) was applied to the content

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/207230-spinner) — Design tab, image 17.*

#### Line length

For the content of the Spinner label, the line of text shouldn’t be longer than 80 characters. This helps users with certain reading or visual disabilities that have trouble keeping their place when reading long lines of text. If the width of the text container is resized, it should be allowed to scale in a way so 80 characters or less are shown.

Note: This is based on a [W3C guideline](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/page-structure/styling/).

#### Internationalization

For RTL (right-to-left) languages, the fill of the Spinner loading continues to spin clockwise.

![Spinner with an RTL Arabic loading label](/assets/spinner/internalization-rtl.png)

### Resources

Find this component under: `Cobalt Design System > Core Components > Spinner`

* [Spinner Loader](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?node-id=160%3A3661) — Core Components library
* [Spinner Handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?node-id=263%3A167383) — Specs

### Installation

> **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Examples

### Props

### Content

everywhere, see [Grammar and mechanics](/foundations/content/content-grammar-and-mechanics/).

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Development

* Expose the busy state to assistive tech (`role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"`).
* Provide a text alternative like "Loading".

For accessibility guidance that applies to every component, see
[Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

narrative.markdown:
Stepper is a group of steps in a prescribed order with statuses that reflect progress.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

If a flow is divided into multiple pages or steps, the Stepper helps the user to understand the progression, navigate between the steps, and know how long it takes until completion. It also provides a better experience to the user while focusing on tasks one at a time.

### Anatomy

![Stepper anatomy: visited, connecting bar, current step, unvisited](/assets/stepper/anatomy.png)

1. **Visited** - Steps that have already been visited
2. **Connecting Bar**: It shows users their progress in completing a task.
3. **Current step:** It shows the current step that the user is on.
4. **Unvisited:** Shows steps that the user has not visited.

### Variants

#### Sizes

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Orientation

![Vertical Stepper orientation](/assets/stepper/orientation-vertical.png)
*Vertical*

![Horizontal Stepper orientation](/assets/stepper/orientation-horizontal.png)
*Horizontal*

#### Quantity

![Stepper with 3 steps](/assets/stepper/quantity-3.png)
*3 steps*

  ![Stepper with 4 steps](/assets/stepper/quantity-4.png)
*4 steps*

![Stepper with 5 steps](/assets/stepper/quantity-5.png)
*5 steps*

  ![Stepper with 6 steps](/assets/stepper/quantity-6.png)
*6 steps*

#### Progress

This is a progress visual indicator in Figma to help designers provide more context in their explorations.

![Progress indicator, 1 of 6 steps, start](/assets/stepper/progress-1.png)
*1/6 steps (start)*

  ![Progress indicator, 2 of 6 steps](/assets/stepper/progress-2.png)
*2/6 steps*

  ![Progress indicator, 3 of 6 steps](/assets/stepper/progress-3.png)
*3/6 steps*

![Progress indicator, 4 of 6 steps](/assets/stepper/progress-4.png)
*4/6 steps*

  ![Progress indicator, 5 of 6 steps](/assets/stepper/progress-5.png)
*5/6 steps*

  ![Progress indicator, 6 of 6 steps, complete](/assets/stepper/progress-6.png)
*6/6 steps (complete)*

### Guidelines

#### Placement

In general, the Stepper is positioned below the header. However, the Stepper can be placed inside the Header. In this case, the Header should not have the bottom border. As always, the Stepper should be full width.

![Stepper placed inside a page header, below the title and above the page content](/assets/stepper/placement.png)

#### Use cases

![Stepper used across a full page](/assets/stepper/usecase-full-page.png)
*Full page*
General use case

![Stepper used inside a Modal](/assets/stepper/usecase-modal.png)
*Inside a Modal*
Use for critical and/or small forms.

![Stepper used inside a Panel](/assets/stepper/usecase-panel.png)
*Inside a Panel*
Use when the user might need to reference details on the page.

#### Best practices

##### Do

* Use it when requiring a user to complete a linear workflow that includes 3 to 6 steps.
* When you have complex processes that benefit from being broken down into smaller tasks.

##### Don't

* Avoid using a workflow that contains fewer than 3 or more than 6 steps.
* Don't use it when presenting a non-linear workflow.
* Don't mix the vertical and the horizontal steps in the same flow.

### Behavior

#### Responsiveness

##### Horizontal

The Stepper component should always be full-width.

##### Vertical

The component should have its values fixed. The vertical orientation may change to horizontal on mobile devices.

#### Spacing

![Stepper with default spacing](/assets/stepper/spacing-default.png)
*Default*

![Stepper with padding around it](/assets/stepper/spacing-with-padding.png)
*With padding*

### Resources

Access this Cobalt component from: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Stepper (or VerticalStepper)`

* [Stepper Component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?type=design\&node-id=280-10413\&mode=design) — Core components library
* [Stepper Handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?type=design\&node-id=349%3A198065\&mode=design\&t=G7viA6EPpOShSmI1-1) — Specs

### Code

### Installation

> **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Examples

### Props

### Content

### Writing guidelines

This component has no component-specific copy rules yet. For copy rules that apply
everywhere, see [Grammar and mechanics](/foundations/content/content-grammar-and-mechanics/).

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Development

* Convey step order and current/completed status (e.g. `aria-current="step"` plus text, not color alone).
* Use an ordered list structure.

For accessibility guidance that applies to every component, see
[Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

narrative.markdown:
The nav component allows the user to navigate between different areas of the page or page segment (e.g. panel) without leaving it.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

Nav is used to separate different content available on the same page or page segment.

### Anatomy

![Nav anatomy: tab, tag, badge, divider, navigation buttons](/assets/tab/anatomy.png)

1. **Tab**. Each tab represents a different area where the user can navigate.
2. **Tag**. Tabs can have associated tags to provide valuable communication to the user.
3. **Badge**. Tabs can have associated badges to notify the user.
4. **Divider**
5. **Navigation**. These buttons allow the user to see hidden tabs.

### Variants

#### Sizes

There are three sizes available (Large, Medium, and Small), each to be applied to the respective viewport.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### States

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Modifiers

##### Nav

![Nav with divider](/assets/tab/modifier-nav-with-divider.png)
*with divider*

  ![Nav without divider](/assets/tab/modifier-nav-without-divider.png)
*without divider*

  ![Nav with navigation buttons](/assets/tab/modifier-nav-with-navigation.png)
*with navigation*

##### Tab

![Tab with badge](/assets/tab/modifier-tab-with-badge.png)
*with badge*

  ![Tab with tag](/assets/tab/modifier-tab-with-tag.png)
*with tag*

  ![Tab with tag and badge](/assets/tab/modifier-tab-with-tag-and-badge.png)
*with tag and badge*

#### Quantity

Navs can have as many tabs as needed.

![Nav with many tabs](/assets/tab/quantity.png)

### Guidelines

#### Placement

The Nav should be placed right after the header component.

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a large viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-large.png)

### Behavior

#### Responsiveness

Navs left and right paddings follow the general rules for each viewport, **L:24px / M:16px / S:12px**

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a small viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-small.png)
*small*

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a medium viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-medium.png)
*medium*

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a large viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-large.png)
*large*

#### Overflow

When the group of tabs width is larger than the container width, the user can access hidden tabs by using the navigation buttons positioned on the right.

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a small viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-small.png)

The core `Tab` package is a single tab and does not scroll. The scrolling row with navigation buttons is the Cobalt Marketplace [Nav](/components/marketplace/nav/) component, which is built on `Tab`.

#### Text truncation

Tabs can be truncated.

We recommend, optionally, setting a max width for each tab dependent on the viewport.

* **128px** for the small viewports;
* **148px** for the medium viewports;
* **168px** for the large viewports.

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a small viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-small.png)
*max width - small*

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a medium viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-medium.png)
*max width - medium*

![Page header with pre-title, heading and description at a large viewport width](/assets/tab/sizes-large.png)
*max width - large*

#### Spacing

Spacing between tabs is always 16px.

![Seven tabs spaced 16px apart](/assets/tab/spacing.png)

### Resources

* [Nav](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?node-id=608%3A29236\&t=AVgi4HZIy2fgEObs-1) — Core components library
* [Nav handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?node-id=12%3A17461\&t=Aj3KLvOYbnQHsyFy-1) — Handoff guidelines

### Code

### Props

### Examples

### Content

* Write short tab labels and use plain language, rather than made-up terms. Tab labels should usually be 1–2 words. Short labels are more scannable; if you need longer labels, it’s a sign that the choices are too complicated for a tab control.
* Avoid abbreviations and acronyms unless you’re sure that the user is already familiar with them.
* Use sentence case unless it’s the name of a specific app, feature, or product.

**Do:** Use clear and concise labels.
![Do example](/assets/tab/content-do.png)

**Don't:** If the name of a tab is the same as the page header, it should be the first tab.
![Don't example](/assets/tab/content-dont.png)

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Development

Each tab renders a link (`<a>`); a disabled tab renders a `<span>` with `aria-disabled`. The component
does not add a landmark or mark the current tab, so the page using it must:

* Wrap the tabs in a `<nav>` landmark, with an `aria-label` when the page has more than one.
* Mark the selected tab with `aria-current="page"` as well as the `active` prop, which is visual only.
* Give every tab an `href`, so it stays reachable with `Tab` and opens with `Enter`.

If you use the Cobalt Marketplace [Nav](/components/marketplace/nav/) for overflow, see its
Accessibility tab for a gap in its navigation buttons.

For accessibility guidance that applies to every component, see
[Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

narrative.markdown:
Tables are used to organize and display information from a data set. This way, users can have a more detailed comparison with other elements.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

Tables display information in a grid-like format of rows and columns. They organize information in a way that’s easy to scan so that users can look for patterns and develop insights from data.

Use when a data structure includes two or more columns of data. For a single data column, use a **List Group** instead.

### Anatomy

**Tables may contain:**

* Interactive components - Checkbox, Radio buttons, Links, Buttons (all types + button groups), Dropdown, Tags
* Non-interactive - Avatar, Basic Text
* Tools to interact with Data queries - Filters, Search, Pagination (they are placed on a Toolbar before and/or after the table)

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

1. **Draggable interaction.** By interacting with this component the user can reorder the items.
2. **Checkbox.** By interacting with this component the user can select the item.
3. **Avatar**
4. **Link.** By interacting with this component the user will be forwarded to the item info page.
5. **First column**
6. **Text column**
7. **Sorted column.** All items are organized starting from the most recent.
8. **Monospaced column**
9. **Tag column**
10. **Status column**
11. **Actions column**
12. **Hovered row**
13. **Selected row**
14. **Toolbar**
15. **Pagination**

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/36db72-table) — Design tab, image 1.*

### Variants

Tables are a common element in our applications. They can be customized in different ways to adapt to every single use case.

#### Modifiers

##### Basic table

This table example is showing cell elements with no advanced interactions.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/36db72-table) — Design tab, image 2.*

##### Scrollable table

A scrollable table fixes the Header on the page and allows for the table body to scroll underneath it.

| ☢️ | This variation should only be used inside modals or panels (where the height of the element is fixed) and it should occupy all the available height of the component. It should also load more rows by lazy-loading instead of a pagination toolbar. |
| -- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/36db72-table) — Design tab, image 3.*

### Guidelines

#### Use cases

##### Table options

Several table options can be edited by the user which will impact the table content visibility, placement, and others. Each of these options is optional and will not be available on all products consistently.

Table options can be accessed by interacting with the button “table options” available on the toolbar. When active, this button opens a popup with all available option actions.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/36db72-table) — Design tab, image 4.*

Small viewports don't have enough space to place two popups side by side, so it should be used one single popup and added back action when necessary.

![Table example — Use cases Table options: Table options selection](/assets/table/options-table-options-selection.png)
*Table options selection*

  ![Table example — Use cases Table options: Table options / Option selection](/assets/table/options-table-options-option-selection.png)
*Table options / Option selection*

Only for large viewports, when the table has up to three table options available they can be placed in the toolbar instead of using the table options button action.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/36db72-table) — Design tab, image 7.*

##### Items per page

Allow the user to define the number of items/results (rows) per page. Other items/results can be accessed by using the pagination.

By default, a table should display 10 items and the user can change it to 20, 50, or 100.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/36db72-table) — Design tab, image 8.*

##### Pinned columns

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

### Behavior

#### Interaction

##### Draggable rows

##### Expandable rows

When data doesn’t fit on a single row and needs more room to display primary and secondary info, you can use expandable rows. You can place any information inside an expanded row, as it doesn’t need to be tabular data.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

##### Resizable columns

Lets users adjust the **column width** in a table so they can prioritize the content that matters most to them, instead of relying on a fixed layout.

![Table example — Interaction Resizable columns](/assets/table/interaction-resizable-columns.png)

New button in toolbar called Resize columns

Clicking on the "**Resize columns" button** in the toolbar, enters the **resize mode.** It activates vertical lines in all resizable columns. When hovering a resizable border, the cursor changes to a left-right resize icon.

![Table example — Interaction Resizable columns](/assets/table/interaction-resizable-columns-2.png)

Resize mode activated

The toolbar adapts to show a tile on the left "**Resize Columns**" and a set of actions related to resizing: **Reset sizes**, **Cancel** and **Save**

![Table example — Interaction Resizable columns](/assets/table/interaction-resizable-columns-3.png)

Resize toolbar

All row-level interactive elements are disabled while in this mode: checkboxes, bulk actions, inputs, end-row actions...

![Table example — Interaction Resizable columns](/assets/table/interaction-resizable-columns-4.png)

Disabled actions in a row

**Column border states**  While in resize mode, resizable column borders become 2px wide, with color changing by state:

| **State**     | **Border color** |
| ------------- | ---------------- |
| Default       | Secondary 4      |
| Hover / focus | Secondary 6      |
| Dragging      | Secondary 8      |

**To resize,** drag a border to increase or decrease the column's width.

**Accessibility**

A resize divider can be focused with the keyboard. Once focused, the arrow keys increase or decrease the column's width — dragging isn't required to use the pattern.

**Cell content** On resize, cell content adapts immediately to the new width. If content is truncated, increasing the column's width reveals more characters; decreasing it truncates further.

**Interacting with elements outside of the table** Interacting with anything outside the table content — a header action, the drawer, or switching to another app — cancels the resize.

![Table example — Interaction Resizable columns](/assets/table/interaction-resizable-columns-5.png)

On resize UI changes

##### Sortable columns

* Improve table usability by making data sortable. Column headers will display the controls by showing an icon.
* A sorted table has three states: unsorted (arrows up and down), sorted-ascending (arrow up), and sorted-descending (arrow down).
* The sort icon should always be visible in the column header. If a table just has 1 row yet, the sort icon should be visible in the disabled state.

![Unsorted column header](/assets/table/sortable-unsorted.png)

* The examples below show, on the left, the Checkbox selection which allows the user to select multiple rows. The table header provides interaction to select all rows.
* On the right, the Radio button selection will allow the user to strictly select only one row. In this case, the column header has no interaction.

The checkbox on the column header will display different states, depending on if the user interaction is single or multiple:

![Column header checkbox states for single vs multiple row selection](/assets/table/selectable-header-checkbox-states.png)

A table with selectable rows has a deep integration with the toolbar component. So when selecting a few rows, the Toolbar will display the number of selected items.

##### Actions for each row

The last column of each row can have a set of actions that can be performed. Usually, it’s just simple transparent icon buttons, but we can add any kind of action here.

Each row can have a maximum of three actions. For rows with more than three, a more options button should be added as a third action. When active a popup with all hidden actions should be visible.

![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg)

*Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/36db72-table) — Design tab, image 30.*

##### Status rows

Rows can change their background to display the status of its contents.

![Table rows with status background colors](/assets/table/status-rows.png)

#### Loading

##### Lazy loading

Tables may be sourcing information from large data sets and so processing may take a few moments. That's why we use [skeleton](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/243842-skeleton) states on these data-based components.

The size of the loading is defined by the size of the item itself.

![Table skeleton loading state](/assets/table/lazy-loading.png)

#### Spacing

Independently of the viewport, if a table is the central element of the page, then it should also stretch to **full width**. If it’s not the central element and it shares the screen with multiple other elements, then it should follow the inner page padding (**L:24px / M:16px / S:12px**).

##### On panels and cards

Tables inside panels and cards should always be displayed at **full-width**, touching the borders of the container they’re in.

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Design

* [1.3.1 Correctly marking up table headers](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG20-TECHS/F91.html)
* [05.1 Identify row and column headers for data tables.](https://amp.levelaccess.net/public/standards/view_standard.php?rule_id=64)

#### Development

Screen reader users can navigate data tables from cell to cell, in a multi-directional way (up, down, right, left), much like navigating a spreadsheet. As they move from cell to cell, screen readers will read the associated header labels (if the table has been created with accessibility in mind). This structure and easy navigation ability with screen readers make tables well-suited to tabular data.

##### Provide semantic markup for tabular data

Tabular data SHOULD be represented in a `<table>`.

###### Table caption/name

The `caption` element is the most straightforward way to give a name to a table. It is also possible to use `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

On a page with multiple tables, screen reader users can pull up a list of all tables on the web page, which will show the captions (such as "1st Quarter Results") along with the table size (such as "3 columns, 4 rows").

Here is a table list as viewed with the VoiceOver screen reader table list:

![VoiceOver screen reader table list example](/assets/table/accessibility-voiceover-table-list.png)

Voice over example of a table list

The purpose of the caption or name is to allow users to identify the table and/or understand the purpose of the table, so **the caption or name should be meaningful**.

**Do:** <caption> Table 1: First Quarter Earnings </caption>

**Don't:** <caption> Table 1 </caption>

The name/caption of each data table SHOULD be unique within the context of other tables on the same page.

###### Table headers

The only way that screen readers can know if a table cell is a header is by marking it with `<th>`. For more complex tables, explicit associations may be needed using `scope`, `id`, and `headers` attributes.

If the text in the header cell is vague (for example, naming it "Column 2"), or if it contains extraneous information (like links, buttons or extra descriptions that aren't the name of the column), it can confuse for screen reader users. **It's best to keep the header text accurate and simple.**

**Table data cells MUST be associated with their corresponding header cells.**

Each header is marked with either `<th scope="col">` or `<th scope="row">` as appropriate.

**Good example (on html)**

```html
<table>
	<caption><strong>Activities table</strong></caption>
	<thead>
		<tr>
			<th scope="col">Name</th>
			<th scope="col">1 mile</th>
			<th scope="col">5 km</th>
			<th scope="col">10 km</th>
		</tr>
    </thead>
	<tbody>
		<tr>
			<th scope="row">Mary</th>
			<td>8:32</td>
			<td>28:04</td>
			<td>1:01:16</td>
		</tr>
     </tbody>
</table>
```

### Guidelines

#### Group

![Four tags spaced 4px apart horizontally](/assets/tag/group-spacing.png)

Tags should always have **4px** spacing between them, horizontally.

![Tag example — Guidelines Group](/assets/tag/guidelines-group.png)

The horizontal spacing between tags and transparent buttons should be **4px**.

![Tag example — Guidelines Group](/assets/tag/guidelines-group-2.png)

The horizontal spacing between tags and labels should be **8px**.

![Tag example — Guidelines Group](/assets/tag/guidelines-group-3.png)

The horizontal spacing between tags and text should be **8px**.

![Filter name with two descriptive tags and a numeric +1 tag](/assets/tag/group-overflow.png)

When multiple tags are combined and are not all visible, the first 2 tags should be descriptive tags, and the third tag should be numerical, showing the total number of hidden tags. In several use cases when this happened (e.g. in a toolbar), 2 descriptive tags are secondary with a label, and the numeric tag is a primary tag.

![Tag example — Guidelines Group](/assets/tag/guidelines-group-4.png)

When multiple tags are combined and they are all visible, the horizontal spacing between them should be **4px** and the vertical **8px**.

#### Text truncation

Tags can be truncated at the end of the copy or in the middle.

* Default truncation:
  * add an ellipsis (…) at the end of the copy.
* Mid truncation can be useful when several tags copy only change at the end or in the beginning.
  * add an ellipsis (…) before a specific number of characters;
  * add an ellipsis (…) after a specific number of characters.

We set an optional maximum width of:

* **160px** for the small Tag;

### Content

Tags can be helpful in labeling objects for faster recognition. Use tags in moderation as they easily increase the amount of visual noise on a screen — especially when combined with other visual elements.

* Be clear and concise.
  * To choose the right wording, consider first all the tags for that particular product/feature. If there’s a tag named *Completed with errors*, there should be one named *Completed* (and not *Done* or *Successful*).
  * Furthermore, pay attention to the meaning of the words and what they entail. For example, *Suspended* usually implies the ability to resume something whereas *Stopped* doesn’t.
* Avoid line-wrapping and truncating text. If necessary, check guidelines for [text truncation](/components/core/tag/).
* Colors can be used to help distinguish tags more quickly, but can never be the only method to do it. [The wording is absolutely crucial.](https://zeroheight.com/51aaf6147/v/latest/p/36ed56-word-choice/b/405dff)

**Do:** Example of tags with names from the same family: "Completed", "Completed with errors".
![Do example](/assets/tag/content-do-status-names.png)

**Don't:** "Done" and "Unsuccessful" are not antonyms. "Cancelled" should be spelled "Canceled". "Resume" is not a status. "Incomplete" is not the same as "Completed with errors".
![Don't example](/assets/tag/content-dont-status-names.png)

#### Text truncation

Tags can be truncated at the end of the copy or in the middle.

* Default truncation:
  * add an ellipsis (…) at the end of the copy.
* Mid truncation can be useful when several tags copy only change in the end or in the beginning.
  * add an ellipsis (…) before a specific number of characters;
  * add an ellipsis (…) after a specific number of characters.

![Text truncation examples: default truncation and mid truncation](/assets/tag/content-text-truncation-examples.png)
*Text truncation examples*

* If interactive (removable/selectable), expose it as a control with an accessible name.

knownGaps.summary: TagGroup's remove button is 12×12px and is named just "Remove" for every tag, so a screen reader can't tell which filter it removes. TagGroup also won't take size tiny or small ("interactive tags are at least 24px"), although that floor applies to the tag, not to its 12px remove target. Designs with 20px removable tags (the Users app filter bar) have to use a standalone small Tag with a clickable Icon and an accessibilityLabel instead. Needs a fix in cobalt: name each remove button after its tag, and either allow a small size or document why not.
knownGaps.source: Measured in the browser against @talkdesk/cobalt-react-tag 3.0.0 (published); types in its dist/index.d.ts

narrative.markdown:
A text area is a large text input form field that can be used to add multiple lines of text.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Variants

#### Medium

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Small

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Theming

*Describe the rules related to colors, shapes or others, that may be affected when changing the theme*

#### Size

Textarea can accept the modifiers to **Size** them. will be used only one size (**small**), please take a look at the specs above ☝️

### Guidelines

The text area input, much like the regular text input (input type=”text”) defines an unless developer specified, input that will hold an unlimited number of user-inputted characters, regardless of the “visual” size defined in a multi-line presentation.

Its size is defined by the cols and rows attributes, or via the width and height CSS properties.

### Behavior

#### Internationalization

No special steps are needed to be extended to the textarea component/element when dealing with i18n concerns apart from its text direction through the `dir` attribute (which can be `ltr` or `rtl`)  and defined by the end-users (apps). Furthermore, the only concern is to address the copy of the label wrapping the textarea component/element and again this is a concern passed on to the apps.

### Resources

|                      | **Medium**                                                                                                  | **Small** |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| Min height           | `40px`                                                                                                      | `32px`    |
| Width                | `100%`                                                                                                      |           |
| Font size            | `14px`                                                                                                      | `12px`    |
| Font weight          | `400`                                                                                                       |           |
| Color                | `basic-800`                                                                                                 |           |
| Background color     | `basic-000`                                                                                                 |           |
| Padding              | `12px`                                                                                                      | `8px`     |
| Border radius        | `4px`                                                                                                       |           |
| Border width / style | `2px solid`                                                                                                 |           |
| Border color         | `basic-400`                                                                                                 |           |
| Resize               | `vertical`                                                                                                  |           |
| box sizing           | `border-box`                                                                                                |           |
| Outline              | `none`                                                                                                      |           |
| Transition           | `transition-property: box-shadow, border; ``transition-duration: 0.2s; ``transition-timing-function: ease;` |           |
|                      | `touch-action: manipulation;`                                                                               |           |

Textareas are fully available in Figma under `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Form Elements > Textarea`

* [Textarea](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Cobalt-Core-Components?node-id=289%3A12204) — Cobalt component

#### Modifiers

A text area can hold an unlimited number of characters, to set the size of the text area, just use the rows attribute. A placeholder text can also be added using the placeholder attribute.

```html
<textarea id="text1" rows="5" placeholder="Write something here"></textarea>
```

### Placeholder

Form Textarea placeholder attributes are helpful for providing hints to (sighted) users in forms. Often times, due to design decisions, a placeholder is used to replace a more semantic label element. Unfortunately, accessible placeholder browser support isn’t complete and placeholders often lack sufficient color contrast by default.

Read more: [https://a11yproject.com/posts/placeholder-input-elements/](https://a11yproject.com/posts/placeholder-input-elements/)

| **Font weight** | `400`       |
| --------------- | ----------- |
| **Color**       | `basic-500` |

![Placeholder state, medium size](/assets/textarea/state-medium-placeholder.png)

### Disabled

| ☢️ | To avoid remove pointer events, make sure that status (eg.Hover,…) will be applied with CSS pseudo-class:not(\[disabled]). You can see an example being used in Button component styles. |
| -- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

The `disabled` and `readonly` attributes have similar effects — in fact, they look the same from the user's perspective.

In both cases, what the user sees is a field that is slightly “**grayed out**” over opacity, which cannot be clicked on or edited.

Read more: [https://html.com/attributes/input-disabled/#ixzz6D5h6B1gv](https://html.com/attributes/input-disabled/#ixzz6D5h6B1gv)

|                  | Disabled                  | Read-only   |
| ---------------- | ------------------------- | ----------- |
| Cursor           | not-allowed               | not-allowed |
| Background color | `basic-200`               | `basic-200` |
| Label color      | `basic-800 (opacity 40%)` | `basic-800` |
| Border color     | `basic-300`               | `basic-500` |

![Disabled state, medium size](/assets/textarea/state-medium-disabled.png)
*Disabled*

![Read-only state, medium size](/assets/textarea/state-medium-readonly.png)
*Read-only*

### Status color

| Border wolor | `error-700` | `warning-700` |
| ------------ | ----------- | ------------- |
| Border width | `2px`       | `2px`         |

![Error state, medium size](/assets/textarea/state-medium-error.png)
*Error*

  ![Warning state, medium size](/assets/textarea/state-medium-warning.png)
*Warning*

### Code

### Installation

> **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Examples

### Props

### Content

* Use a combination of a concise label and supportive helper text for clarification of the field input. Don’t rely solely on placeholder text as it is not visible at all times.
* Use a concise label to indicate what information goes in the text area input. For example, if the text area appears in a modal called *Create component*, the label for a description text area should only say *Description* and not repeat the modal’s title.
* Place helper text above the text input (below the area label) if it is necessary to understand the field.
* If appropriate, you can have pre-filled information in the text input. (see image 1).

**Do:** Label and helper text clarify what the user needs to do/know. The pre-filled information in the text area expedites the user's work.
![Do example](/assets/textarea/content-do-prefilled.png)

**Don't:** Don't rely solely on placeholders.
![Don't example](/assets/textarea/content-dont-placeholder-only.png)

#### Placeholder text

In general, placeholder text should only be used if it adds value. In recurrent tasks it’s particularly important to have this in mind to prevent cognitive overload.

**Note:** Do not use a placeholder as the label of the field.

**Do:** When appropriate, help users to know what is expected of them, by giving examples.
![Do example](/assets/textarea/content-do-example.png)

**Don't:** Do not add extra text just to fill space.
![Don't example](/assets/textarea/content-dont-extra-text.png)

![Do example](/assets/textarea/content-do-blank.png)
*Do*
Leave it blank if the label is self-explanatory.

### Accessibility

* Keep it simple - not all browsers correctly expose multiple labels that are linked to the same form element.
* Use labels for every textarea and make the `for=""` and i`d=""` values match. IDs must be unique on each page, only one label can be associated with each unique form element.
* Make required fields obvious by using an indicator - border color change, asterisk, description text, etc.
* Fields with error validation should have `aria-describedby` to insure that the associated field-level error message is read by assistive technology. If the error message has an `id="my-error-message"`, then the input should have `aria-describedby="my-error-message"`.
* Similarly to other inputs the textarea must either be wrapped in a label with matching (and unique) `for=”...”` and `id=”...”` attribute pairs.
* If resorting to a non textarea native tag to implement this behaviour the `role=”textbox”` is used on the container and some other attributes should be set to ensure that all users can interact properly with this component/element like `aria-multiline=”true”`, for example.

narrative.markdown:
A Toggle lets people turn a single setting on or off immediately.

### Design

> **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Overview

Use this selection control when the user needs to toggle a single item on or off. They are an effective way to quickly define settings or preferences at an account or system level.

### Anatomy

![Toggle example — Anatomy](/assets/toggle/anatomy.png)

1. **Toggle** - Element with different states available and determinates if something is on or off
2. **Label** - Text to clarify the action that the Toggle performs

### Variants

#### Sizes

Toggles come in two different sizes: Small and Medium. Toggle size is dependent on the viewport. The Small is to be used in Small viewports and the Medium is to be used in Medium and Large viewports.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### States

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Modifiers

Toggles should always have labels. When the Label is not defined, a Toggle becomes standalone. Standalone toggles should only be used when their connection to other components is clear, and they give sufficient context.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

#### Orientation

![Label on the left of the toggle](/assets/toggle/orientation-ltr.png)
*Default - LTR (Left to Right)*

  ![RTL (Right to Left) orientation](/assets/toggle/orientation-rtl.png)
*RTL (Right to Left)*
The RTL version is not implemented in Storybook.

#### Position

When creating an on/off Toggle, you can choose to have the Toggle on the left or right of the label. The label on the right is the default and most frequently used option.

> **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Guidelines

#### Group

You can include multiple Toggles together when necessary keeping one per line.

#### Best practices

##### No partial states

Toggles can only be on or off. If you need to show a partial state, use a checkbox instead of a Toggle.

**Do:** 
![Do example](/assets/toggle/behavior-no-partial-do.png)

**Don't:** 
![Don't example](/assets/toggle/behavior-no-partial-dont.png)

##### Visual language

**Do:** Be concise.
![Do example](/assets/toggle/behavior-visual-language-do.png)

**Don't:** There is no need to pair two labels with a Toggle.
![Don't example](/assets/toggle/behavior-visual-language-dont.png)

##### Toggle copy

Don’t change the toggle copy dependent on its state.

**Do:** 
![Do example](/assets/toggle/behavior-toggle-copy-do.png)

**Don't:** 
![Don't example](/assets/toggle/behavior-toggle-copy-dont.png)

### Behavior

#### Interaction

Example of the Toggle being used with the applied states.

![Animated toggle switching between its on and off states](/assets/toggle/interaction.gif)

#### Overflow

When the Label is too long for the horizontal space available in a Toggle, it wraps to form another line.

![A long label wrapping to a second line next to a toggle](/assets/toggle/overflow.png)

#### Toggle vs checkbox

Toggles are best used for communicating activation (e.g., on/off states), while checkboxes are best used for selection (e.g., multiple table rows). Toggles, unlike checkboxes, can't have an error state.

**Do:** 
![Do example](/assets/toggle/checkbox-do.png)

**Don't:** 
![Don't example](/assets/toggle/checkbox-dont.png)

#### Toggle vs radio buttons

Toggles are very similar to [Radio buttons](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/085bf5-radio) where they're both single selectors: there can only ever be one option selected. However, unlike Radio buttons, **a Toggle can only have 2 options**, which usually relate to something being active or inactive.

**When you should use Toggles:**

* If there are only 2 options.
* If the 2 options relate to something being "On" or "Off" or being "Active" or "Disabled".
* If you want the action to be instant.

**Do:** 
![Do example](/assets/toggle/behavior-visual-language-do.png)

**Don't:** 
![Don't example](/assets/toggle/radio-dont1.png)

**When you should use Radio buttons:**

* If there are more than 2 options.
* If the options aren’t referring to something being on or off.
* If you want the user to confirm settings.

**Do:** Direct and unambiguous.
![Do example](/assets/toggle/radio-do2.png)

**Don't:** This label is neutral and makes the users second-guess what to do.
![Don't example](/assets/toggle/radio-dont2.png)

#### Internationalization

For RTL (right-to-left) languages, the layout of the Toggle is mirrored. The track is placed on the right side of the text and the handle is positioned to the left when the Toggle is turned on.

![RTL toggle example with the track mirrored to the right](/assets/toggle/internationalization.png)

### Resources

Access this Cobalt component from: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Toggle`

* [Toggle component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?node-id=475%3A16299) — Core Component library
* [Toggle handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?node-id=178-119867) — Handoff guidelines

### Code

### Installation

> **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site.

### Examples

### Props

### Content

### Introduction

The Toggle component is a switch that allows users to turn a feature on or off. This component is commonly used in settings, preferences, or options.

### Tone and voice

Be clear, informative, and directive. Use friendly and conversational language while still being concise.

### Word choice

Use words that clearly indicate the state of the toggle, such as **"on",** **"off", "active", "inactive", "enabled", or "disabled".**

Give preference to synonyms, as they can be clear on the state of the toggle.

Avoid using ambiguous language that may confuse users.

### Concise and clear writing

Clearly explain what the toggle does and how to use it. Keep labels short and direct. Labels should describe what the control will do when the switch is on; they should not be neutral or ambiguous.

Avoid asking questions.

### Examples

**Do**
- Use action verbs to clearly indicate what will happen if the toggle is on/off.
- 
- 
![Do example](/assets/toggle/content-example-disabled.png)

**Don't:** Without context, labels like these are not clear.
![Don't example](/assets/toggle/content-example-enabled.png)

### Accessibility

### Considerations

#### Development

* Expose it as a switch (`role="switch"` with `aria-checked`) or rely on native checkbox semantics with a clear label.
* Don't signal on/off by color or position alone.

For accessibility guidance that applies to every component, see
[Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

narrative.markdown:
A Tooltip is a small piece of contextual information about an element on the screen that is displayed when a user hovers or focuses on the element. ### Design > **Interactive demo — Playground.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site. ### Overview **A Tooltip or a StatefulPopup should only be used if the information in the tooltip is not necessary for users to complete a task.** Otherwise, the information should be present on the screen and it is not necessary to use a tooltip. ### Variants #### Sizes Tooltips don’t have fixed sizes, their size adapts to the content. However, should be considered a max width of: * **300px** for small viewport; * **520px** for medium and large viewports. > **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site. #### Colors There are three color variations for tooltips. By default, they have dark text on a white background, but we can choose to invert it by using white text on a dark background. There is also an error variant that uses a red background that can be used to display error messages in tooltips. ![Tooltip example — Variants Colors: Dark](/assets/tooltip/colors-dark.png) *Dark* ![Tooltip example — Variants Colors: Light](/assets/tooltip/colors-light.png) *Light* ![Tooltip example — Variants Colors: Error](/assets/tooltip/colors-error.png) *Error* > **Interactive demo — Demo.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site. #### When to use error, light or dark tooltips? Use the error variant to display error messages where the screen real estate is too small to show a regular error message. ![Tooltip example — Colors When to use error, light or dark tooltips?](/assets/tooltip/colors-when-to-use-error-light.png) | | **Error tooltip** | **Dark tooltip** | **Light tooltip** | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | Light background | Used to display error messages in tooltips. | Used to display text-only information in tooltips. | Used to display multiple types of information in tooltips. | | Dark background | Used to display error messages in tooltips. | Used to display multiple types of information in tooltips. | Used to display text-only information in tooltips. | | Visual example | | | | ![Tooltip example — Colors When to use error, light or dark tooltips?](/assets/tooltip/colors-when-to-use-error-light-2.png) ![Tooltip example — Colors When to use error, light or dark tooltips?](/assets/tooltip/colors-when-to-use-error-light-3.png) ![Tooltip example — Colors When to use error, light or dark tooltips?](/assets/tooltip/colors-when-to-use-error-light-4.png) #### Theming This component might be impacted by theme, in a sense that a theme might choose to change the default color (light or dark) of the tooltips to better adapt to it. ### Guidelines #### Placement Tooltips can be positioned in all corners of a hovered element. Unless there is a really good and critical reason, we should avoid the bottom positioning. Left and right positioning helps when the hovered element is on the edge of the screen so the tooltip can always be visible in the window viewport. ![Tooltip example — Guidelines Placement](/assets/tooltip/guidelines-placement.png) **Do:** Position the tooltips in order to make sure they are always visible. This is particularly important on items that are on the edge of the screen. ![Do example](/assets/placeholder-image.svg) **Don't:** Avoid using positions that will make the tooltip go outside of the viewport. Also, avoid using the bottom position so that it doesn't go under the mouse cursor. ![Don't example](/assets/placeholder-image.svg) *Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/94ad96-tooltip) — Design tab, image 12, image 13.* #### Use cases #### Disabled paired element A tooltip can be used associated with a disabled paired element (e.g. disabled button) but this should be avoided. Whenever possible the information should be provided on the screen by using a hint, error message, or another text element. ![Caution example](/assets/tooltip/use-cases-disabled-paired-element-caution.png) *Caution* ![Do example](/assets/tooltip/use-cases-disabled-paired-element-do.png) *Do* #### Tooltip vs StatefulPopup | Initiated by | **On hover** | **Focused** | **On click** | | -------------- | ------------ | ----------- | ----------------- | | Component | **Tooltip** | **Tooltip** | **StatefulPopup** | | Visual example | | | | ![Tooltip example — Tooltip vs StatefulPopup](/assets/tooltip/tooltip-vs-statefulpopup.png) ![Tooltip example — Tooltip vs StatefulPopup](/assets/tooltip/tooltip-vs-statefulpopup-2.png) ![Tooltip example — Tooltip vs StatefulPopup](/assets/tooltip/tooltip-vs-statefulpopup-3.png) ### Behavior #### Text truncation Tooltips can be helpful in displaying the entire content of a truncated text string. ![Placeholder: image still to be added from ZeroHeight](/assets/placeholder-image.svg) *Image to add: [original on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/94ad96-tooltip) — Design tab, image 16.* #### Spacing Tooltips should be placed at a distance of `8px` from the triggering element. Tooltips can be placed in [multiple positions](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/94ad96-tooltip/t/02f775), so be sure to align them according to your context ![Tooltip example — Variants Spacing](/assets/tooltip/variants-spacing.png) ### Resources Find this component under: `Cobalt Design System > Core Components > Tooltip` * [Tooltip](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/Cobalt-Core-Components?node-id=279%3A10410) — Cobalt core component * [Tooltip handoff](https://www.figma.com/file/o1okDlSciNFIyJzEmB7Vws/5---%F0%9F%94%8D-Handoffs?node-id=200%3A131811\&t=ufnda0LUTEiS6ulr-1) — Handoff guidelines * [V1](https://talkdesk.github.io/cobalt-react-components/?path=/story/tooltip--positions) — Cobalt ### Code ### Installation > **Interactive demo — Install.** Not reproducible in text; see the documentation site. ### Examples ### Props ### Content * In general, be brief and concise. * Tooltips can only accept simple text strings (one sentence). They do not support line breaking or any text style other than the default one. * Use them to provide supplementary information to help users accomplish a task, or help minimize any concerns that might prevent people from achieving their goal. * Never use tooltips to hide important information for task completion. * Avoid using tooltips too often, as users might ignore them. * Use sentence case. **Do:** Use simple text strings. ![Do example](/assets/tooltip/do.png) **Don't:** Avoid using large strings and don't use custom text styles. ![Don't example](/assets/tooltip/dont.png) ### When to use "?" or "i" icons in your tooltip? When using a tooltip, you can either choose to use a **"?"** (**question mark icon)** or an **"i"** (**info icon)**. It depends on what you're trying to write on the tooltip. Here's the difference between them: * the **"?"** must be used when users need help (or to avoid that), trying to give answers to potential questions. * the **"i"** must be used to provide more information, knowledge, details, and context that add value to the user. ### Accessibility ### Considerations #### Development Tooltip is built on react-aria's `TooltipTrigger` and `Tooltip`, which meet the requirements below: the tooltip opens on hover and on keyboard focus, `Esc` closes it, it has `role="tooltip"`, and the trigger is linked to it with `aria-describedby`. The trigger must be focusable, such as a Cobalt `Button`. #### Keyboard Tooltips are activated when hovering over an element if the user is using a pointing device, like a mouse. Users who rely on the keyboard to navigate should also be able to see the tooltip when the item is focused. When using the keyboard and an item is focused and displaying a tooltip, pressing ESC should close the tooltip. An important notice is that tooltips should never receive focus. #### ARIA The tooltip component should have the correct ARIA role assigned to it and the triggering element should use the ARIA-describedby attribute to be associated with the corresponding tooltip ID. ```html
...
... ``` For guidance that applies to every component, see [Accessibility](/foundations/accessibility/overview/).

Used to highlight portions of a text such as a word or a phrase.

### Design

### Overview

**Mark** allows the user to determine parts to highlight inside content with different colors. It also can be used to get snippets of search results with matching keywords highlighted. It helps to improve an application’s search experience.

### Anatomy

![Mark example — Anatomy](/assets/mark/anatomy.png)

1. **Label**
2. **Highlight**

### Variants

#### Types

![Mark example — Variants Types: Paragraph](/assets/mark/types-paragraph.png)
*Paragraph*

  ![Mark example — Variants Types: Microcopy](/assets/mark/types-microcopy.png)
*Microcopy*

#### Colors

Please also consider checking the [Color | Color usage](/foundations/tokens/color/#color-usage) page when applying different colors to the Mark component.

### Guidelines

#### Placement

It should always be placed inside Paragraphs and Microcopies.

#### Best practices

![Do example](/assets/mark/guidelines-do-s-don-ts-do.png)
*Do*
Use it inside Paragraphs

**Do:** Use it inside Microcopies.
![Do example](/assets/mark/guidelines-do-s-don-ts-do-2.png)

**Don't:** Don't use it on different typography components.
![Don't example](/assets/mark/guidelines-do-s-don-ts-dont.png)

![Don't example](/assets/mark/guidelines-do-s-don-ts-dont-2.png)
*Don't*
Don't mix different colors when highlighting.

### Behavior

#### Interaction

When the user marks a word or sentence inside a text the content is highlighted with the Mark component.

#### Dimensions

The width is always the same as the size of its content.

narrative.markdown:
Sliders allow users to quickly select a value.

### Design

### Overview

Use Sliders to let users select a value within a given range of minimum and maximum values or an isolated value.

### Anatomy

![Slider example — Anatomy](/assets/slider/anatomy.png)

1. **Active fill** - Displays the track already filled
2. **Handle** - Dragged position indicator that can be moved along the track to change the value
3. **Track** - Displays the range available for the user to select from
4. **Value** - Tooltip that specifies the selected value
5. **Minimum value** - Dual range slider for setting a minimum value
6. **Maximum value** - Dual range slider for setting a maximum value

### Variants

#### States

![Slider example — Variants States: Default](/assets/slider/states-default.png)
*Default*

  ![Slider example — Variants States: Active (Dragging)](/assets/slider/states-active-dragging.png)
*Active (Dragging)*

  ![Slider example — Variants States: Disabled](/assets/slider/states-disabled.png)
*Disabled*

#### Modifiers

The Slider can be either a single-point slider for setting a single value or a dual-range slider for setting a minimum and maximum value.

![Slider example — Variants Modifiers: Single-point](/assets/slider/modifiers-single-point.png)
*Single-point*

  ![Slider example — Variants Modifiers: Single-point with Tooltip](/assets/slider/modifiers-single-point-with-tooltip.png)
*Single-point with Tooltip*

![Slider example — Variants Modifiers: Range](/assets/slider/modifiers-range.png)
*Range*
Allows users to select both an upper and a lower limit.

  ![Slider example — Variants Modifiers: Range with Tooltip](/assets/slider/modifiers-range-with-tooltip.png)
*Range with Tooltip*

#### Progress

This is a progress visual indicator in Figma to help designers provide more context in their explorations.

![Slider example — Variants Progress: 0%](/assets/slider/progress-0.png)
*0%*

  ![Slider example — Variants Progress: 25%](/assets/slider/modifiers-single-point.png)
*25%*

  ![Slider example — Variants Progress: 50%](/assets/slider/states-default.png)
*50%*

![Slider example — Variants Progress: 75%](/assets/slider/progress-75.png)
*75%*

  ![Slider example — Variants Progress: 100%](/assets/slider/progress-100.png)
*100%*

### Guidelines

#### Use cases

Use sliders when you want users to see their options instead of reading them.

**When you should use a slider**

* When you want users to see their minimum and maximum options more visually.
* When you have enough space.
* When dealing with degrees of comparison (e.g. size, money, etc).

#### Best practices

##### Single-point

A slider by default will **always have a preselected value**. As a general rule, when it comes to anything dealing with money, you should set the default to the lowest option, and for everything else, you can choose to set it to the middle or default.

**Do:** In general, choose to set it to the middle or default (lowest).
![Do example](/assets/slider/do-s-don-ts-single-point.png)

**Don't:** Related to money, don't set it to the middle
![Don't example](/assets/slider/do-s-don-ts-single-point-2.png)

##### Range

**Do:** Use it to indicate a range of simple values. For range sliders, set the whole range preselected as the default.
![Do example](/assets/slider/do-s-don-ts-range-do.png)

**Don't:** Don't use a range if choosing a specific value is important. The slider interaction isn't as precise as explicitly typing or choosing an option from a list.
![Don't example](/assets/slider/do-s-don-ts-range-dont.png)

![Don't example](/assets/slider/do-s-don-ts-range-dont-2.png)
*Don't*
Dont use ranges that are too small, for example, 1-3.

![Don't example](/assets/slider/do-s-don-ts-range-dont-3.png)
*Don't*
Don't use for ranges extremely largers, for example, 1-1000.

### Behavior

#### Interaction

The user should be able to move the slider to whatever value they feel is necessary. Whenever the Handle is moved, the informative Popup must appear with the corresponding value.

#### Dimensions

The width of a slider can be customized appropriately for its context.

![Slider example — Variants Dimensions](/assets/slider/variants-dimensions.png)

### Resources

Access this Cobalt component from: `Cobalt Design System > Cobalt Core Components > Slider`

* [Slider component](https://www.figma.com/file/F3P45YCDsmcmsm01iFIM8s/2---%E2%9A%9B%EF%B8%8F-Core-Components?type=design\&node-id=2307-476509\&mode=design) — Core components library
