:::note
Sourced from Cobalt's live Accessibility docs, which the Cobalt team has flagged as under review —
treat as a starting point, not settled guidance.
:::

The audit process will require accessibility knowledge such as performing automated testing, operating
only using the keyboard, testing with assistive technologies, and creating the ACR, among other
examples, so, before starting, we highly recommend taking the accessibility courses previously listed.
This process has as a result an Accessibility Audit Report that identifies all accessibility issues.
After fixing all issues identified in the Accessibility Audit Report, an Accessibility Conformance
Report (ACR) should also be created.

## Methods

The audit process combines three different testing methods: automated testing, manual testing and
assistive technology (AT) testing.

Automated testing can only identify less than 30% of accessibility violations, so we must perform
manual and AT testing. Ideally, manual and AT testing should only start when no issues are already
identified by automated testing, however, because some important issues are only identified by manual
and AT evaluation and solving all issues identified by automated testing can take significant time, we
also recommend performing manual and AT testing after automated testing.

### Automated testing

We recommend testing with as many automated tools as possible because different tools provide
different, complementary results.

**Mandatory:**

* IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker

To perform an automated test using the IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, first install the
browser extension and then follow these steps:

1. Enter the webpage you want to test
2. Right-click on the page and select Inspect
3. Choose "IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker" tab
4. Select the "Scan" button
5. After the scan, choose "Download current scan" by selecting the dropdown on the left of the "Scan"
   button
6. Add the report insights to the Accessibility audit report

**Important:**

* Lighthouse
* axe DevTools - Web Accessibility Testing
* webhint
* LERA
* ANDI - Accessibility Testing Tool
* WAVE Evaluation Tool
* Accessibility Insights for Web

**Color contrast and color blindness tools:**

* Are My Colours Accessible
* Adobe Color
* Color Contrast Checker - TPGi
* Leonardo
* Accessibility features reference - Chrome Developers

Other tools: Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools List, Section508.gov web software.

### Manual testing

To perform manual testing you should follow at least the first provided checklist, IBM Accessibility,
Verify - manual checklist. We encourage you to also follow the other checklists and add new topics that
are not covered by the provided checklist but that you identified as important from a training course,
to answer a user request, and/or to improve a specific product use case's accessibility.

* IBM Accessibility — Verify - manual checklist
* LearnAccessibility! — Checkpoints for navigation and wayfinding
* University of Washington — Accessibility checklist
* Microsoft — Accessibility checklist
* The A11Y project — Accessibility checklist
* Section 508 ICT Testing Baseline — ICT Testing Baseline for Web Accessibility

### Assistive technology testing

The assistive technology testing will be focused on testing using one of the following screen readers:
NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, Narrator, TalkBack, Orca.

Before starting the AT testing it is essential to complete the recommended training, which instructs
how to test with a screen reader. Additionally, it is highly recommended to attend the University of
Washington webinar, *Testing with Screen Readers, April 2023 Edition*.

To perform this test you should follow the provided checklist using a screen reader. We encourage you
to add new topics that are not covered by the provided checklist but that you identified as important
from a training course, to answer a user request, and/or to improve a specific product use case's
accessibility.

* IBM Accessibility — Test with a screen reader checklist

## Accessibility audit report template

Use this template to add insights from automated, manual and AT testing. The template shows a table
composed of the following columns:

| Column                   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Method                   | The method used: Automated testing (IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, Lighthouse, axe DevTools, webhint, LERA, ANDI, WAVE, Accessibility Insights for Web), Manual testing, or Assistive technology testing.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Product                  | The product where the issue was identified.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Screenshot               | Screenshot(s) related to the issue.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Link                     | The link where the issue was identified.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Criteria                 | The related WCAG criteria.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Conformance Level        | The provided criteria's conformance level: A, AA or AAA.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Rule                     | The WCAG rule(s) related to the provided criteria.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Issue                    | A description of the identified issue.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Code                     | The code related to the issue that must be fixed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Technique(s)             | The WCAG technique(s), related to the provided criteria, that should be adopted.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Recommendations          | Recommendations and resources on how to fix the issue.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Remarks and Explanations | From the international edition of VPAT®, this section may include: information regarding the testing of a given criteria, information on application dependencies to support accessibility (e.g. OS, app frameworks, browsers recommended), how the customer can find more information about accessibility issues (e.g. a bug ID for customer support), and known workarounds for accessibility issues. |
| Jira ticket              | The Jira ticket related to this fix.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

## Additional recommendations

A product without any accessibility issue identified by automated or manual testing is not necessarily
accessible by all users.

Accessibility is an on-going process and your users may have specific accessibility needs that should
be answered. It is important to continuously research accessibility opportunities to guarantee that
your product answers all your users' accessibility needs. To find new accessibility opportunities we
suggest:

* Testing with users with disabilities
* Testing with users with disabilities that use assistive technologies
* Performing automated or manual testing as new developments are launched
* Following analytics metrics and KPIs
* Requesting evaluation reports from accessibility experts

:::note
The live source page linked most tool/checklist names and listed several accessibility-consultancy
URLs directly; this migration kept the names as plain text since the transcription method used
couldn't reliably capture link targets. Re-add the actual URLs when this page gets a proper editorial
pass.
:::

Sourced from Cobalt's live Accessibility docs, which the Cobalt team has flagged as under review —
treat as a starting point, not settled guidance.
:::

Talkdesk firmly believes that web and software experiences should be accessible for everyone. TDS
(Talkdesk design system) is committed to following and complying with accessibility best practices.

## What is accessibility?

Accessibility is the qualities that make an experience open to all. The ability to see, hear, speak,
think and touch affects the human capacity to use technology so when designing an experience we should
consider different abilities levels.

By designing experiences that can be used by people with different abilities we are increasing the
number of people with disabilities that can use our products and also improving the experience for all
users. As an example closed captioning was initially designed to support people who are deaf and hard
of hearing however, it is now used by people without physical disabilities when in contexts where this
technique is useful such as in public places (when using public devices or when using their own mobile
device in silent mode), in loud environments, by someone who is learning a new language, among others.

The [World Health Organization](https://www.afro.who.int/health-topics/disabilities) defines that,

> "Disability is an umbrella term, covering impairments, activity limitations and participation
> restrictions. Impairments are problems in body functions or structures while activity limitations
> are difficulties encountered by an individual in executing tasks or actions. Problems experienced by
> an individual in life situations are called participation restrictions. In other words, disability is
> not just one health problem. It is a complex phenomenon, reflecting the interaction between features
> of a person's body and features of the society in which he or she lives."

Human disability can be permanent, temporary or situational.

| Permanent disability             | Temporary disability           | Situational disability                  |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Someone deaf or hard of hearing. | Someone with an ear infection. | Someone that is in a noisy environment. |

The [World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro/#what)
defines web accessibility as follows,

> "Web accessibility means that websites, tools, and technologies are designed and developed so that
> people with disabilities can use them. More specifically, people can: perceive, understand,
> navigate, and interact with the Web; contribute to the Web."

Examples of different disability use cases applied to ICT are,

|           | Permanent                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Temporary                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Situational                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Auditory  | A user who is deaf and relies on captions or sign language interpretation to communicate and understand customer inquiries.                                                                                                                             | A user who has recently undergone ear surgery and is experiencing temporary hearing loss. They may use captions or request written communication until their hearing recovers.                                                       | A user working in a noisy environment with loud background noise, such as construction noise or a bustling call center. They may use captions to ensure they can accurately understand customer conversations.                |
| Cognitive | A user with a cognitive disability, such as autism or a learning disability, who benefits from written communication. They may rely on captions or chat-based interfaces to effectively communicate with customers.                                     | A user recovering from a concussion or experiencing temporary cognitive difficulties due to illness. They may require written communication, including captions, to support their understanding and responsiveness.                  | A user working during a time of extreme fatigue or high stress, which may impair their cognitive abilities. They may use captions or written communication as a support tool to ensure accurate information exchange.         |
| Physical  | A user with a physical disability that affects their mobility or dexterity, such as paralysis or limb loss. They may use assistive technologies, like speech recognition software or alternative input devices, to interact with customers effectively. | A user who recently underwent surgery and is recovering from a broken arm, making it difficult to type or use a mouse. They may rely on voice recognition software or speech-to-text tools to assist in their customer interactions. | A user working in an environment with limited mobility, such as a temporary workspace due to renovations or holding a baby. They may use assistive devices or alternative setups to accommodate their physical limitations.   |
| Speech    | A user with a speech impairment that affects their ability to articulate spoken words clearly. They may rely on alternative communication methods, such as text-based chat or pre-recorded messages, to assist in their interactions.                   | A user who has undergone throat surgery and is unable to speak fluently during the recovery period. They may use text-based communication, including chat or captions, to communicate with customers effectively.                    | A user working in a noisy environment or experiencing voice strain due to a cold or illness. They may use written communication, such as captions or chat, to ensure accurate customer interactions.                          |
| Visual    | A user who is blind or visually impaired and relies on screen reader software or Braille displays to access information. They may use these assistive technologies to navigate customer requests and respond effectively.                               | A user recovering from eye surgery or wearing temporary eye patches, which affects their vision. They may require screen magnification tools or enlarged captions to assist in their customer interactions.                          | A user working in a dimly lit environment or experiencing temporary vision difficulties due to eye strain. They may rely on high-contrast interfaces, larger fonts, or captions to ensure clear communication with customers. |

## Talkdesk accessibility goals

Our ambition should be to make **Talkdesk products WCAG 2.1 level A and level AA compliant**.

This achievement will contribute to being compliant with standards and guidelines such as,

* [EN 301 549 "Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services"](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/301500_301599/301549/02.01.02_60/en_301549v020102p.pdf) from the European Standards Organizations (ESOs), [CEN](https://www.cen.eu/), [CENELEC](https://www.cenelec.eu/), and [ETSI](https://www.etsi.org/)
* ["National accessibility requirements and standards for products and services in the European single market: overview and examples"](https://ec.europa.eu/social/BlobServlet?docId=14840\&langId=en) from the [European accessibility act (EAA)](https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1202)
* [ICT Accessibility 508 Standards and 255 Guidelines](https://www.access-board.gov/ict/)
* [Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)](https://www.ada.gov/resources/web-guidance/)

## Talkdesk Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR)

ACRs are statements of conformance to accessibility standards that answer how the products meet the
criteria. ACRs can be created internally or by external accessibility experts and must always identify
that automated, manual and assistive technology testing was performed.

ACRs should have internal and external access because they inform about the degree of accessibility
conformance of products and also contribute to potential organizations'/customers'/users' decision-making
during the procurement process.

By default, the Talkdesk Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) uses the WCAG edition of the ITI
Voluntary Product Accessibility Template® (VPAT®), which is "the leading global reporting format for
assisting buyers and sellers in identifying information and communications technology (ICT) products
and services with accessibility features," and because — according to a training course created by the
Information Technology Industry Council (ITI) — WCAG level AA fully applies, without exceptions, all US
Revised Section 508 and EU EN 301 549 criteria for web software, web-based documentation and authoring
tool functionalities, converging with the current Talkdesk accessibility goals.

The international edition of VPAT® should be used if you need to:

* Evaluate non-web software, non-web documentation and/or closed functionality software (on products
  like ATMs, printers, etc.)
* Provide an ACR that fully evaluates all Section 508 (U.S.), EN 301 549 (EU), and W3C/WAI WCAG
  criteria

This is because WCAG doesn't fully apply to US Revised Section 508 and EU EN 301 549 criteria for
non-web software, non-web documentation and/or closed functionality software (on products like ATMs,
printers, etc.); however, the international edition is the only VPAT® edition that fully addresses all
US Revised Section 508 and EU EN 301 549 criteria, and its last version includes "the leading ICT
accessibility standards: Section 508 (U.S.), EN 301 549 (EU), and W3C/WAI WCAG."

Alternatively, or when requested, the 508 and/or EU editions could be used to provide separate reports.

Despite VPAT® being considered "the leading global reporting format" — and mentioned in the DHS OAST
Training Resources as "The ACR is created using a template called the Voluntary Product Accessibility
Template (or VPAT)" — we should keep evaluating new opportunities such as the new reporting methodology
suggested by Standard Accessibility Reporting (SAR).

## Meeting the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)

WCAG is developed through the W3C process in cooperation with individuals and organizations around the
world, with the goal of providing a single shared standard for web content accessibility that meets
the needs of individuals, organizations, and governments internationally.

The WCAG documents explain how to make web content more accessible to people with disabilities.

TDS follows the WCAG 2.1 which are stable, referenceable technical standards.

They have guidelines that are organized under 4 principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and
robust. For each guideline, there are testable success criteria, which are at three levels: A, AA, and
AAA.

## Standards compliant markup

The semantic markup is what makes content readable and understandable by assistive technologies by
representing the type of content that is being presented.

Accessible Rich Internet Applications (ARIA) or Web Accessibility Initiative – Accessible Rich Internet
Applications (WAI-ARIA) specification adds accessibility information to HTML elements making them more
accessible to people with disabilities specialty who use assistive technology.

* ARIA Authoring Practices Guide
* Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.2
* Using ARIA

ARIA applies special attributes to HTML; roles, states, and properties.

The course *Get Started with Web Accessibility* offered by Salesforce defines,

> "Roles are a way to give semantic meaning to HTML elements that traditionally do not have any
> semantic meaning, such as `<div>` or `<span>`."

> "States are attributes that describe the status of an ARIA component to a browser's accessibility
> tree."

Properties as, "attributes that describe the nature of an object."

## Assistive technology

Tools used by users with disabilities can be grouped into two main groups: Assistive technologies and
Adaptive strategies.

What mainly distinguishes these two groups is that,

Adaptive strategies are applied by using standard software and hardware such as keyboard, web browsers.
Adaptive Strategies examples include resizing text, reducing mouse speed, turning on captions,
switching to dark mode, using keyboard only, among others.

* Better Web Browsing
* Tips for Customizing Your Computer

Assistive technologies require the use of non-standard software and/or hardware such as screen readers,
screen magnifiers, voice recognition software, among others.

Different disabilities require different tools and techniques. The next section explains some of them.

## Assistive technologies

**Screen readers.** Read aloud information from web pages and other documents for people who cannot
read the text. Some of the most used screen readers are NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, Narrator, TalkBack, and
Orca.

**Refreshable braille.** Used combined with screen readers. The screen reader is capable of adapting
electronic content to braille and, by using a refreshable braille display, blind users can read the
content.

**Screen magnifiers.** Allow users to magnify the entire screen or a part of a screen. Used by people
with some types of low vision to enlarge visual content (type, images, and others).

**Text-to-speech / voice recognition software.** Lets a person use spoken commands to enter text or
control a computer. Used by people who cannot use a keyboard or mouse.

**Selection switches.** Used by people who cannot use a keyboard or mouse.

**Alternative input software and hardware.** Allow users to navigate without using a keyboard or a
mouse. Used by people with mobility impairments. As an example, software that displays a keyboard
on-screen allows users to activate virtual keys by blinking or using head stick, mouth stick, foot
pedals, among others.

This guide aims to help us deliver a consistent and positive product writing experience across all
Talkdesk products. As a result, we will *be* more professional and our users will trust us more. It's a
win-win situation for everyone involved.

If you ever need to deviate from these guidelines, talk to someone in charge of the Design System. It's
important to understand why it needs to be done and what's the best way to achieve it.
