narrative.markdown:
## Abbreviations and acronyms

### Abbreviations

To avoid misunderstanding, before referring to something with its abbreviation, write the full version on the first mention, with the abbreviation in parentheses. On subsequent mentions, you can start using the abbreviation.

**Example:** Amazon Web Services (AWS)

* Avoid using internal abbreviations in the product.
* Well-known abbreviations, like **API** or **SMS**, can be used.
* Don't use apostrophes for plural abbreviations.
* When you want to display an example of something to offer more context and information to the user, use the abbreviation **e.g.**

### Acronyms

An acronym is formed from the first letters of words. The letters can either be pronounced as a word itself or separately.

**Example:**

* EMEA (**Europe, Middle East, and Africa**)
* USD (**United States dollar**)
* FAQ (**Frequently Asked Questions**)
* CSAT (**Customer Satisfaction Score**)

---

## All caps

All caps are harder to read than regular sentence-case text. Users tend to read all caps text slightly more slowly, or even more aggressively. You should avoid it except for [acronyms](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/23fa55-grammar-and-mechanics/t/45073b) and [file extensions](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/23fa55-grammar-and-mechanics/t/916c11).

---

## Articles

* The use of articles (*a*, *an, the*) depends on whether the message is conversational or action-based microcopy.
* Avoid articles in buttons and labels.
* Use articles in more conversational sections of the interface, like empty states or messages. This makes the language more approachable and helps with understanding when introducing new, complex concepts.

**Do** In the title, the definite article "the" was used to provide a more conversational experience with the user. The button, however, does not require an article.

---

## Avoid saying “sorry”

Use “sorry” only in error messages that result in serious problems for the user (for example, data loss, the user can’t continue to use Talkdesk, or the user must contact Support).

![Do — a “Service unavailable” error screen reading “We’re sorry, our service is temporarily unavailable, but we should be back up shortly. Please contact us if the problem persists.”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-avoid-sorry-do.png)
*Do We should apologize because is Talkdesk is down.*

![Don’t — a sign-in form error reading “Sorry, but you must include a symbol in your password”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-avoid-sorry-dont.png)
*Don't The user made a mistake. No need for us to apologize.*

**Note:** Before you use “sorry” in UI text, ask yourself if you could change the design to avoid the situation.

---

## Contractions

They give our writing an informal, friendly tone. Some can be used, some can’t.

**Do:** We'll, Can’t, Don’t, You’re, Shouldn't, It’s, You’ve, Couldn’t, Haven’t.

**Don't:** Needn’t, Mustn’t, There’re, You’d, That’ll, Gotta, It’d, Could've, They've.

**The difference between *its* and *it's***

Don't confuse *its* (possessive pronoun) with *it's* (personal pronoun *it* + verb). *It’s* is a contraction of “it is” or “it has” while *its* is used to refer to something or to say that something belongs to someone/something.

**Do** The computer looked as though its power supply had failed.

**Do** It’s a good idea to read the Cobalt Design System guidelines.

---

## Currency

When writing about currency, give preference to the acronym instead of the symbol. The acronym should always be placed before the amount.

Since we write our product in American English, we should always use a decimal point.

**Do:** USD 250.00

**Don't:** $250.00 USD

---

## Dates and Times

Dates and times are represented according to examples in the table below.

| **When did it happen?**   | **How to use**                              |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Current day               | Today, 3:54 PM                              |
| Next day                  | Tomorrow, 2:16 AM                           |
| Previous day              | Yesterday, 2:25 PM                          |
| More than 48h ago         | May 3, 4:12 PM                              |
| In a previous/future year | Dec 25, 2019, 5:19 PM Apr 1, 2025, 11:12 PM |

### Dates

* Traditional US format: Month Day, Year (MMM D, YYYY).
* Months are usually abbreviated.
* The year is only represented if it’s not the current one.
* A comma between month/day and year.
* A comma between the date and time.
* “Today”, “Tomorrow” and “Yesterday” are the only relative dates used.
* Values are displayed without the leading “0”.
* In a graphic or a table, spell out the day of the week only if necessary.
* A comma between weekday and month.
* Choose to abbreviate weekdays over months.

| **Weekdays** | **Abbreviation** |
| ------------ | ---------------- |
| Monday       | Mon              |
| Tuesday      | Tue              |
| Wednesday    | Wed              |
| Thursday     | Thu              |
| Friday       | Fri              |
| Saturday     | Sat              |
| Sunday       | Sun              |

| **Months** | **Abbreviation** |
| ---------- | ---------------- |
| January    | Jan              |
| February   | Feb              |
| March      | Mar              |
| April      | Apr              |
| May        | May              |
| June       | Jun              |
| July       | Jul              |
| August     | Aug              |
| September  | Sep              |
| October    | Oct              |
| November   | Nov              |
| December   | Dec              |

| **Word**       | **Abbreviation** | **Example**  |
| -------------- | ---------------- | ------------ |
| **Year/Years** | yr.              | 1 yr. 12 yr. |
| **Years**      | yrs.             | 10 yrs.      |
| **Month**      | mo.              | 1 mo.        |
| **Months**     | mos.             | 3 mos.       |
| **Day/Days**   | d.               | 7 d.         |
| **Week**       | wk.              | 1 wk.        |
| **Weeks**      | wks.             | 6 wks.       |

Abbreviations for these words should be avoided, and you should prioritize writing the complete word.

In cases where there is a lack of space, or you want to specify the duration of something - when a subscription is ending or for how long the user is a member - use the abbreviations above.

![Example of date format and different abbreviations — a client details panel showing “Membership: Jan 12, 2019 (3 yr., 3 mos.)”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-date-abbreviations-example.png)
*Do Abbreviations for January, "years", and "months".*

**Time**

* 12-hour format.
* “AM” and “PM” are capitalized, without periods, and with a space between the numbers and “AM/PM”.
* Values are displayed without the leading “0”.
* Relative time (e.g. 20 minutes ago) is not used.

### Date and time ranges

To display a date or time range, show an en dash (without spaces) between dates or times.

| **Range** | **How to use**                                                                                                                                                                                                           | **Example**                           |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| Year      | Date ranges are formatted based on whether the range covers the same year or the current year: Show the year on both the start and end. If both dates have the current year, show the year only at the end of the range. | Dec 6, 2013–Jan 2, 2014 Jan 4–6, 2014 |
| AM/PM     | If both times have the same AM/PM, use a single AM or PM at the end of the range.                                                                                                                                        | 8:00–10:30 AM                         |

---

### Other date and time formats

If the US date format is not applicable, you can use one of these, according to the [language/country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Date_format_by_country) in question:

* Day Month, Year (D MMM, YYYY)
* Year Month Day (YYYY MMM D).

If the 12-hour format is not applicable, you can use the 24-hour format. In this format, values are displayed with the leading “0”.

The table below shows you how to represent date and time according to the Day Month, Year (D MMM, YYYY), and the 24-hour format.

| **When did it happen?**       | **How to use**                         |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| **Current** day               | Today, 15:54                           |
| **Previous** day              | Yesterday, 14:25                       |
| More than **48 hours** ago    | 3 May, 16:12                           |
| In a previous/future **year** | 25 Dec, 2019, 17:19 1 Apr, 2025, 23:12 |

**Labels for the first 24 hours:**

* less than a minute ago, a minute ago, 2-59 minutes ago, 1 hour ago, 2-24 hours ago

**Label for the next 24 hours:**

* Yesterday, 9:43

**Label after the first 48 hours:**

* Thursday, January 19, 9:45 / Thu, January 19, 9:45 / Thu, Jan 19, 9:45

### Duration

Events with a duration (e.g., a call duration, a recording duration) are represented in the format 00:00. If the event reaches the hour mark, the format updates to 00:00:00.

In tables, these values should be right-aligned.

**Do:** 00:07

**Don't:** 7sec / 7s

**Do:** 01:23:42

**Don't:** 00:23:42 — The event did not reach the hour mark, so the format should be “23:42”.

---

## Decimals and fractions

### Decimals

Use commas and decimal points in accordance with standard American number formatting.

### Fractions

Use fractions when referring to multiple steps, as seen in our [progress bars](https://cobaltdesignsystem.zeroheight.com/styleguide/s/64259/p/63389d-progress-bar/b/06f00a).

---

## Emojis

Emojis are a fun way to express emotions and add humor, but let’s keep them out of our product. 💜

*Please bear in mind that we use icons in some of our [messages](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/04b4cd-message/b/35e7dd) and this does not mean you have to exclude them, as they're different from emojis.*

---

## File extensions

Use all caps to refer to a file extension type.

When referring to a specific file, you should include the word *file* after the filename and use their exact spelling. **Example: a CSV file**

When asking for the user to interact with a file, don’t use the file type as a verb.

**Do:** Open the ZIP file.

**Don't:** Unzip a ZIP file.

Use the file type name and not the filename extension.

**Do:** Drop your CSV file here.

**Don't:** Drop a .csv file here.

---

## Languages

* Write names of languages without abbreviations. When space is an issue, write out the name of the language on the first mention, and then on subsequent mentions, abbreviations are fine.
* Always mention the country of the language in parentheses.
* Write the name of the language in its own language.

**Do:** Français (CA) Français (FR)

**Don't:** Portuguese (PT) Spanish (ES)

When there is no space, follow the ISO norm. Capitalize the country, not the language.

**Example:** pt-PT, pt-BR

---

## Lists

* Use lists to make content easier to scan and reduce cognitive load.
* Use punctuation if you’re writing complete sentences.
* Avoid including more than 5 items on a list. If you need more, it might be better to create multiple lists.
* All lists and dropdowns should be sorted alphabetically if no other field is defined by default.

---

## Percentages

Use the % symbol instead of spelling out "percent."

---

## Punctuation

To help readers scan text at a glance, avoid using punctuation in places where it isn't necessary.

### Bold

Use **bold** for elements like titles, buttons, labels, or anything else you want to draw the user’s eye to. Try not to overdo it.

### Commas

Use the Oxford comma with “and” and “or”. The Oxford comma is placed after the penultimate item in a list of three or more items.

![Do — a search field placeholder reading “Search by name, number, or company”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-oxford-comma-do.png)
*Do*

![Don’t — a search field placeholder reading “Search by name, number or company”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-oxford-comma-dont.png)
*Don't*

**Note:** Why use the Oxford comma? **Example:** “We invited the mechanics, J.F.K. and Stalin.” With no Oxford comma, this sentence implies that the mechanics share their names with the 35th U.S. president and a Soviet dictator.

### Dashes and hyphen

Use a hyphen (-) without spaces on either side to link words into a single phrase.

**Do:** “First-time user”

**Don't:** “First time user”

You can often use an em dash (—) without spaces on either side to replace parentheses or colons.

**Do:** “Studio—released last year—is used by everyone at Talkdesk” “You can have two pets in the office—a dog and a cat”

**Don't:** 

Use the en dash (–) without spaces to indicate spans of time or ranges of numbers.

**Do:** “The 2020–2021 fiscal year was when it all started”

**Don't:** “The 2020-2021 fiscal year was when it all started”

### Exclamation points

Use exclamation points sparingly, and never more than one at a time, to be encouraging or generate excitement. Avoid using exclamation points in error messages, confirmation messages, or instructional text.

**Do:** “Almost there!” (To show progress during a process.)

**Don't:** “Your changes were saved!”

### Italics

Use *italics* for emphasis, citations, or defining a term.

### Periods

Avoid using periods on solitary sentences within these UI descriptions:

* Labels
* Tooltips
* Bulleted lists
* Modal dialog body text
* Toasts

**Do:** “Please check your internet connection and try again”

**Don't:** “Please check your internet connection and try again. “

Use periods on multiple sentences.

**Do:** “The interaction is already assigned to a different agent. Please try again shortly.”

**Don't:** “The interaction is already assigned to a different agent. Please try again shortly”

### Quotes

Use curly double quotes (“ ”) for initial quotations, and curly single quotes (‘ ’) for quotations within the initial quotation. Leave a space between a single and a double when they are next to each other.

**Do:** “Let’s explore the meaning of the quote ‘a misplaced phone is a Bastos phone,’ ” said Daniel.

**Don't:** ‘Let’s explore the meaning of the quote “a misplaced phone is a Bastos phone,”’ said Daniel.

### Underline

Use underline for hyperlinks, preferably giving it more emphasis with bold. Don’t underline text that will not be clickable, as users are used to that behavior.

## Phone numbers

Use the country code to help identify that the number is from another country. When space is not an issue, you can also add a flag to the country code.

All phone numbers are separated with non-breaking spaces, regardless of their origin.

The North American phone number format is: **+CC DDD DDD DDDD**

**Do:** +1 234 567 8999

**Don't:** +1 214-208-2146

**Phone numbers outside North America**

Numbers with 9 digits: **+CC DDD DDD DDD**

Numbers with 10 digits: **+CC DDD DDD DDDD**

---

## Sorting

When sorting items such as names, titles, or any other kind of data, it's important to follow a consistent and intuitive order.

Here's the suggested sorting order:

1. **Spaces**
2. **Symbols other than numerals, letters, and punctuation marks**
3. **Numerals (0 through 9)**
4. **Letters (A through Z)**

---

## States, provinces, cities, and countries

Spell out all city, state and province names without abbreviations. For countries or federations, when space is an issue, write out the name on the first mention, and then on subsequent mentions, abbreviations are fine.

**Do** United States of America, US United Kingdom, UK Brazil, BR

---

## Symbols and special characters

For accessibility purposes, avoid symbols. Don’t use *&* (ampersand) instead of *and*.

### The use of +

In [BadgeContainer](https://zeroheight.com/51aaf6147/p/86f1ac) and [Tag](https://zeroheight.com/51aaf6147/p/26887e), it's usual to represent a group of items through a number. When the maximum has been reached, a + is used to represent that there are more than a certain amount of items attached to that item.

In cases like this, **the + should be placed at the right of the number.**

The only case where we **represent the + on the left side of the number** is when representing [phone numbers](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/48e27a-grammar-and-mechanics/t/6809ef) and their **country code**.

---

## Titles and headings

Titles and headings should be descriptive but concise. It’s easier to navigate throughout the product if the headings and titles are different and unique.

* Use sentence case for headings and titles
* Keep it simple: headings with one sentence only.
* Don’t use punctuation.
* Don't put a link in a heading because it can easily be confused as a style applied to a heading instead of a link

**Do:** Simple and concise information.

**Don't:** Avoid title case.

---

## The use of "please"

Use “please” sparingly and only if an action is really serious, and important, or if you’re asking the user to complete a task that is not that easy. Sometimes, an imperative CTA is all that’s necessary.

Don't use "please" in the normal course of explaining how to use a product, even if you're explaining a difficult task.

Use "please" when you're asking for permission or forgiveness—for example, when what you're asking for benefits us, inconveniences a reader, or suggests a potential issue with a product.

---

## Units of measurement

When you specify a number with the unit, use a non-breaking space between the number and the unit. **Example: 65 MB**

However, when the unit of measure is [percentage](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/23fa55-grammar-and-mechanics/t/859ac1), don’t use a space. **Example: 50%**

On ranges of numbers with units, repeat the unit for each number and add the word *to* to separate the two numbers. **Example: 50% to 60%**

For [Currency](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/23fa55-grammar-and-mechanics/t/63b318), give preference to the acronym instead of the symbol.

---

## Use consistent words

Don’t use different words for the same thing. **Example:** if the correct term is “Notification Center”, don’t tell the user to go to his “Notifications area”. If the correct term is “interaction”, don’t call it “conversation” somewhere else, as it will only confuse the user.

### Delete vs Remove

Use the word “delete” when it’s impossible or nearly impossible to undo a certain action.

![Do — a confirmation dialog titled “Delete flow?” with “You can’t undo this action”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-delete-vs-remove-delete-do.png)
*Do*

![Don’t — the same irreversible action labeled “Remove flow?” instead of “Delete flow?”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-delete-vs-remove-delete-dont.png)
*Don't*

Use the word “remove” when the user can easily undo a certain action. When appropriate, reassure the user that the “removal” is reversible (see “optional” in the example below).

![Do — a confirmation dialog titled “Remove agents from the list?” with “You can add them back anytime”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-delete-vs-remove-remove-do.png)
*Do*

**Don't**

### Select vs Choose

You can **select** some text, one or more items in a table, one or more icons.

You **choose** a menu command or a toolbar command, an item in a popup menu, an item in a segmented control.

**Select** is to **choose** one or more elements of a set, especially a set of options. If you can apply a menu command to the item, then it’s a **selection**. To **choose** is to pick.

**Do** You select different ring groups

**Do** You choose the preferred language

### Settings vs Preferences vs Configuration

There isn't a single consistent style followed by all applications/websites. They are (broadly) synonyms. However, we will do our best to define them so we can be consistent across Talkdesk products and make sure our users always understand what the words mean.

**Configuration** is a deep, fundamental property of the system. These are things that the IT department might set up, and that the user may never change, unless you have very specific needs and knowledge.

On the other end of the scale there are **Preferences**. These are the user's personal choices. They may involve whether spell-check is active, choice of language, speed of the mouse-pointer, etc.

**Settings** is very similar to Preferences, with a less personal touch to it. It's where the user views or modifies the list of things that can be set. *Account settings* (where we change our Role and Team) would be a viable option for our Workspace, for example. Note that **setting** and **option** can also be used interchangeably in the singular (“check the option labeled *never*” or "You don't have permission to change this setting").

---

## Use numerals

![Do — “You have 3 messages”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-use-numerals-do.png)
*Do Faster to read.*

![Don’t — “You have three messages”](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-use-numerals-dont.png)
*Don't Takes longer to read.*

**Exception 1:** When using numbers two different ways, refer to one in numerals and the other in text. E.g.: “Enter two 3s.”

**Exception 2:** If it's an expression that typically uses spelled-out numbers, leave them that way. E.g. “A friendly welcome email can help you make a great first impression.”

---

## Use sentence case

Capitalize only the first word in a phrase. It’s easier to read and to remember as a rule.

![Do — a button labeled “Create flow” in sentence case](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-sentence-case-do.png)
*Do*

![Don’t — a button labeled “Create Flow” in title case](/assets/content-grammar-and-mechanics/grammar-sentence-case-dont.png)
*Don't*

---

## When you're stuck

You can always ping the Product Design team in our design-private channel.
narrative.title: Grammar and mechanics

narrative.markdown:
### Address users clearly

Use "you" and "your" to address users or use a "no point of view" approach.

### Avoid saying "sorry"

Use "sorry" only in error messages that result in severe problems for the user (for example, data loss,
the user can't continue to use Talkdesk, or the user must contact Support).

### Be concise, simple, and direct

Avoid unnecessary and redundant information. Avoid large blocks of text and long, complex sentences.
This will help users to be more efficient in their tasks and prevent cognitive overload.

### Be inclusive

Use gender-neutral language. A lot of Portuguese words are masculine, but there is *always* a way to be
as neutral as possible.

### Buttons should have verbs

Avoid unnecessary words and articles such as *a, o, as*, or *os.* **Use verbs.** Avoid saying "New" when
you're asking the user to create/add something.

### Do not translate Product names

Facebook Messenger is a name, and you should not translate that to Mensagens do Facebook, for example.
Not translating Product names is different from translating features and option names.

### English words

Use English words only if there is no translation or if they're known by the majority of the users. How
do you know that? If you're in doubt if the word is regularly used, just translate it. Common sense is
the key to this one.

### Punctuation isn't always necessary

Avoid using punctuation in places where it isn't necessary. Do not use periods in solitary sentences.
Use periods in multiple sentences.

### Use European Portuguese

Bad translations and/or a mix between European Portuguese and Brazilian Portuguese can cause a sense of
confusion and lack of confidence, as it is often something related to spam websites.

### Use positive language and an active voice

The subject of the sentence is the person or thing performing the action. With passive voice, it's
often hard for readers to figure out who's supposed to do something.

### Use the informal "you"

Always always always use "tu" instead of "você", preferably without having to say "tu" in the sentence.

### Write according to the latest Portuguese Language Orthographic Agreement

[Acordo Ortográfico da Língua Portuguesa](https://www.portoeditora.pt/lingua-portuguesa/conversor-acordo-ortografico)
narrative.title: Portuguese

narrative.markdown:
### Be concise, simple, and direct

Avoid unnecessary and redundant information. Avoid large blocks of text and long, complex sentences.
This will help users to be more efficient in their work and prevent cognitive overload. By the way,
direct does not mean insensitive.

**Do:** "Save changes?"

**Don't:** "Would you like to save your changes?"

---

### Be honest and specific

Be honest and specific about what the product can or cannot do. Don't oversell or overpromise.

**Do:** "You can add up to 50 guests to a conversation."

**Don't:** "You can add as many guests as you want to a conversation."

---

### Use positive language

**Do:** To open Callbar, click Open.

**Don't:** You can't open Callbar if you don't click Open.

**Note:** Positive language doesn't mean you cannot use "negative" words. *You can disable Callbar
anytime* is a sentence that gives the user confidence despite having the word "disable" in it. It's more
about the message and how we make the users feel than the words individually.

---

### Use active voice

**Do:** "Please install the app first."

**Don't:** "The app must be installed first."

**Exception:** When you want to specifically emphasize the action over the subject. In some cases, this
is fine. E.g., *Your account has been flagged.*

---

### Write for all reading levels

Use technical and industry terminology when it's relevant but keep your language as simple as possible.

**Do:** "Preparing video…"

**Don't:** "Buffering..."

---

### Address users clearly

Use "you" and "your" to address your users or use a "No point of view" approach.

**Do:** "Please check your internet connection."

**Don't:** "I have to check my internet connection."

**Do:** "Account"

**Don't:** "My Account"

**Exception:** There are some cases in which it's industry standard to use "I" and "my" to emphasize the
user's ownership of content or actions.

**Do:** "I agree to follow the terms of service."

**Don't:** "You agree to follow the terms of service."

---

### Write in the present tense

Use the present tense to describe product behavior. Avoid using the future tense to describe the way a
product always acts. When you need to write in the past or future tenses, use simple verb forms.

**Do:** "Contact created"

**Don't:** "Contact has been created"

---

### Avoid slang and jargon

Use a conversational, casual tone with our users, but don't be overfamiliar or condescending.

**Do:** "Well done"

**Don't:** "You're the real deal, bro!"

---

### Don't exclude people

Never rely on shape, size, color or location alone to communicate something, because not all users will
know what you're talking about. Avoid saying things like:

* "Click the blue button."
* "Go to the menu on the top of the page."
* "Fill out your details in the square box."

---

### When you're stuck

You can always ping the Product Writing team on Slack (@frederica.lopes), request a
[design-review](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/UX/pages/1103662259/Design+Reviews+a.k.a.+Sketchbusters)
or create an issue on
[our Jira board.](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/jira/software/projects/CDS/boards/1041?issueType=11376)
narrative.title: Principles

narrative.markdown:
Our writing has two dimensions: voice and tone.

Our voice reflects who we are, it never changes. We should always sound like Talkdesk.

In contrast, some aspects of our personality might be more or less apparent, depending on the audience
and their context (think different users, like an admin vs a regular agent; empty state vs description
of a header; a recurrent message vs a rare one). That's tone.

---

## Voice

Talkdesk is a young, vibrant company that has taken the contact center industry by storm with its
innovative products and a new way of tackling perennial, quasi-unsolvable problems.

We should all be proud of what we've accomplished so far, but youth and hypergrowth have drawbacks: it's
difficult to deliver consistency and intuitiveness – cornerstones of any leading software. And when these
are lacking, trust becomes an issue.

So what can we do? We make sure our voice is as clear and predictable as water. Building trust is our top
priority, and that's why our writing is always **clear**, **positive**, **concise**, and **honest**. We
sound like a friendly and knowledgeable colleague, who uses everyday language to guide everyone through
all of our products.

---

## Tone

As the good, friendly and knowledgeable colleague that we are, there will come times when we'll show more
enthusiasm. We will be witty and irreverent, but never awkward or offensive. We'll know when the time is
right because we understand the context. The same joke told over and over again stops being funny very
quickly. We'll congratulate a user for creating something complex but not for something as simple as
closing a window. If we know the user is in a hurry, we'll get out of their way.

**If something serious has gone wrong**, we say "sorry". For instance, if the product has stopped working
completely.

However, we avoid saying "sorry" in other types of error messages. We also **avoid humor when writing for
errors**. People use our products for serious tasks and can sometimes be under stress.

There's usually no need to say "please" or "thank you". It's alright to say "Contact created" rather than
"Thank you for creating a contact".

Remember to focus on the specifics of the situation and adapt the tone accordingly.
narrative.title: Voice and tone

narrative.markdown:
### Avoid saying "sorry"

Use "sorry" only in error messages that result in serious problems for the user (for example, data
loss, the user can't continue to use Talkdesk, or the user must contact Support).

![A generic 'ERROR 504 - Service unavailable' page reading 'We're sorry, our service is temporarily unavailable, but we should be back up shortly. Please contact us if the problem persists.'](/assets/content-word-choice-consistent-words/word-choice-avoid-sorry-do.png)
*Do We should apologize because is Talkdesk is down.*

![A generic Talkdesk sign-in form showing the error 'Sorry, but you must include a symbol in your password'](/assets/content-word-choice-consistent-words/word-choice-avoid-sorry-dont.png)
*Don't The user made a mistake. No need for us to apologize.*

**Note:** Before you use "sorry" in UI text, ask yourself if you could change the design to avoid the
situation.

---

### The use of "please"

Use "please" sparingly and only if an action is really serious and important, or if you're asking the
user to complete a task that is not that easy. Sometimes, an imperative CTA is all that's necessary.

Don't use "please" in the normal course of explaining how to use a product, even if you're explaining a
difficult task.

Use "please" when you're asking for permission or forgiveness—for example, when what you're asking for
benefits us, inconveniences a reader, or suggests a potential issue with a product.

---

### Using "We" and "You" in messages

#### We - Our product, Talkdesk

Using "we" in messages can:

* Establish a relationship between the user and the product.
* Give the user the idea that the product is working together with them to achieve a shared goal.
  **e.g.** *"We've made some improvements based on your feedback"* can help the user feel like they are
  part of the process.
* Shift the responsibility of something going wrong to us, Talkdesk, when needed. **e.g.** *"We
  apologize for the inconvenience caused"* helps reassure the user that the company is working to fix
  the problem.
* Create a more positive experience and can help celebrate the user's accomplishments, when used in
  success messages. **e.g.** *"We've received your payment and your subscription will be ready soon"*
  is more friendly than *"Payment received"*.
* Help explain why certain actions or information are necessary for the user. **e.g.** "We need your
  location to provide an accurate timezone" is more informative than "Allow us to access your
  location".
* Create excitement and anticipation for the user, when used in Onboarding. **e.g.** *"We want to
  introduce our new feature that allows you to customize your profile"* rather than *"Check out our new
  feature"*.

Other things to take into consideration:

* "We" should be mentioned to refer to our product.
* Do not use "we" to mention both the user and the product.
* Do not overuse "we", as the content/messages can become more self-centered and can create a sense of
  distance between the user and the product.

#### You - The user

Using "you" in messages can:

* Help address the user directly when sending a message or a notification.
* Create a more personalized experience and helps the user feel more engaged with the product.
* Make the user take action, helping create a sense of urgency and encourage the user to take the
  desired action. **e.g.** *"You can now assign users to your seats"*.
* Address the user's needs, creating a more empathetic and user-centric experience. **e.g.** *"Orders
  \#189 and #186 need your attention"*.
* Help soften and create a more supportive experience, when used in error messages. **e.g.** *"Your
  seats couldn't be updated. Please try again or contact Talkdesk"* is more friendly than *"Seats update
  failed"*.
* Engage, when introducing the user to a new feature. **e.g.** Saying *"You're going to take so much
  advantage of our new feature"* instead of *"Check our new feature"*.

Other things to take into consideration:

* Avoid using "you" too much. Just like any word that becomes too much repetitive, can be overwhelming.
  Use "you" sparingly and strategically to avoid overloading the user with too much language.

---

### View more, show more, see more

#### View more

Can be used when the user is browsing through a list of items and needs to view more names, numbers,
etc from that list;

#### Show more

Can be written when the user is viewing a specific page and needs/wants to see more content;

#### See more

A more generic terminology. Must be written when the user needs to see more options, for example.

---

### When to "Cancel", "Close", "Reset", and "Clear"

#### Cancel vs Reset

* Use "Cancel" when you want the user to confirm they want to abandon or dismiss an action. **e.g.**
  *"Cancel call!*
* Use "Reset" when you want to give the user the option to revert to the original state of the
  interface. e.g. *"Reset filters"*
* Make sure the "Cancel" button is clearly visible and positioned in a prominent location, such as on
  the bottom right-hand side of the interface.
* Use "Reset" sparingly (compared to "Cancel") and only when it's necessary to give users the option to
  start over from scratch.

#### Cancel vs Close

* Use "Cancel" when the action being taken can be undone or reversed, such as canceling a call, an
  order, or a subscription. **e.g.** *"Cancel call"*
* Use "Close" when the action being taken cannot be reversed, such as closing a window. **e.g.** *"Close
  chat"*

#### Reset vs Clear

* Use "Reset" when you want to give the user the option to revert to the original state of the
  interface. **e.g.** *"Reset filters"*
* Use "Clear" when you want the user to erase any input or selection they have made when filtering or
  to erase their input. **e.g.** *"Clear filters"*
* Make sure the "Reset" and "Clear" buttons are clearly labeled and easy to distinguish from one
  another.

**For all scenarios:**

* Consider using a warning/confirmation message to double-check if the user really wants to cancel or
  reset the action.
* Be consistent with the terms you use across the product to avoid confusing the user.
narrative.title: Consistent words

narrative.markdown:
Talkdesk is a global company, so it's crucial that our communication remains free from bias. On this
living page you'll find some rules of conduct, as well as inclusive alternatives for terminology that
has been **widely** considered inappropriate or contentious.

* **Avoid making generalizations about people, countries, regions, and cultures.**
* **Avoid using slang,** especially if it could be considered cultural appropriation, such as "spirit
  animal".
* **Don't use profane or derogatory terms.**
* **Avoid culturally sensitive terms,** such as the terms associated with military or political actions
  or other historic events and eras.
* **Focus on people, not disabilities.** Don't use words that imply pity, such as "stricken with" or
  "suffering from". Don't mention a disability unless it's relevant.

| Do (inclusive language)                             | Don't (non-inclusive/contentious language)          |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Primary/replica Leader/follower                     | Master/slave                                        |
| Safelist/blocklist                                  | Whitelist/blacklist                                 |
| Team, everyone, people, y'all                       | Gendered nouns (e.g., guys)                         |
| Firefighter, chair                                  | Gendered nouns (e.g., fireman, chairman)            |
| They/them/their                                     | Gendered pronouns (e.g., he/him/his or she/her/her) |
| Synthetic, manufactured                             | Gendered adjectives (e.g., manmade)                 |
| People with disabilities                            | Handicapped, differently-abled                      |
| Woman/Women (when referring to someone 18 or older) | Girl/Girls                                          |
| Underrepresented groups                             | Minorities                                          |
narrative.title: Inclusive language

narrative.markdown:
Here you'll find a list of words/phrases that you should use in our UI to ensure consistency and, in
many cases, correctness.

| Do                           | Don't                       | Comments                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Activity                     | Activity App                | Avoid using prefixes or suffixes (like "App") to refer to the Atlas apps.                                                                                                                                                 |
| Analyze                      | Analyse                     | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Behavior                     | Behaviour                   | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Blocklist                    | Blacklist                   | Contentious language.                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Canceled                     | Cancelled                   | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Center                       | Centre                      | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| CSV                          | csv                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Email                        | E-mail                      |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Favorite                     | Favourite                   | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| internet                     | Internet Network            | "internet" is immediately understood by everyone. "Network" is slightly more technical and more ambiguous. **Note**: Please capitalize "internet" only at the beginning of a sentence (e.g., "Internet connection lost"). |
| Keypad                       | Dialpad Dial pad            |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| License                      | Licence                     | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| No.                          | Nr.                         | "No." is the correct abbreviation for Number. "Nr." is the abbreviation used in Portuguese.                                                                                                                               |
| Organize                     | Organise                    | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| On a call                    | On call                     | "On call" means that someone is available for work at a moment's notice. It does not mean you are on a telephone call with someone.                                                                                       |
| Recognize                    | Recognise                   | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Safelist                     | Whitelist                   | Contentious language.                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Setup (noun)                 | Setup (verb)                |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Set up (verb)                | Set up (noun)               |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Sign-in (noun or adjective)  | Login (noun or adjective)   | Correct: "You have one more sign-in attempt." Incorrect: "Please sign-in again."                                                                                                                                          |
| Sign in (verb)               | Log in (verb)               | Correct: "Please sign in again." Incorrect: "You have one more sign in attempt."                                                                                                                                          |
| Sign-out (noun or adjective) | Logout (noun or adjective)  |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Sign out (verb)              | Log out (verb)              |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Time zone                    | Timezone                    |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Traveled                     | Travelled                   | Always use the American English variant.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Try again                    | Retry                       |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| You can't undo this action   | This action can't be undone | Active voice is usually better than passive voice.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Wi-Fi                        | WiFi                        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

### When you're stuck

You can always ping the Product Writing team on Slack (@frederica.lopes), request a
[design-review](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/UX/pages/1103662259/Design+Reviews+a.k.a.+Sketchbusters)
or create an issue on [our Jira board.](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/jira/software/projects/CDS/boards/1041?issueType=11376)
narrative.title: Vocabulary

narrative.markdown:
:::note
This page doesn't map to the current Foundations taxonomy (Tokens / Content / Accessibility) — flagged for review.
:::

Talkdesk products can be developed with 5 different layout types; Block, Column, Modular, Hierarchical, and Flow.

Layout types differ by the used grid type, number of containers, number of push panels, and other characteristics and guidelines.

## Overview

|                 |         | **Block** | **Column** Tables and Calendars | **Column** Forms | **Modular** | **Hierarchical** | **Flow** |
| --------------- | ------- | --------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------- | ----------- | ---------------- | -------- |
| **Grid**        | Fluid   | ❌         | ✅                               | ✅                | ✅           | ✅                | ✅        |
|                 | Fixed   | ✅         | ❌                               | ✅                | ✅           | ❌                | ❌        |
| **Containers**  | One     | ✅         | ✅                               | ✅                | ✅           | ✅                | ✅        |
|                 | Two 1/3 | ❌         | *Rarely*                        | *Rarely*         | *Rarely*    | ❌                | ❌        |
|                 | Two 2/2 | ❌         | *Rarely*                        | *Rarely*         | *Rarely*    | ❌                | ❌        |
| **Push Panels** | 0       | ❌         | ✅                               | ✅                | ✅           | ✅                | ❌        |
|                 | 1       | ✅         | *Sometimes*                     | *Sometimes*      | *Sometimes* | ❌                | ✅        |
|                 | 2       | ❌         | *Rarely*                        | *Rarely*         | *Rarely*    | ❌                | ✅        |

---

## Block layouts

Block layouts use a centered aligned fixed grid type and only have one container.

The max width is applied for each viewport.

Usually, all MainApp elements, vertically and horizontally centered aligned, are inside the four columns positioned in the center.

![Abstract diagram of a Block layout: one centered, fixed-width container](/assets/layout/block-xlarge.png)

![Example of a Block layout: a dialer screen centered on the page](/assets/layout/block-example.png)

| Column 1           | Column 2                                                                             |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Responsiveness** | Block layouts support all viewports                                                  |
| **Push panels**    | Block layouts can use one panel. By default, the panel is open but can be collapsed. |
| **Actions**        | Block layout actions are fixed and positioned on the bottom of the Main App area.    |
| **Background**     | Block layouts use a white background.                                                |

#### Responsiveness

![Block layout at the small viewport](/assets/layout/block-small.png)
*Block small*

![Block layout at the medium viewport](/assets/layout/block-medium.png)
*Block medium*

![Block layout at the large viewport](/assets/layout/block-large.png)
*Block large*

![Block layout at the xlarge viewport](/assets/layout/block-xlarge.png)
*Block xlarge*

---

## Column layouts

Column layouts use different grid types, usually fluid, and have one or two containers.

MainApp elements are positioned according to the grid columns.

Column layouts are usually applied to the following layouts:

* Tables
* Forms
* Calendars

| Column layouts     | Table and Calendar                                                                                                       | Forms                                                                                        |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Responsiveness** | Depending on the product, column (Table and Calendar) layouts might support all viewports                                | Depending on the product, column (Forms) layouts might support all viewports                 |
| **Push panels**    | Column (Table and Calendar) layouts can use one panel. By default, the panel is open but can be collapsed.               | Column (Forms) layouts can use one panel. By default, the panel is open but can be collapsed |
| **Actions**        | Column (Table and Calendar) layout actions are fixed and positioned in the top right corner, associated with the header. | Column (Forms) layout actions are positioned below the form.                                 |
| **Background**     | Column (Table and Calendar) layouts use a white background.                                                              | Column (Forms) layouts use a white background.                                               |

#### Responsiveness

![Column layout at the small viewport](/assets/layout/column-small.png)
*Column small*

![Column layout at the medium viewport](/assets/layout/column-medium.png)
*Column medium*

![Column layout at the large viewport](/assets/layout/column-large.png)
*Column large*

![Column layout at the xlarge viewport](/assets/layout/column-xlarge.png)
*Column xlarge*

### Tables

Tables usually use a column layout, fluid grid type, and have one container.

Table columns' width can be dynamic or fixed, depending on the content.

![Abstract diagram of a Column layout used for a table](/assets/layout/column-table-xlarge.png)

There are use cases where Tables have one push panel.

#### Responsiveness

![Column table layout at the small viewport](/assets/layout/column-table-small.png)
*Column table small*

![Column table layout at the medium viewport](/assets/layout/column-table-medium.png)
*Column table medium*

![Column table layout at the large viewport](/assets/layout/column-table-large.png)
*Column table large*

![Column table layout at the xlarge viewport](/assets/layout/column-table-xlarge.png)
*Column table xlarge*

### Calendar

Calendars usually use a column layout, fluid grid type, and have one container.

![Abstract diagram of a Column layout used for a calendar](/assets/layout/column-calendar-xlarge.png)

![Example of a Column calendar layout: a monthly schedule view](/assets/layout/column-calendar-example.png)

#### Responsiveness

![Column calendar layout at the small viewport](/assets/layout/column-calendar-small.png)
*Column calendar small*

![Column calendar layout at the medium viewport](/assets/layout/column-calendar-medium.png)
*Column calendar medium*

![Column calendar layout at the large viewport](/assets/layout/column-calendar-large.png)
*Column calendar large*

![Column calendar layout at the xlarge viewport](/assets/layout/column-calendar-xlarge.png)
*Column calendar xlarge*

### Forms

Forms usually use a column layout, fluid or fixed grid type, and have one container.

Form inputs use the total width only in small viewports. In other viewports, they use half of the total width.

Explore more about forms in the [Forms pattern documentation](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/04cbc6-forms).

![Abstract diagram of a Column layout used for a form](/assets/layout/column-form-xlarge.png)

![Example of a Column form layout: a create-contact form](/assets/layout/column-form-example.png)

There are use cases where Forms have one push panel.

![Example of a Column form layout with one push panel: an add-case form](/assets/layout/column-form-example-one-push-panel.png)

#### Responsiveness

![Column form layout at the small viewport](/assets/layout/column-form-small.png)
*Column form small*

![Column form layout at the medium viewport](/assets/layout/column-form-medium.png)
*Column form medium*

![Column form layout at the large viewport](/assets/layout/column-form-large.png)
*Column form large*

![Column form layout at the xlarge viewport](/assets/layout/column-form-xlarge.png)
*Column form xlarge*

---

## Modular layouts

Modular layouts use different grid types, usually fluid, and have one or two containers.

Modular layouts are usually used to show Cards, in Modules (fluid or fixed) or Rows.

| Column 1           | Column 2                                                                                                  |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Responsiveness** | Depending on the product, modular layouts might support all viewports                                     |
| **Push panels**    | There are no use cases where a Modular layout uses push panels but they can use one panel when necessary. |
| **Actions**        | Modular layout actions are fixed and positioned in the top right corner, associated with the header.      |
| **Background**     | Modular layouts usually use a gray background but can also use a white background.                        |

#### Responsiveness

![Modular layout at the small viewport](/assets/layout/modular-small.png)
*Modular small*

![Modular layout at the medium viewport](/assets/layout/modular-medium.png)
*Modular medium*

![Modular layout at the large viewport](/assets/layout/modular-large.png)
*Modular large*

![Modular layout at the xlarge viewport](/assets/layout/modular-xlarge.png)
*Modular xlarge*

### Cards - Modules

Cards Modules usually use a modular layout and only have one container.

Sometimes, in Cards Modules, cards have fixed dimensions. In these cases, they don't follow the grid structure.

#### Fluid grid type

![Example of a modular Cards - Modules layout with a fluid grid type: an AI Launchpad screen](/assets/layout/modular-cardmodules-example-fluid.png)

#### Responsiveness

![Cards - Modules fluid layout at the small viewport](/assets/layout/hierarchical-small.png)
*Hierarchical small*

![Cards - Modules fluid layout at the medium viewport](/assets/layout/hierarchical-medium.png)
*Hierarchical medium*

Usually used fluid grid types.

## Hierarchical layouts

Hierarchical layouts usually use fluid grid types and only have one container.

Hierarchical layouts are usually used to show Cards with different dimensions.

| Column 1           | Column 2                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Responsiveness** | Depending on the product, hierarchical layouts might support all viewports                                     |
| **Push panels**    | There are no use cases where a Hierarchical layout uses push panels but they can use one panel when necessary. |
| **Actions**        | Hierarchical layout actions are fixed and positioned in the top right corner, associated with the header.      |
| **Background**     | Hierarchical layouts use a gray background.                                                                    |

## Flow layouts

Flow layouts usually use fluid grid types and only have one container.

Usually, they have one or two push panels.

![Abstract diagram of a Flow layout](/assets/layout/flow-xlarge.png)

![Example of a Flow layout: the Automation Designer canvas](/assets/layout/flow-example.png)

**Responsiveness** —
Flow layouts don't support small and medium viewports —

**Push panels** —

Flow layouts can use two panels. As an exception, only in this kind of layout, panels don't overlap the header and the toolbar.

In flow layouts we should provide to our users the largest canvas area possible so panels should only be open when the user needs to interact with them. Examples of actions that can contribute to this are,

* Only one panel is open at a time. When the user opens a panel the other one automatically closes. This also contributes to a better experience when the secondary area and the drawer are open avoiding having multiple panels open simultaneously.

* Use float buttons that overlap the flow.

  Because in flow layouts the user needs to use several panels you should not close the panel to open another one when selecting a new card. Instead of that replace the panel content with the new one maintaining the panel open.
  —

  **Actions** —

  Flow layouts have Flow and View actions.

  Flow actions are actions with who the user interacts to create and manage the flow. Examples of these actions are searching or creating/configuring variables.

  View actions are actions with who the user interacts to change the way the flow is observed. Examples of these actions are adding notes, zooming in/out, or Fit screen.
  —

  **Flow actions** —
  Flow actions, such as search or create/configure variables, should be placed on the top of the flow, right, or left. Can be positioned floating, on the panel, or on the toolbar. —

  **View actions** —

  View actions, such as adding notes, zoom and view modes should have a fixed floating position, overlapping the flow.

  Should not have a label and a tooltip should be used to show the label.

  They should always be placed on the bottom, right, left, horizontally or vertically.
  —

  **Background** —

  Flow layout uses a background with a dotted pattern.

  They can assume different colors to represent different flow modes. Gray is the recommended default color to use in the background.
  —

#### Responsiveness

*Flow large*

*Flow xlarge*

:::note
This page doesn't map to the current Foundations taxonomy (Tokens / Content / Accessibility) — flagged for review.
:::

The Right-To-Left (RTL) writing is a system widely used in the Middle East and languages such as
Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, and Urdu are read and written from right-to-left.

Designing for the Middle East region poses some unique challenges, to produce a user experience that
will look and feel natural when presented to RTL users.

---

## RTL General Principles

To design an RTL project, we use the principle of mirroring every piece of content, with a few key
exceptions. To understand what to mirror and what to change entirely, it's important to imagine the UI
directionality flowing from right to left, as you can consult in the image below.

Starting from the top right corner of the page, they scan across the top and then scan down the
right-hand side of the content.

RTL websites tend to right-justify even the elements of the page. So the logo of the site will be on
the top right instead of the top left. Everything else naturally follows.

*The "image below" referenced here — a real-product "Voicemails" screenshot showing the same table
mirrored LTR vs. RTL — is not reproduced here because it pairs several fictional names with fictional
phone numbers (e.g. "Carly Yates" / "+1 563-212-2237"). See the data-handling note at the top of this
file. [View on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/07d484-right-to-left).*

## Typography & Text

Proper attention should be given to typography since Arabic and Hebrew, are displayed with characters
appearing from right to left and the typography needs to be specific because of characters
representation.

Another aspect to take into account is that those fonts may appear smaller than Latin ones at the same
font size, requiring adjustments to line spacing and alignment so that the typography works well in
that UI for all languages.

**Noto font** is the recommended font to use, it aims to support all languages with a harmonious look
and feel.

![Roboto font compared with Noto font in Arabic](/assets/rtl/font-rtl.png)

To maintain easy readability, **bold typeface should be avoided**. The italicized font is also not used
in Arabic.

**[Noto Sans Arabic](https://noto-website-2.storage.googleapis.com/pkgs/NotoSansArabic-unhinted.zip)**
— Download
**[Noto Sans Hebrew](https://noto-website-2.storage.googleapis.com/pkgs/NotoSansHebrew-unhinted.zip)**
— Download

**Features to take into consideration include:**

* Aligning text to the right side;
* **Words in LTR languages don't change their direction and neither do digits** (like phone numbers
  with international dialing codes). These are still displayed on RTL websites as they would be on LTR
  websites;
* **Abbreviating** days of the week, month, etc is commonplace in English, but **is not appropriate in
  Arabic**;
* Dates do not change direction either;
* Capital letters are often omitted.

Languages such as Arabic tend to have a great number of spoken and written variations, and if you're
making a product catered specifically to some region, it should really display the language version
used there.

### Text Reading Order

The direction depends on the language — Any time Arabic is used it will always appear RTL. However, as
we can see in the image below, there are instances where English (or other LTR languages) texted will
be mixed in amongst Arabic. In those cases, the LTR language text will always appear left to right.

![LTR reading order vs RTL reading order of a mixed Arabic/English sentence](/assets/rtl/text-reading-order.png)

Note that LTR words continue to appear left to right.

### Differences In Word Sizes Between Languages

Sometimes, when a website is translated into Arabic, the sizing of elements changes due to some words
becoming bigger or smaller after translation.

Consider the following example:

![Cancel and Save buttons in LTR compared with the same buttons in Arabic](/assets/rtl/differences-in-word-sizes.png)

The buttons 'Cancel' and 'Save' look smaller in Arabic, which can cause usability problems. It would be
better to have a min-width for the button to account for such cases.

---

## Logos and Trademarks

Logos and trademarks do not flip, but they do switch locations. So if a logo is typically in the upper
left, it will move to the upper right.

![A sidebar with the app logo shown on the left (LTR) and on the right (RTL)](/assets/rtl/logos-and-trademarks.png)

Note that the logo doesn't need to be flipped but moves to the top right instead of the top left.

---

## Icons

Mirroring icons in an Arabic interface should be done with proper caution. Sometimes mirroring or
flipping isn't necessary and sometimes it is.

Basic guidelines are as follows:

* **Symmetrical icons and** icons without an explicitly specified direction (such as camera, download,
  user profile, etc.) **don't need to be flipped.**

![A row of symmetrical icons: person, trash, settings, bell, alert, bookmark, diamond, calendar, wifi, stop, mail, headset, close, more, expand](/assets/rtl/symmetrical-icons.png)

Using the dock as an example, we can see in the image below that some icons don't need to be flipped
since they are symmetrical.

![A dock with the home icon highlighted, noting it doesn't need to be mirrored](/assets/rtl/dock-symmetrical-icons.png)

* The majority of users in RTL-writing countries are also **right-handed**, so such icons **should not
  be mirrored.**

![Coffee cup, wrench, and search icons that should not be mirrored](/assets/rtl/right-handed-icons.png)

* \*\*Icons with slashes: \*\*the slashes don't need to be flipped. This is true in both text and
  iconography.

---

* \*\*Icons with an explicit direction should be mirrored. \*\*For example, the back button should point
  to the right in the RTL version.

![LTR and RTL rows of directional icons such as arrows, send, log out, and call decline, mirrored](/assets/rtl/mirrored-icons-specific-direction.png)

* \*\*Icons that depict movement or text direction should be mirrored \*\*(such as text alignment icons,
  progress charts, etc.)

![LTR and RTL rows of icons depicting alert, chat, list, bar chart, calendar, and trend, mirrored](/assets/rtl/mirrored-icons-depict-direction.png)

* **Icons featuring English characters don't need to be mirrored**.

![Bold, underline, text size, strikethrough, and underlined A icons that don't need to be mirrored](/assets/rtl/english-characters.png)

* \*\*Icons that show directionality (like clocks) should not be flipped. \*\*While the linear
  representation of time is mirrored in RTL, the circular direction of time is not. A clock icon or a
  circular refresh or progress indicator with an arrow pointing clockwise should not be mirrored.

![Refresh, clock, and history icons that should not be flipped](/assets/rtl/time-icons.png)

* **Ensure that the icons you're using are appropriate.** For example, using a wine glass as a symbol
  for a restaurant or bar could be misunderstood because alcohol consumption is prohibited in Islam.
  Cultural peculiarities need to be taken into account, and designers should double-check that the
  symbols and icons they're using are appropriate for the target market.

---

## Numbers

**Numbers don't change direction** — Under no circumstances are "English" numbers flipped.

This includes both the number itself and the order of the numbers. So a phone number will still appear
in the LTR format with no changes. Even if you are listing out a number that is mixed with letters or
characters, numbers always appear left to right.

For example, **something like A58B265 would stay the same in LTR and RTL**. However, if you are
translating the phrase, from the year 2001 – 2010, in Arabic it will appear as 2010 – 2001.

---

## Images

Images and illustrations don't flip, although choosing an image requires appropriate selection, taking
into account cultural peculiarities when it comes to perception.

---

## UI Elements

Not all interface elements need to be mirrored. Below is a comprehensive overview of elements found in
a website's layout and whether these should be mirrored in RTL projects.

### Calendars

Calendars need to be mirrored. Monday will be displayed on the right side and Sunday on the left one.

![A calendar in LTR (Sun–Sat, left to right) compared with the same calendar in RTL (Sat–Sun, right to left)](/assets/rtl/calendars-rtl.png)

Note that Saturday is the official first day of the week in most Muslim countries.

**Hijri vs. Gregorian Calendar**

The Arabic Hijri calendar is primarily used in Saudi Arabia is lunar-based, consisting of 12 lunar
months in a year of 354 or 355 days. While they still acknowledge and follow the Gregorian calendar to
some extent, many publications and sites use the Hijri.

As we can see in the image below, some sites allow the **display of both Gregorian and Hijri at the
same time**.

There is also a Persian and Hebrew calendar. You will need to make specific calendar changes based on
who you are localizing for.

![A date picker showing both the Hijri and Gregorian calendar in Arabic and in English](/assets/rtl/hijri-calendar.png)

Examples of the Gregorian/Hijri calendar in Arabic and English.

### Dropdowns

Dropdown arrows will still face downward but will be placed on the left-hand side of the dropdown menu.

![A dropdown field in LTR with the arrow on the right, compared with RTL with the arrow on the left](/assets/rtl/dropdown-rtl.png)

### Buttons with icons

The icon's position should be flipped in the RTL layout.

![New contact and Resolve buttons with their icons mirrored between LTR and RTL](/assets/rtl/button-icons-rtl.png)

### Toasts

As you might expect, "close" and check icons should be flipped.

![A success toast with the close and check icons mirrored between LTR and RTL](/assets/rtl/toasts-rtl.png)

### Tabs

In RTL, the tabs should be flipped.

![Two tabs mirrored in position and underline between LTR and RTL](/assets/rtl/tabs-rtl.png)

### Media Controls

Media controls like playback buttons and media progress indicators always run LTR.

This is because media controls are reflecting the way a cassette players rolls the tape in a cassette.
So elements containing a play/pause/stop button will never flip.

![A media player control bar that stays LTR in both the LTR and RTL layouts](/assets/rtl/media-controls-rtl.png)

### Scroll Bars

Scroll bars within UI and within the browser will flip to be on the left.

### Toggle switches and checkboxes

On/off switches should be mirrored with the off position on the right and the on position on the left.

Checkmark buttons should not be mirrored with the longer leg positioned on the left.

![Toggle switches mirrored between on/off positions and a checkbox that is not mirrored, between LTR and RTL](/assets/rtl/toggle-switches-checkboxes-rtl.png)

### Sliders

Horizontal sliders should be mirrored in most cases with the minimum range on the right and the maximum
range on the left.

Horizontal sound volume sliders are the exception and inherit their directionality from media controls,
which are not mirrored.

![A slider control mirrored between LTR and RTL, and a sound volume slider that is not mirrored](/assets/rtl/sliders-rtl.png)

### Rating & Page selectors

Rating selectors often used to collect user feedback, should be mirrored, with the lowest rating on the
right and the highest rating on the left.

Page selectors are also mirrored with the Previous Page button on the right and the Next Page button on
the left.

The numerals that are used to indicate the page number should also be rearranged in right to left
order. For Arabic languages, the page numerals should be displayed using Eastern Arabic digits.

![A star rating selector and page selector, both mirrored between LTR and RTL](/assets/rtl/rating-page-selectors-rtl.png)

### Forms

Despite most text being right-to-left, users often need to switch keyboard layout to input email
addresses, logins, or passwords — which are usually written left-to-right.

Basic guidelines are as follows:

* Placeholders need to be aligned to the right;
* The text being input needs automatically to occupy the left or right-hand side of the field,
  depending on its direction;
* Text being input in fields for inputting a phone number or URL should always occupy the left-hand
  side of the field;
* Fields for inputting an email address should expect left-to-right text, but also be prepared for
  right-to-left text;
* Cursors in empty fields for inputting an email address, phone number, or URL should be left-aligned.

![A form with Name, Email, and Password fields, mirrored between LTR and RTL, with the Name field showing a name and the Email field being typed left-aligned](/assets/rtl/forms-rtl.png)

Once the input is focused and the user starts typing in an LTR language, the alignment will be flipped
to the left.

---

## RTL in a nutshell

**When a UI is mirrored, these changes occur:**

* Text field icons are displayed on the opposite side of a field;
* Navigation buttons are displayed in reverse order;
* Icons that communicate direction, like arrows, are mirrored;
* Icons that imply text direction are mirrored;
* Icons that imply the location of UI elements in the screen, like sidebars, also change;
* Text (if it is translated to an RTL language) is aligned to the right.

**Exception items that are not mirrored:**

* Icons containing text/numbers;
* Icons that don't communicate horizontal/diagonal direction;
* Numbers, such as those on a clock and phone numbers;
* Checkmark icons;
* Dashes in icons;
* Product logos;
* Charts and graphs;
* Order of size dimensions (e.g., 1920x1080 should not become 1080x1920);
* Order of size units (e.g., 10 px should not become px 10);
* Paths(e.g., C:\Users\username\Desktop);
* Full URLs;
* Usernames & passwords (most sites on the web expect LTR usernames/passwords, but there may be
  exceptions);
* Other text fields where only LTR text is expected.

---

## Next steps

These insights are just a starting point and need to be validated. Getting deep into a language and its
society will help understand the user's needs and present a better solution for them.

As a next step, a study is being prepared to validate and to clarify some specific use cases, through
usability testing and user interviews. This documentation will be updated, as soon as we get more
information.

---

## Useful links

**[Evaluate RTL on Cobalt](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COB/pages/2610922642/Evaluate+RTL+on+Cobalt)**
— Confluence documentation
