Cobalt Design System comes with its own color palette. Some colors are defined by the brand, others
are static.

## Theme

### Semantic colors

In code, each token is a CSS variable from the theme stylesheet (see [Develop](/get-started/develop/)):
`Colors.Primary.9` is `var(--primary-9)`, `Colors.Text.Default` is `var(--text-default)`. The tables below
give each token's variable.

#### Primary

The primary color is the most prominent color of Talkdesk interfaces. It establishes brand awareness
and must be used in the most important elements.

| Token                     | CSS variable         | Value   | Usage                                                |
| ------------------------- | -------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Colors.Primary.1`        | `--primary-1`        | #FCFCFF | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Primary.2`        | `--primary-2`        | #F9F8FF | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Primary.3`        | `--primary-3`        | #F2F0FF | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Primary.4`        | `--primary-4`        | #E8E4FF | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Primary.5`        | `--primary-5`        | #DED8FF | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Primary.6`        | `--primary-6`        | #D1C8FF | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Primary.7`        | `--primary-7`        | #BEB3FF | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Primary.8`        | `--primary-8`        | #A794FF | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Primary.9`        | `--primary-9`        | #5405BD | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Primary.10`       | `--primary-10`       | #4600A6 | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Primary.11`       | `--primary-11`       | #6A41D2 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Primary.12`       | `--primary-12`       | #331E6B | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Primary.contrast` | `--primary-contrast` | #FFFFFF | Used over shade 9                                    |

**Primary or Static Purple:** the primary brand color is variable and updates automatically with
future brand changes. If you want something to always be "purple," independent of brand, use the
static Purple color instead.

#### Secondary

The canvas of the UI — a neutral-based palette, leaving accents to the brand color. Mainly used for
components, interactive elements, and text.

| Token                       | CSS variable           | Value   | Usage                                                |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Colors.Secondary.1`        | `--secondary-1`        | #FCFCFD | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Secondary.2`        | `--secondary-2`        | #F8F9FA | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Secondary.3`        | `--secondary-3`        | #EEF0F2 | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Secondary.4`        | `--secondary-4`        | #E6E9EB | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Secondary.5`        | `--secondary-5`        | #DEE2E4 | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Secondary.6`        | `--secondary-6`        | #D6DADD | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Secondary.7`        | `--secondary-7`        | #CACFD3 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Secondary.8`        | `--secondary-8`        | #B7BCC1 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Secondary.9`        | `--secondary-9`        | #888E92 | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Secondary.10`       | `--secondary-10`       | #7E8387 | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Secondary.11`       | `--secondary-11`       | #5F6568 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Secondary.12`       | `--secondary-12`       | #1C2023 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Secondary.contrast` | `--secondary-contrast` | #FFFFFF | Used over shade 9                                    |

#### System colors

System colors stay unchanged regardless of brand, guaranteeing product consistency. They're widespread
and important, but — unlike Primary — don't represent an identity.

**Error** — communicates a dangerous consequence or an error.

| Token                   | CSS variable       | Value   | Usage                                                |
| ----------------------- | ------------------ | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Colors.Error.1`        | `--error-1`        | #FFFCFC | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Error.2`        | `--error-2`        | #FFF8F7 | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Error.3`        | `--error-3`        | #FFEBE8 | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Error.4`        | `--error-4`        | #FFDBD4 | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Error.5`        | `--error-5`        | #FFCDC4 | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Error.6`        | `--error-6`        | #FFBDB2 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Error.7`        | `--error-7`        | #F7A89C | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Error.8`        | `--error-8`        | #EE8D7F | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Error.9`        | `--error-9`        | #DB362A | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Error.10`       | `--error-10`       | #CC2018 | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Error.11`       | `--error-11`       | #D22B21 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Error.12`       | `--error-12`       | #621F18 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Error.contrast` | `--error-contrast` | #FFFFFF | Used over shade 9                                    |

**Success** — communicates a positive consequence or success.

| Token                     | CSS variable         | Value   | Usage                                                |
| ------------------------- | -------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Colors.Success.1`        | `--success-1`        | #FBFEFC | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Success.2`        | `--success-2`        | #F4FBF6 | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Success.3`        | `--success-3`        | #E6F6EB | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Success.4`        | `--success-4`        | #D6F1DF | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Success.5`        | `--success-5`        | #C4E8D0 | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Success.6`        | `--success-6`        | #AEDDBF | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Success.7`        | `--success-7`        | #90CEA7 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Success.8`        | `--success-8`        | #61B885 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Success.9`        | `--success-9`        | #00874F | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Success.10`       | `--success-10`       | #007942 | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Success.11`       | `--success-11`       | #00814A | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Success.12`       | `--success-12`       | #1D3B29 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Success.contrast` | `--success-contrast` | #FFFFFF | Used over shade 9                                    |

**Warning** — communicates a possible, non-critical, dangerous consequence.

| Token                     | CSS variable         | Value   | Usage                                                |
| ------------------------- | -------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Colors.Warning.1`        | `--warning-1`        | #FEFDFB | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Warning.2`        | `--warning-2`        | #FFF9E7 | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Warning.3`        | `--warning-3`        | #FFF1C4 | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Warning.4`        | `--warning-4`        | #FFE7AC | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Warning.5`        | `--warning-5`        | #FFDC8E | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Warning.6`        | `--warning-6`        | #FFCC61 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Warning.7`        | `--warning-7`        | #F7BB52 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Warning.8`        | `--warning-8`        | #E7A200 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Warning.9`        | `--warning-9`        | #EDA813 | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Warning.10`       | `--warning-10`       | #E29D00 | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Warning.11`       | `--warning-11`       | #A26A00 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Warning.12`       | `--warning-12`       | #4B3718 | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Warning.contrast` | `--warning-contrast` | #2C1F09 | Used over shade 9                                    |

**Information** — communicates informative content.

| Token                  | CSS variable      | Value   | Usage                                                |
| ---------------------- | ----------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Colors.Info.1`        | `--info-1`        | #FDFDFE | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Info.2`        | `--info-2`        | #F6FAFF | Backgrounds                                          |
| `Colors.Info.3`        | `--info-3`        | #ECF2FF | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Info.4`        | `--info-4`        | #DDEAFF | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Info.5`        | `--info-5`        | #CCE0FF | Interactive elements and states                      |
| `Colors.Info.6`        | `--info-6`        | #B8D3FF | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Info.7`        | `--info-7`        | #A0C0FC | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Info.8`        | `--info-8`        | #7FA7F3 | Borders and separators                               |
| `Colors.Info.9`        | `--info-9`        | #003FBD | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Info.10`       | `--info-10`       | #002BAA | Solid — buttons, toasts, messages, large UI graphics |
| `Colors.Info.11`       | `--info-11`       | #275DCC | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Info.12`       | `--info-12`       | #162E5E | Accessible text over shades 1–2                      |
| `Colors.Info.contrast` | `--info-contrast` | #FFFFFF | Used over shade 9                                    |

Use system colors (Error/Success/Warning, etc.) to indicate status rather than their static
equivalents — since these can be adapted per theme in the future and your product updates
automatically. Static colors ("green", "yellow", "red") are for things that must always be that color
regardless of theme — e.g. a REC button should always be red, so use the static Red rather than the
semantic Error color.

### Static colors

Static colors never change, no matter which brand is applied — useful when you want a color's meaning
to be independent of the active theme's semantic mapping (e.g. a static Red guarantees "red" even if a
theme redefines what "Error" means visually). Each system color has its own static version.

In code, a static color's shades are CSS variables named after the palette: `--blue-1` to `--blue-12`, and
the same for green, neutral, orange, purple, red, teal, yellow and gray.

| Palette                                                     | 1 (bg)  | 9 (solid) | 11 (text) |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | --------- | --------- |
| Blue                                                        | #FDFDFE | #003FBD   | #275DCC   |
| Green                                                       | #FBFEFC | #00874F   | #00814A   |
| Neutral *(primitive behind Secondary — don't use directly)* | #FCFCFD | #888E92   | #5F6568   |
| Orange                                                      | #FEFCFB | #FF6300   | #D94300   |
| Purple                                                      | #FCFCFF | #5405BD   | #6A41D2   |
| Red                                                         | #FFFCFC | #DB362A   | #D22B21   |
| Teal                                                        | #FAFDFE | #4BC4C9   | #008085   |
| Yellow                                                      | #FEFDFB | #EDA813   | #A26A00   |
| Gray                                                        | #FBFCFD | #898E93   | #606569   |

**Gray or Secondary?** The Neutral primitive should never be used directly — it only backs the
Secondary semantic. Use **Gray** for non-interactive elements (text, dividers); use **Secondary** for
interactive elements (buttons) and/or when color needs semantic connotation (e.g. tags).

### Background and surfaces

**Background colors** — a `background-color` variable translates automatically between light (`#FFFFFF`)
and dark (`#1A1A1A`, not full black) mode.

**Surface background colors** — introduced for Dark theme, since shadows aren't "inverted" in dark mode
the way borders/surfaces need distinguishing:

* `surface-elevation-1` — maps to `background-color` (light) / `neutral-2` (dark). E.g. a side panel or
  popup/card sitting above the main content.
* `surface-elevation-2` — maps to `background-color` (light) / `neutral-3` (dark). For a surface above
  `surface-elevation-1` — e.g. a dropdown opened from within a side panel.
* `surface-elevation-3` — maps to `background-color` (light) / `neutral-4` (dark). An extra overlap
  level, rarely used — e.g. a dropdown opened from a card that's already inside a panel.

### Text variables

Theme-level text variables ensure accessibility over `background-color`:

* `text-default` — regular text color.
* `text-description` — descriptions, hints, supporting text.
* `text-placeholder` — placeholders on a field that has its own label. If a component has no label at
  all (e.g. a toolbar search with only a placeholder), use `text-description` instead — a
  placeholder-only color doesn't pass contrast, a recognized exception, so the description color is
  used instead in that specific case.
* `text-error`, `text-warning`, `text-success`, `text-info` — for text conveying that specific state.

### Helper colors

Helper colors exist only for documentation purposes in Figma.

### Library

**Color tokens** — the color libraries are available on Figma.

## Dark theme

In dark mode, our variables change automatically. The overall visual creates a darker color palette
for all screens, views, menus, and controls, and it uses more vibrancy to make foreground content
stand out against the darker backgrounds.

Dark themes reduce the luminance emitted by device screens, while still meeting minimum color
contrast ratios — some people with visual impairments do better with dark mode (in users with normal
vision, light mode leads to better performance most of the time). Another advantage is facilitating
screen use in dark environments and improving visual ergonomics by reducing eye strain, preventing
long-term effects associated with light mode.

In dark mode, there are two sets of background colors — called **base** and **elevated** — to enhance
the perception of depth when one dark interface is layered above another. The base colors are darker,
making background interfaces appear to recede; the elevated colors are lighter, making foreground
interfaces appear to advance.

:::note
The mobile dark-color guidelines below don't follow the current updated color algorithm.
:::

Dark theme UIs use predominantly dark surfaces, with sparse color accents. They emit low levels of
light while maintaining a high standard of usability.

For mobile, the background color is always `#000000` so that content can vary, with enough contrast,
against the other 3 main dark colors (Dark 300, 200, 100) — the rule being that the higher a
surface's elevation (raising it closer to an implied light source), the lighter that surface becomes.

Complementary gray colors can be used in rare cases where the main dark colors don't work well — for
example, intersecting or overlapping elements such as lines or bars in a grid.

## Accessibility

### Color contrast

Color contrast is an essential aspect of accessibility. Good contrast makes it easier for people with
visual impairments and helps in poor conditions like low-light environments or older screens.

Contrast ratios represent how different one color is from another; they range from 1 to 21 (commonly
written 1:1 to 21:1). The greater the difference between the two numbers in the ratio, the greater the
difference in relative luminance between the colors.

We are committed to complying with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines AA standard contrast
ratios and Section 508, which sets a legal standard for the contrast level between text and its
background. The exception is brand logos, which do not have to meet color contrast requirements.

**Recommended contrast ratios (Level AA)**

| Element type  | Contrast ratio                                                                                                      |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Standard text | 4.5:1 against the background                                                                                        |
| Large text    | 3:1 against the background — defined as 18pt (typically 24px) or larger, or bold 14pt (typically 18.66px) or larger |

If you choose colors beyond what is documented here, a color contrast tool is a helpful resource to
test color combinations, or use a Figma plugin such as Contrast, A11y - Color Contrast Checker, Low
Vision, or Stark.

It's also important to ensure graphical icons provide enough contrast: when choosing colors for an
icon, consider the color(s) next to it and test that the contrast ratio is at least 4.5:1.

### Color blindness

Color-blindness (color vision deficiency) is the inability to distinguish certain shades of color.
The most common types are protanomaly (reduced sensitivity to red light), deuteranomaly (reduced
sensitivity to green light), and tritanomaly (reduced sensitivity to blue light).

Relying solely on color for readability and affordance makes a website difficult to use, which
ultimately affects readership and sales. This includes conveying information, indicating an action,
prompting the user for a response, or distinguishing one visual element from another — for example, a
text field's error state should be communicated through multiple cues, not just a colored stroke.
Use a color blindness simulator to analyze how different types of color blindness affect an image.

**Useful tools:** a color contrast checker (to calculate the contrast between two colors) and Color
Oracle (to simulate how a colorblind person sees colors).

## Color usage

The following components are affected by color usage: Tag, Avatar, LabeledIcon, Mark, ProgressBar,
ChatBubble. Some other components have color usage associated but can't be applied in a non-semantic
context, so they follow their own specific guidelines.

### Semantic vs. non-semantic

**Semantic** — color applied with a consistent meaning keeps cognitive load low and creates a unified,
engaging experience:

* Brand — e.g. new, brand product
* Warning — e.g. pending, on hold, processing, close to limit
* Negative — e.g. error, alert, rejected, failed
* Positive — e.g. approved, complete, success, new, purchased, licensed
* Informative — e.g. active, in use, live, published
* Neutral — e.g. archived, deleted, paused, draft, not started, ended, N/A

Semantic color helps users identify a standard status quickly and simply — avoid misusing semantic
opportunities in status categories, since it must stay as clear as possible for the user.

**Non-semantic** — colors used to indicate conventional meaning for color-coded categories and
customization settings (e.g. Purple for Healthcare/support, Yellow for Sales/dedicated, Red for
Marketing/VIP customers, Green for Digital connect/chat, Blue for Agent, Gray for Call center, White
for order issues, plus Orange/Teal/Midnight for other categories). White tags can be used the same way
as gray tags, or when the layout's color logic needs to be "inverted" for darker backgrounds.

Use the same background color for related items and let the content's color differentiate individual
items — avoid multiple background-colored avatars in the same list (for a contacts list, prefer
light-primary).

### Emphasis level

Color can also be chosen based on the emphasis needed:

* **Default** — bold emphasis, best isolated to highlight a specific element (e.g. "New").
* **Light** — subtle emphasis, can be applied across items in the same category or group (e.g. ring
  groups).

Keep the same emphasis level within a category or group for consistency, and reserve stronger,
isolated emphasis for highlighting a single element — mixing emphasis levels within the UI, or across
categories, causes confusion. Exception: when a tag is used to indicate more tags are available (a
"+N" tag), always emphasize it — don't invert the emphasis or change its main (Primary) color in that
case.

narrative.markdown:
The Grid is the geometric foundation of all the visual elements, from typography to columns, boxes,
icons, and illustrations. It provides structure and guidance for all creative decision-making.

## Baseline Grid

We use a **4px** baseline grid to help achieve the vertical rhythm of elements throughout a page.

This means that everything will be a multiple of 4 (0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, and so on). The result is a
subconscious recognition of balance and congruity.

![Text with 4px baseline grid](/assets/grid/baseline-grid-text.png)

Always try to align objects on the 8px grid, but where necessary, use good judgment to fine-tune your
designs to 4px.

The 4px baseline is there allows more flexibility for line heights and smaller adjustments.

![Example of the 4px baseline grid](/assets/grid/baseline-grid-example.png)

---

## Anatomy

![Anatomy of the MainApp grid, numbered 1 through 9](/assets/grid/anatomy.png)

1. **Title bar**
2. **Dock**
3. **Drawer**
4. **MainApp container with Inner Padding,** fixed values based on the viewport
5. **Column,** the number of columns is based on the viewport
6. **Gutter,** fixed values based on the viewport
7. **First container**
8. **Second container**
9. **Secondary Area**

The amount of columns is based on the viewport:

* Small, from 424 to 640px, 4 columns
* Medium, from 641 to 960px, 8 columns
* Large, from 961 to 1440px, 12 columns
* XLarge, from 1441px ou 1601px, 12 columns

Gutters are fixed values based on the viewport:

* Small, from 424 to 640px, gutters width is 12px
* Medium, from 641 to 960px, gutters width is 16px
* Large, from 961 to 1440px, gutters width is 24px
* XLarge, from 1441px ou 1601px, gutters width is 24px

---

## MainApp container grid types

### Fluid

In fluid grids, column widths are dynamic, dependent on the main app width.

![Fluid grid diagram](/assets/grid/fluid.png)

![Fluid grid applied to a real product screen](/assets/grid/fluid-example.png)

#### Responsiveness

![Fluid grid, small viewport](/assets/grid/fluid-small.png)
*Small*

![Fluid grid, medium viewport](/assets/grid/fluid-medium.png)
*Medium*

![Fluid grid, large viewport](/assets/grid/fluid-large.png)
*Large*

![Fluid grid, xlarge viewport](/assets/grid/fluid-xlarge.png)
*XLarge*

Columns width in fluid grid types should be defined in percentage and calculated as, if
MainAppViewportWidth is L=1440px, M=860px, S=434px:

**4/4 column width** = 100% —
**4/4 column width** = 100% —

**3/4 column width**,

* `L = ((100%-(24\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth)\*3)/4)\*3`

* `M = ((100%-(16\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth)\*3)/4)\*3`

* `S = ((100%-(12\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth)\*3)/4)\*3`

  —

  **3/4 column width**,

* `L = ((100%-(24\*100%/1440)\*3)/4)\*3 = 71,25%`

* `M = ((100%-(16\*100%/860)\*3)/4)\*3 = 70,81%`

* `S = ((100%-(12\*100%/434)\*3)/4)\*3 = 68,78%`

  —

  **2/4 column width**,

* `L = (100%-(24\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth))/2`

* `M = (100%-(16\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth))/2`

* `S = (100%-(12\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth))/2`

  —

  **2/4 column width**,

* `L = (100%-(24\*100%/1440))/2 = 49,17%`

* `M = (100%-(16\*100%/860))/2 = 49,07%`

* `S = (100%-(12\*100%/434))/2 = 48,62%`

  —

  **1/4 column width**,

* `L = (100%-(24\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth)\*3)/4`

* `M = (100%-(16\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth)\*3)/4`

* `S = (100%-(12\*100%/MainAppViewportWidth)\*3)/4`

  —

  **1/4 column width**,

* `L = (100%-(24\*100%/1440)\*3)/4 = 23,75%`

* `M = (100%-(16\*100%/860)\*3)/4 = 23,60%`

* `S = (100%-(12\*100%/434)\*3)/4 = 22,93%`

  —

### Fixed

Fixed grids have a max width.

The max width can be applied only for large viewports or for each viewport.

![Fixed grid diagram](/assets/grid/fixed.png)

![Fixed grid applied to a real product screen](/assets/grid/fixed-example.png)

#### Responsiveness

![Fixed grid, small viewport](/assets/grid/fixed-small.png)
*Small*

*Medium*

![Fixed grid, large viewport](/assets/grid/fixed-large.png)
*Large*

![Fixed grid, xlarge viewport](/assets/grid/fixed-xlarge.png)
*XLarge*

Each container has its own scroll.

## Push panels

Layouts can have one or two push panels with fixed widths that push the content, influencing its grid.
We suggest using push panels only for [one container grid](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/582820-grid/t/156f31).

Push panels paddings and gutters should follow the viewport padding.

* Small, from 424 to 640px, paddings and gutters value is 12px
* Medium, from 641 to 960px, paddings and gutters value is 16px
* Large, from 961 to 1440px, paddings and gutters value is 24px
* XLarge, from 1441px ou 1601px, paddings and gutters value is 24px

Push panels can be closed and their width will be 60px.

The push panel is usually small size.

For main app widths below 1041px the push panels, when open, will overlap the main app container.

For main app widths below 1237px, the push panels cannot be opened simultaneously.

Each push panel has its own scroll.

narrative.markdown:
:::note
Sourced from the live Cobalt DS's Assets > Icons page and its App Icons / Feature Icons / Icons /
Guidelines / How to add a new icon tabs. The asset browsers themselves (live, filterable icon
galleries) aren't reproduced here — these sections carry the surrounding guidance only.
:::

Icons are a symbol or image-based visual representation of commands or common actions, used to
provide visual context and improve user experience.

## App Icons

Must be used only in the dock, to identify a product, and should not be reused for different
meanings. Organized in the asset library as `Cobalt Design System / Assets / Icons / App Icons /
app_(icon_name)`. Creation is owned by the Creative Team — request one by following the
[guidelines below](#how-to-add-a-new-icon).

## Feature Icons

Can be used in different components, but only to identify a feature — they can be reused for
different meanings as long as they stay related to the same feature. Organized as `Cobalt Design
System / Assets / Icons / Feature Icons / (feature_group) / feature_(icon_name)`. Creation is also
owned by the Creative Team.

## Icons

Can be used in different components and contexts/actions, and can carry different meanings. Organized
as `Cobalt Design System / Assets / Icons / (icon_group) / (icon_name)`. Unlike App and Feature icons,
these are created by Product Design following the guidelines below.

In code, an icon is drawn by core Icon with its name: `<Icon name="refresh" />`. Every name it accepts:

Every icon name is listed as the `name` prop of [Icon](/ai-docs/components/core/icon/icon.md).

## Guidelines

### Categorization

Icons are categorized into 3 categories: **App Icons**, **Feature Icons** and **Icons.**

| Category         | App Icons                                                                                                                   | Feature Icons                                                                                                               | Icons                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Usage**        | Must be used only in the dock                                                                                               | Can be used in different components                                                                                         | Can be used in different components                                                                                       |
| **Context**      | Must be used only to identify a product                                                                                     | Must be used only to identify a feature                                                                                     | Can be used in different contexts/actions                                                                                 |
| **Meaning**      | Should not be used for different meanings                                                                                   | Can be used for different meanings but always related with the same feature                                                 | Can have different meanings                                                                                               |
| **Organization** | Cobalt Design System / Assets / Icons / App Icons / app\_(icon\_name)                                                       | Cobalt Design System / Assets / Icons / Feature Icons / (feature\_group) / feature\_(icon\_name)                            | Cobalt Design System / Assets / Icons / (icon\_group) / (icon\_name)                                                      |
| **Creation**     | Creative Team. Request by following [these guidelines](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/32d352-icons/b/18b165) | Creative Team. Request by following [these guidelines](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/32d352-icons/b/18b165) | Product Design following [these guidelines](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/32d352-icons/b/18b165/t/2271cb) |

*An illustrative screenshot normally appears here on ZeroHeight but is not reproduced — it showed
fictional full names paired with phone numbers in a "Recent activities" style table. See the data-handling
note at the top of this file.
[View on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/32d352-icons/b/166599).*

---

### Sizing

Icons size uses a 4px baseline grid, the sizes most used are 16px, 20px, 24px and 48px. Make sure that
the icon size is consistent throughout your product.

![Icon size scale showing 12px, 16px, 20px, 24px, 32px, 48px, and 64px icon examples](/assets/iconography/icon-sizes.png)

---

### Usage

Icons with 20px size are used in form elements (`<input>`, `<button>`, etc.)

![Search toolbar using 20px icons for search, sort options, table options, and filters](/assets/iconography/usage-20px-search.png)

The default size (24px) is used on toasts, media controls, and other elements.

![Media player toolbar using 24px icons for play, volume, and skip controls, and a 24px icon in an error toast message](/assets/iconography/usage-24px-media-controls.png)

We use the major icons in alert dialogs and empty states.

![Empty state message using a 48px major icon above a title, description, and Secondary/Primary buttons](/assets/iconography/usage-48px-major-icon.png)

---

### Color

Icons are always a solid, monochromatic color and need to pass the same color contrast ratio as
typography (4.5:1).

For more information, see the
[color accessibility guidelines](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/01309d-colors/b/86f3da).

---

### Alignment

When used next to text, icons should be center-aligned.

![Do — a plus icon center-aligned to the 'Add another row' text](/assets/iconography/alignment-do.png)
*Do Center-align icons when they're next to text.*

![Don't — a plus icon baseline-aligned to the 'Add another row' text](/assets/iconography/alignment-dont.png)
*Don't Don't baseline-align icons to the text.*

---

### Principles

#### Simple over detailed

Limit the creation of icon variations. Different icons should not represent the same concept (e.g.
"admin settings" vs. "user settings")

![Do — a simple upload icon with clean, minimal lines](/assets/iconography/simple-over-detailed-do.png)
*Do Icons should have simple lines and shapes.*

![Don't — an export icon with finer, more detailed linework](/assets/iconography/simple-over-detailed-dont.png)
*Don't Icons should not be too heavy in details, this increases cognitive load on the user.*

#### Clear over conceptual

* Don't reinvent an icon that's already been accepted as a convention.
* Users should be able to understand what the icon represents.
* Interpreting abstract (symbolic) icons can take more time and effort.

#### Family over friends

Users should be able to understand what the icon represents. Interpreting abstract (symbolic) icons can
take more time and effort.

![Do — upload, download, new folder, and cloud icons sharing a consistent filled style](/assets/iconography/family-over-friends-do.png)
*Do The icon set needs to look and feel related.*

![Don't — the same 4 icons mixing inconsistent outline and filled styles](/assets/iconography/family-over-friends-dont.png)
*Don't Icons that aren't related may look out of place.*

---

### Accessibility

#### Specify if an icon is decorative

Icons can either be **decorative** or **informative**. With a decorative icon, it's unnecessary to
inform the user about its existence on the page.

For example, the information provided by the icon might already be given using adjacent text.

#### Give informative icons a title

If an icon isn't decorative, you must provide a title property, so assistive technology can infer equal
meaning as a sighted user would. **To fix this, add an aria-label or the alt attribute if it is an
image.**

![Do — a bell icon with an accessible title of 'notifications'](/assets/iconography/informative-title-do.png)
*Do Provide meaningful information.*

![Don't — the same bell icon with a generic accessible title of 'bell'](/assets/iconography/informative-title-dont.png)
*Don't Don't use generic titles.*

#### Pair icons with text

The combination of icons and a corresponding label helps everyone: people with mental impairments, the
elderly who aren't "internet natives", and even yourself.

![Do — an 'Add event' button pairing a plus icon with a text label](/assets/iconography/pair-icons-with-text-do.png)
*Do*

![Don't — a bare plus icon with no text label](/assets/iconography/pair-icons-with-text-dont.png)
*Don't*

In case you have to use an icon without a label, always provide a tooltip.

*An example screenshot normally appears here on ZeroHeight but is not reproduced — it showed fictional
full names paired with phone numbers in a call-list UI. See the data-handling note at the top of this
file.
[View on ZeroHeight](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/32d352-icons/b/166599).*

---

## How to add a new icon

### Adding a new App icon or Feature icon

1. **Icon category** — review the Icons Categorization board to confirm the new icon complies with
   all guidelines.
2. **Open Cobalt Style** — open the Cobalt Assets library file, or search for App Icons or Feature
   Icons.
3. **Review current icons** — search for the icon; if it's already there, no need to add it.
4. **Request to the Creative Team** — App Icons and Feature Icons must always be created by the
   Creative Team.
5. **Add the icon to the Design System** — once the SVG is available, create a Figma branch in the
   Assets file, adjust the SVG (flatten the color layer), match the needed properties (24×24 bounding
   box, 20×20 inner layer), paste-to-replace into a duplicated icon, rename it following the naming
   convention (lowercase, underscores; e.g. `action/account_balance_wallet` for regular icons,
   `agent_actions/feature_assign_agent_pool` for feature icons — must include "feature" in the name —
   and `app_conversation`-style names with no folder for app icons), match constraints (frame
   Left/Top, color layer Scale/Scale), convert to a component, and have the Design System team review
   the branch.
6. **Add the icon to the Cobalt Assets library** — coordinate in the design and engineering SME
   channels to get it added.

### Adding a new general icon

1. Check the Cobalt Assets library / Icons page — if the icon already exists, stop here.
2. Look for it in Material Symbols and Icons (Google Fonts) or Material Design Icons, in that order.
3. If found, export as SVG, add it as a Figma symbol, categorize/rename it per the Icons
   Categorization board, keep the Material icon settings (Weight 400, Grade 0, Optical size 24px,
   style Material Symbols (New) - Outlined), reduce it to a simple path, and fill it with the
   Gray/gray-12 color variable.
4. If not found, decide whether it can be a **composed icon or variant** of an existing icon (define
   identification/meaning/context, search for reference patterns, prototype, and request review) or
   needs to be **created from scratch** (same identification/meaning/context and reference-search
   process, then request review) — in both cases, coordinate through the design-private and
   eng-sme-cobalt channels before it's added to the library.

---

narrative.markdown:
:::note
Sourced from the live Cobalt DS's Design Tokens > Introduction page.
:::

Learn more about the concept of design tokens with all the values needed to construct and maintain
our design system.

## What does Design tokens mean?

Let's say a brand has a Primary Pink color. Designers and developers should refer to this color by
the same name and identity, regardless of platform (design, web, mobile etc). If the color changes
in design, it should also change on all development platforms automatically (and vice versa).

Design tokens enable this behavior by creating an abstract identity and centralizing the source of
truth for this color. Because they help to establish a source of truth, they are often found in
design systems. They can be used for colors, text styles, spacings, animation values etc.

Design tokens work as design atoms of the design system — specifically, they are named entities that
store visual design attributes.

We are talking about typography, color, spacing, shadow, and more represented as data. They are
directly integrated into our component libraries and can represent anything defined by design: a
color as a hex value, an opacity as a percent, etc. Tokens replace static values, used in place of
hard-coded values in order to ensure flexibility and a consistent visual system for UI development.

A Cobalt token consists of:

* A code-like name, such as `primary-600`
* An associated value, such as `#3E048B`
* A symbol (`$`) to represent the token

So our token is represented as `$primary-600` and every time a designer and/or an engineer try to
implement this color, they will both reference the same token called this primary color, then design
and engineering can be confident that the same color will be used in both places. This consistency
remains in place even when the color value assigned to a token gets updated.

## Why are they important?

Design Tokens provide a design system with a single source of truth. They enable a consistency path
through the entire products at Talkdesk.

They are reusable and can be as generic as possible in order to supply different scenarios and
contexts. This also provide the design system evolution, because even if we change some values of our
styles considering future changes, we can keep the nomenclature and ensure ongoing consistency across
experiences.

## Where to find

* **Design tokens** — check our library on Figma
* **Color tokens** — color styles and palettes
* **Typography tokens** — text styles and more
* **Spacing & more** — spacing, border, opacity and shadow

## Further reading

* [Tokens in Design Systems — Nathan Curtis](https://medium.com/eightshapes-llc/tokens-in-design-systems-25dd82d58421)
* Using design tokens to promote collaboration and maintainability of a design system
* An example of design tokens in a live design system — Lightning Design System

:::note
This page corresponds to the live Cobalt DS's Design Tokens > **Shadow** page — renamed to "Elevation"
here to match this design system's token category naming.
:::

Shadows create a visual hierarchy and impression of depth to convey proximity and prominence to the
user. Use shadows to highlight differences in elevation between two components.

## Appearance and usage

Shadows provide important visual cues about objects' depth and directional movement. They are the
only visual cue showing the amount of separation between surfaces.

There are two types of lights: **key lights** and **ambient lights**. Key lights create sharper,
directional shadows, which are called key shadows. Ambient light appears from all angles so they
create soft shadows, called ambient shadows.

Because shadows express the degree of elevation between surfaces, they must be used consistently
throughout our products. Use the below defined tokens to set shadows consistently.

![Level 1: (X: 0px, Y: 2px, B: 4px) + (X: 0px, Y: 4px, B: 8px)](/assets/shadow/level-1.png)
*$shadow-level-1*

![Level 2: (X: 0px, Y: 4px, B: 8px) + (X: 0px, Y: 8px, B: 16px)](/assets/shadow/level-2.png)
*$shadow-level-2*

![Level 3: (X: 0px, Y: 8px, B: 16px) + (X: 0px, Y: 16px, B: 32px)](/assets/shadow/level-3.png)
*$shadow-level-3*

![Level 4: (X: 0px, Y: 12px, B: 16px) + (X: 0px, Y: 24px, B: 32px)](/assets/shadow/level-4.png)
*$shadow-level-4*

## Scrollable shadows

Scroll shadows are when you can see a little inset shadow on elements if (and only if) you can
scroll in that direction. Most used on Forms, Panels and Modals.

![Example applied on modal: a modal with a scroll shadow at the bottom of its scrollable body](/assets/shadow/example-applied-on-modal.png)

narrative.markdown:
Learn about small pieces that standardize the composition of interfaces providing rules to give your
designs a consistent rhythm, constrain decision making, and help teams stay aligned.

## Guidelines

The purpose of this document is to gather all the spacing rules for different contexts (on a page, on
a panel, on a modal…). The goal is to make it easy for everyone to check if they are applying the
correct spacings.

### General rules

Each viewport has a default spacing that is generally followed by most components.

| Large Viewports | Medium viewports | Small viewports |
| --------------- | ---------------- | --------------- |
| **L**: 24px     | **M**: 16px      | **S**: 12px     |

For example, this means that a **Card** will have different inner paddings if seen on screens with
different sizes.

## Spacing specs

Spacing tokens are used to consistently apply margin and padding across elements, components and
layouts. With a set scale for spacing, information can be structured to have a consistent and
intuitive user interface across the website.

### Types

#### Core

![Nano spacing token, $spacing-nano, 4px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-nano.png)

![Micro spacing token, $spacing-micro, 8px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-micro.png)

![XSmall spacing token, $spacing-xsmall, 12px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-xsmall.png)

![Small spacing token, $spacing-small, 16px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-small.png)

![Medium spacing token, $spacing-medium, 20px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-medium.png)

![Large spacing token, $spacing-large, 24px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-large.png)

![XLarge spacing token, $spacing-xlarge, 32px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-xlarge.png)

![Mega spacing token, $spacing-mega, 40px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-mega.png)

![XMega spacing token, $spacing-xmega, 48px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-xmega.png)

![Giga spacing token, $spacing-giga, 56px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-giga.png)

![XGiga spacing token, $spacing-xgiga, 64px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-xgiga.png)

![Tera spacing token, $spacing-tera, 80px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-tera.png)

![XTera spacing token, $spacing-xtera, 120px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-xtera.png)

#### Inset

Internal spacings (paddings) of a component where all values are exactly the same. Padding is the
space around the content inside a container. This spacing does not affect the total dimension of an
element, but rather shrinks the working space within it.

![Inset Nano spacing token, $spacing-inset-nano, V: 4px, H: 4px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-nano.png)

![Inset Micro spacing token, $spacing-inset-micro, V: 8px, H: 8px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-micro.png)

![Inset XSmall spacing token, $spacing-inset-xsmall, V: 12px, H: 12px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-xsmall.png)

![Inset Small spacing token, $spacing-inset-small, V: 16px, H: 16px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-small.png)

![Inset Medium spacing token, $spacing-inset-medium, V: 20px, H: 20px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-medium.png)

![Inset Large spacing token, $spacing-inset-large, V: 24px, H: 24px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-large.png)

![Inset XLarge spacing token, $spacing-inset-xlarge, V: 32px, H: 32px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-xlarge.png)

![Inset Mega spacing token, $spacing-inset-mega, V: 40px, H: 40px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-mega.png)

![Inset XMega spacing token, $spacing-inset-xmega, V: 48px, H: 48px](/assets/spacing-specs/token-inset-xmega.png)

### Usage

#### When to use

* Whenever you need to space out the inner parts within a component
* Whenever you need to space out one component from another or other elements outside of a component

#### When not to use

Don't use it when you need responsive spacing because the tokens provided are fixed values.

### Do's & Don'ts

**Do:** Always use spacing tokens when spacing out element (either margin or padding).

**Don't:** Avoid going outside the provided spacing tokens and try not to stack the spacing tokens (e.g. 16px + 20px).

### Library

**[Spacing & more](https://www.figma.com/file/wFqyJnLISAbPa0Si9UBTP9/1%29-%F0%9F%A7%AA-Design-Tokens?node-id=6%3A600)**
— Specs for spacing, border, opacity and shadow.

Typography is used to create clear hierarchies, useful organizations, and purposeful alignments that
guide users through the product and experience. It is the core guidance of any well-designed
interface.

## Font

### Font-family

#### Roboto

Roboto has a dual nature. It has a mechanical skeleton and the forms are largely geometric. At the
same time, the font features friendly and open curves. While some grotesks distort their letterforms
to force a rigid rhythm, Roboto doesn't compromise, allowing letters to be settled into their natural
width. This makes for a more natural reading rhythm more commonly found in humanist and serif types.

#### Roboto Mono

We can also count with the **Roboto Mono** family to contextual scenarios like a visual distinct need
on a ChatBubble message, for example.

![$font-family-base token: Aa - Base, Roboto](/assets/typography-font/font-family-base.png)

![$font-family-mono token: Aa - Mono, Roboto Mono](/assets/typography-font/font-family-mono.png)

* **[Roboto](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Roboto)** — Download Google font
* **[Roboto mono](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Roboto+Mono?query=roboto+mono)** — Download Google font

**[Typography tokens](https://www.figma.com/file/wFqyJnLISAbPa0Si9UBTP9/Design-Tokens?node-id=0%3A1)**
— You can find our typography specs on Figma

## Scale

There are **six primary types of headings** available through the standard header HTML tags.
Remember to use a logical tree of headings to maintain a hierarchy of information and accessibility.

![Heading scale (H1–H6) compared across Large, Medium and Small viewports, with pixel/rem sizes for each level](/assets/typography-scale/scale-heading-scale.png)

### Content

#### Paragraph

To use when you need a distinct section of a piece of writing with essential element of running text.

#### Microcopy

To use when you need very tiny content. These short sentences tell a user what to do, address user
concerns, providing context to a situation.

![Paragraph and Microcopy type styles compared across Regular, Italic, Medium and Monospaced variants](/assets/typography-scale/scale-content-paragraph-microcopy.png)

### Responsiveness

Regarding responsiveness, the headings should change according to the resize of the viewport, while
the paragraphs and microcopy should stay with the same font size.

## Accessibility

### Headings

Headings play a vital role in the accessibility level of any document, whether it is a Word, PDF, or
HTML document. They are used for navigation by screen reader users and they provide a clear structure
of a document which benefits all users, making it easier to scan through the content.

#### WCAG 2.0 references

* [1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG20/quickref/#content-structure-separation-sequence)
* [2.4.6 Headings and Labels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG20/quickref/?showtechniques=128%2C14\&currentsidebar=%23col_overview#navigation-mechanisms-descriptive)

#### Steps to take

* Plan heading structure early. Ensure all content and design fits into a logical heading structure.
* Consider reading order. The reading order should be the same as the visual order.

### Legibility

Legibility refers to how easy it is for the reader to decode and differentiate individual letters in
a word.

#### Type Colors

Good quality of contrast between the background and font color is essential to ensuring the
legibility of the content. To learn more about color, contrast, and accessibility design, read
[Colors - Accessibility](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/49728f-color/b/11e5b9).

Color also plays a key role in an interface's typographic hierarchy. Below we can see the established
types.

### Usage

#### Styles

Keeping typography consistent and sticking to logical hierarchies ensures that elements in the UI are
clear and easily recognizable when scanning the page.

#### Formatting

Formatting can be added to the text to call attention, add emphasis, and enhance the meaning of
important content.

### Readability

Readability is about arranging words and groups of words in a way that allows the reader's eye to
access the content easily and in a way that makes sense.

#### Line Height

The line-height values need to be always divisible by 4 so they can support a vertical grid (see
[Spacings](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/764e98-spacing--more)).

#### Line Length

A proper length for lines of text is key to the readability of the text. Long lines of text tire a
reader's eyes, and make it difficult for the reader to properly track back and find the start of the
next line. Short lines interrupt the readers too often, preventing them from establishing a flow.

![Line length - Desktop: too narrow, ideal range (45-80 characters), and too wide examples](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-line-length-desktop.png)
*Line length - Desktop*

![Line length - Mobile: too narrow, ideal range (35-40 characters), and too wide examples](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-line-length-mobile.png)
*Line length - Mobile*

While there is no right way to measure the perfect width for text, a good goal is to aim for between
45 and 80 characters per line including spacing. Setting an optimal line length will break up content
into easily digestible information.

For mobile, is a good choice to keep the number of characters per line within 35–40.

#### Type alignment

By default, the text is left-aligned. Exceptions to this rule include text in tables, the centered
text we use in empty states and some writing system like Arabic and Hebrew, are displayed with
characters appearing from
[right to left](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/57a480-right-to-left).

**Do:** All text should be left-aligned whenever possible.

**Don't:** Never left and right justify text.

#### Capitalization

By default, use sentence case. For more on capitalization guidelines, go to
[Grammar and Mechanics](https://designsystem.talkdesk.com/51aaf6147/p/23fa55-grammar-and-mechanics).

![Activity details tabs in sentence case: Snapshot, Stats & flow, Wrap-up, Transcription](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-capitalization-tabs-do.png)
*Do*

![Activity Details tabs in Title Case: Snapshot, Stats & Flow, Wrap-Up, Transcription](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-capitalization-tabs-dont.png)
*Don't*

![Save button and 'Search by contact' input in sentence case](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-capitalization-button-do.png)
*Do*

![SAVE button and 'Search by Contact' input in all caps / Title Case](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-capitalization-button-dont.png)
*Don't*

### Scalable Content

Browsers, mobile devices, and other assistive technology to scale up content are critical for users
with impaired vision.

To help these users, text can be resized in a browser up to 200% resize of text without dropping any
content or functions. This should be accomplished in a browser and therefore not require any
assistive technology.

![Chat message fully visible after text resize, with no loss of content](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-scalable-content-do.png)
*Do Resize text without loss of content or functionality*

![Chat message vertically cut off after text resize](/assets/typography-accessibility/accessibility-scalable-content-dont.png)
*Don't Vertical text cut off*

Use this set of standard breakpoints to maintain layout integrity across viewport sizes. For best
results, test designs and code at each of these standard breakpoints.

## Overview

A viewport is the area of a screen/window shown to the user. In Workspace, we have 2 viewports: the
Workspace viewport and the Application viewports.

![Diagram showing the Workspace viewport containing the Application viewport](/assets/viewports/viewport.png)

These 2 viewports are needed because Workspace applications are rendered inside iframes, which means
that the application's content reacts to the iframe size. The applications are unable to know the
width of the Workspace viewport, and as a consequence cannot react to it.

---

## Viewport breakpoints

The 2 viewports always respect the use of this set of standard breakpoints to maintain layout
integrity across viewport sizes. For best results, test designs and code at each of these standard
breakpoints.

![Small 424px-640px, Medium 641px-960px, and Large greater than 961px breakpoints](/assets/viewports/breakpoints.png)

Please be aware that the min-width supported by Workspace is 424px. Cobalt supports lower widths since
we also support mobile apps.

### Media queries

```css
// Small devices (landscape phones, up to 640px)
@media (max-width: 640px) { ... }

// Medium devices (tablets, between 641px and 960px)
@media (min-width: 641px) and (max-width: 960px) { ... }

// Large devices (desktops, 961px and up)
@media (min-width: 961px) { ... }
```

---

## Canvas sizes

The Canvas size is the recommended size to design screens for each viewport size. When designing a
screen make sure to use the recommended canvas sizes that will be dependent of:

* App viewport: Small, Medium, or Large
* Drawer visibility (when fixed)
* Secondary Area visibility

By using the component [CanvasTemplate](https://www.figma.com/file/txlnFgFiMVzav4GpRfjeJ3/Workspace-library?node-id=367%3A71247)
available in the Workspace Figma library you can explore and use your designs with all recommended
canvas sizes.

| Workspace viewport size | Drawer         | Secondary Area | Main App viewport size |
| ----------------------- | -------------- | -------------- | ---------------------- |
| Small (424x640px)       | No drawer      | ❌              | Small (370x600px)      |
|                         | Hidden (hover) | ❌              | Small (360x600px)      |
| Medium (860x640px)      | No drawer      | ❌              | Medium (806x600px)     |
|                         | Hidden         | ❌              | Medium (789x600px)     |
|                         | Fixed          | ❌              | Small (593x600px)      |
| Large (1440x900px)      | No drawer      | Open           | Large (986x860px)      |
|                         | No drawer      | Closed         | Large (1386x860px)     |
|                         | Hidden         | Open           | Large (969x860px)      |
|                         | Hidden         | Closed         | Large (1369x860px)     |
|                         | Fixed          | Open           | Medium (773x860px)     |
|                         | Fixed          | Closed         | Large (1173x860px)     |
| XLarge (1920x900px)     | No drawer      | Open           | Large (1466x860px)     |
|                         | No drawer      | Closed         | Large (1866x860px)     |
|                         | Hidden         | Open           | Large (1449x860px)     |
|                         | Hidden         | Closed         | Large (1849x860px)     |
|                         | Fixed          | Open           | Large (1253x860px)     |
|                         | Fixed          | Closed         | Large (1653x860px)     |

ℹ️

* In specific scenarios, designers can use different canvas sizes that better adapt to their use case
  (studio and live - wallboard).
* The drawer can be fixed when the Workspace width is at least 641px;
* The Secondary area can be open if the Workspace width is at least 1041px;
* The drawer and the Secondary area can be fixed open at the same time if the Workspace width is at
  least 1237px.

```css
@media (max-width: 640px) {
  /* drawer: closed, can't be fixed */
  /* secondary-area: closed, can't open */
}

@media (min-width: 641px) and (max-width: 1040px) {
  /* drawer: open */
  /* secondary-area: closed, can't open */
}

@media (min-width: 1041px) and (max-width: 1236px) {
  /* Only 1 component can be opened */
  /* secondary-area or drawer */
}

@media (min-width: 1237px) {
   /* Both components can be opened */
   /* drawer: open */
   /* secondary-area: open */
}
```

### Mobile

When designing for mobile applications it's important to take into consideration smaller devices in
order to understand what's the minimal breakpoint but also the component and layout behavior.

Always test layouts in 2 screen sizes.

* For Android, the standard size is 360x640, which is considered a small screen for today's standards
  (2021).

⚠️ Usually, the second canvas is not a default but instead the device size used for testing. ATM it
was the iPhone XR.

---

## Workspace and Cobalt components in different canvas sizes

The canvas size in use will influence the Workspace and Cobalt components variants. This means that
when you are designing for specific canvas sizes (small, medium, and large) you should use the
available variants from the Figma library, and make sure that your development team applies the
correct variants to each viewport size.

Explore each component documentation to understand which variant should be used in your use case.

**Small components**

![Small components canvas with 8 numbered callouts](/assets/viewports/small-components.png)

1. Main app - **padding 12px**
2. Button component in small size variant - **height 32px / font-size 12px**
3. Heading component h1 for small viewports - **font-size 22px**
4. Nav component in small size variant - **padding 12px / font-size 12px**
5. Toolbar component in small size variant - **padding 12px / buttons without label**
6. Drawer component - **hidden in small size variant**
7. EmptyState component in small size variant - **fixed-width of 320px**
8. Toast component in small size variant - **padding 12px**

**Medium components**

![Medium components canvas with 8 numbered callouts](/assets/viewports/medium-components.png)

1. Main app - **padding 16px**
2. Button component in medium size variant - **height 40px / font-size 14px**
3. Heading component h1 for medium viewports - **font-size 28px**
4. Nav component in medium size variant - **padding 16px / font-size 14px**
5. Toolbar component in medium size variant - **padding 16px**
6. Drawer component - **hidden in medium-size variant**
7. EmptyState component in medium size variant - **fixed width of 484px**
8. Toast component in medium size variant - **padding 16px**

**Large components**

![Large components canvas with 8 numbered callouts](/assets/viewports/large-components.png)

1. Main app - **padding 24px**
2. Button component in medium size variant - **height 40px / font-size 14px**
3. Heading component h1 for large viewports - **font-size 28px**
4. Nav component in large size variant - **padding 24px / font-size 16px**
5. Toolbar component in large size variant - **padding 24px**
6. Drawer component - **hidden in large-size variant**
7. EmptyState component in large size variant - **fixed-width 564px**
8. Toast component in large size variant - **padding 24px**

---

We want to share the guidelines to successfully communicate with the Cobalt team.

## Exploring the documentation

Whatever your need is, you should always start by exploring this documentation guideline first. It might also be
helpful to check out the [React documentation](https://prd-cdn-talkdesk.talkdesk.com/cobalt/docs/index.html?path=/docs/introduction-docs--page).

## Asking a question

If you have any questions for the Cobalt team, please submit them on our Slack channel
[#eng-sme-cobalt](https://talkdesk.slack.com/archives/C79STTSLT) (formerly #cobalt-support).

## Asking for documentation

If you want to ask for documentation, share your need on [#eng-sme-cobalt](https://talkdesk.slack.com/archives/C79STTSLT) (formerly #cobalt-support)
first. Please add to this page if the Cobalt team agrees with the documentation needed.

## Reporting a bug

If you want to report a Bug to Cobalt Team, first also confirm the need for this on our Slack channel
[#eng-sme-cobalt](https://talkdesk.slack.com/archives/C79STTSLT) (formerly #cobalt-support) to avoid creating unnecessary issues.

If the Cobalt team agrees with the bug need, please fill out
[this form](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/secure/CreateIssueDetails!init.jspa?labels=Writing\&labels=support\&issuetype=3\&pid=14300\&assignee=5c572f5f7e444742bb2497e6).

## Checking Cobalt board

You can access our open Cobalt board whenever you need to take a look at what the Cobalt Team is doing.

## Submitting a request

If you want to submit a specific request to the Cobalt team, first share your need on
[#eng-sme-cobalt](https://talkdesk.slack.com/archives/C79STTSLT) (formerly #cobalt-support). If the Cobalt team agrees with the need, you can use
the [Cobalt Requests](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/secure/CreateIssueDetails!init.jspa?labels=Design\&labels=support\&issuetype=3\&pid=14300\&assignee=61ead92398cd610070722d08)
board to create a **request** issue type and the associated labels.

Remember to fit your issue into one of the following categories:

* New features, components, or patterns
* Improvements

## Asking for a design review

If you want to ask for a design review please follow this
[documentation](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/UX/pages/1103662259/Design+Reviews).

1. Add or update the cover with a "Design Review"
2. Go to the [Cobalt support and design-review form page](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/secure/CreateIssueDetails!init.jspa?labels=Design\&labels=support\&issuetype=3\&pid=14300\&assignee=6143a2e1ea73af006a70b079)
3. Add the Summary as "**Design Review, (review title)**"
4. Fill the Description input with the **design-review link** and a **message for the reviewers**.
5. For Task Category select,
   1. **Review**
   2. **Design** if it requires cobalt review
   3. **Writing** if it requires product writing review
6. Add a **Due date**. Cobalt collects the due date to know your expectation, however, it is not guaranteed that it
   will be met.

## Signing up for an interview

If you're interested in sharing your experience with the Cobalt team please fill out
[this form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScKFbZhngk1QHI3tVGIzJDjZu0m9OfUhBcX7rHlil96ifQLMA/viewform).

## Contributing to Cobalt

This will be available soon.

[Collaboration Workflow](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1aN5gwimyPPLAezwWoe_4umIWjEnYdLxWb1rEA6iRp4k/edit?usp=sharing) — Cobalt & Workspace

started," distinct from Foundations > Content's own "Principles" page, which covers writing
principles, not the design system's core values).
:::

## Introduction

Let's start from the beginning and remind the vision and principles that guide our design system.

We are and we'll always strive to be trendsetters. We want to lead, not follow. Our design is brave,
modern, but not over-complex or unpredictable. Visual coherence, better UI decisions, better
communication, and efficiency are what define us and help us create incredible experiences for our
users. Driven by new challenges and ever-rising expectations, we'll keep evolving, supported by our
principles. These will never change.

### Get started

This documentation explains all the specs and proper use of the Cobalt design system components for
designers, developers, and interested parties.

The information here on the design system is not set in stone. It is a set of patterns, behaviors and
rules that any business unit should follow and use.

### Libraries

The Cobalt Design System is made of a few main libraries: design tokens, core components, patterns, assets
and helpers. [Design › Libraries](/get-started/design/#libraries) links each one in Figma, with the DesignOps
files behind them.

## Principles

We are and will always strive to be trendsetters. We want to lead, not follow. Our design is brave,
modern, but not overcomplex or unpredictable. Consistency, simplicity, and reliability define us and
help us create incredible experiences for our users. Driven by new challenges and ever-rising
expectations, we'll keep evolving, supported by our principles. These will never change.

* **Brave** — We dare to innovate. Our avant-garde vision gives users the chance to experience the
  future today.
* **Dynamic** — We embrace new challenges, pushing our limits to adapt to a rapidly changing
  environment.
* **Straightforward** — We favor simplicity to boost efficiency and make users' lives easier.
* **Reliable** — We seek to provide a consistent experience that delivers on its promises and builds
  trust.
* **Human** — We strive to understand our users' state of mind and connect with them empathically.

For anyone looking for some great templates, look at some of the following. This collection includes
basic/empty page templates that can be used as a guide for creating your pages. After all, sometimes all
you need is to know where to start.

Using a template as a starting point for your user flows might be the quickest way to build a page
structure in seconds. There are plenty of decent templates here to quick-start your project, and all of
them are good-looking and functional.

---

## General layout

Usually, pages should have the main header on top, followed by a content area.

The header should be placed at the very top of the page and should be full-width.

The content area (unless stated otherwise, e.g. see **Headers** and **Tables** sections below) follows
