narrative.markdown:
:::note
This page doesn't map to the spec's Interaction Patterns categories (Forms & Validation, Search/
Filtering/Sorting, Empty States & Loading, System Notifications & Alerts, Onboarding & Wizards, Data
Visualization) — flagged for review. Sourced from the live Cobalt DS's Actions pattern page.
:::

Actions are usually associated with the header or the bottom of the page — their position depends on
the use case.

## When the user needs to interact with elements before interacting with the actions

* Actions go at the bottom of the page, aligned left.
* The primary action is positioned on the left.
* Destructive actions align to the right, separated from primary/secondary actions by a vertical
  divider.

## When the user is editing a form and doesn't need to interact with all fields first

* Actions go at the bottom of the page, aligned left, and stay always visible.
* The primary action is positioned on the left.
* Destructive actions align to the right, separated by a vertical divider.

## When the user doesn't need to interact with (most) elements before interacting with the action

* Actions associate with the header, aligned right.
* The primary action is positioned on the right.
* Destructive actions are positioned to the left, separated by a vertical divider.
narrative.title: Actions

narrative.markdown:
:::note
This page doesn't map to the spec's Interaction Patterns categories (Forms & Validation, Search/
Filtering/Sorting, Empty States & Loading, System Notifications & Alerts, Onboarding & Wizards, Data
Visualization) — flagged for review. Sourced from the live Cobalt DS's Bulk actions pattern page.
Image-heavy sections have been condensed to their essential guidance — figures/screenshots referenced
by the source page were not migrated in this pass.
:::

Bulk actions let users execute custom actions or logic on a large set of items at once — typically
seen in paginated lists or tables (users, contacts, voicemails, etc.).

## Types

1. **In a list or table** — select at least one item to enable bulk actions on the interface.
2. **Through file import** — apply the same kind of logic via a specific file that contains it.

## Empty and selection states

* **No content yet** — if the screen has no items at all, remove the toolbar's table actions (Search,
  Sort, Table options, Filters), since none of them would change anything.
* **Filtered to nothing** — follow the general Empty state pattern.
* **Error loading results** — use an error state on the results area.
* **No items selected** — the toolbar keeps its default actions (Search, Sort, Table options, Filters).
  These only change how items are shown, not the items themselves; each search/filter/sort still
  triggers a new backend query.

## Enabling bulk actions

Once one or more items are selected via checkboxes, the toolbar updates: the left side shows how many
items are selected, and the right side's table options (search, filter, sort) become unavailable —
re-querying while a selection is active risks showing a list that no longer matches the user's
selection. The bulk actions list sits on the left of the toolbar, with a 12px margin from any other
left-side content.

Clearing an active filter or search while items are selected keeps the selection intact.

## Pagination

Bulk actions work across a paginated list — selections persist as the user navigates pages, so they can
act once instead of per page.

## Overflow

If there are too many bulk actions to fit the toolbar, the ones that don't fit are grouped into a
"More actions" dropdown.

## Destructive actions

Destructive actions (Deactivate, Delete, Logout, etc.) can be part of the bulk actions list. They
should look the same as non-destructive actions for consistency, whether in the toolbar or a "More
actions" popup. Use a confirmation dialog after a destructive bulk action (see below).

## Actions that depend on item attributes

When a bulk action changes an attribute (e.g. voicemail "Status": Open/Resolved):

* **All selected items share the same value** — offer the opposite action, disabling the one that
  doesn't apply (so both actions stay visible for accessibility, one just disabled).
* **Selected items have mixed values** — either present both possible actions, or group them into one
  action that opens a modal where the user picks the specific value to apply.

## Long button labels

Prefer short labels, but when a label doesn't fit (especially after translation), move the action into
a "More actions" button rather than truncating with an ellipsis.

## Confirmation and modal dialogs

* **Non-destructive confirmation** — a simple acknowledge/confirm dialog with a primary action and a
  cancel.
* **Non-destructive, needs input** — the primary button stays disabled until the required input
  criteria are met.
* **Destructive, not critical** — use the standard error modal dialog.
* **Destructive and potentially breaking** (e.g. deleting an account, deleting users in bulk, deleting
  users currently on a call) — use a more deliberate confirmation requiring explicit user input, so the
  action can't be triggered accidentally. Use this sparingly, only when justified.

## Feedback states

After confirming a bulk action, show feedback:

* **Loading** — an info toast; disable checkboxes and actions to prevent duplicate requests.
* **Success** — clear the selection and show a success toast describing what happened to how many
  items.
* **Error** — keep the selection so the user can retry, and show an error toast.
* **Warning (partial success)** — keep only the items that failed selected, so the user can retry just
  those.

## Bulk actions through file import

Useful when users need to change many/all attributes at once, already have a tracking file (CSV,
Excel, etc.), or need to change large sets of items without manually working through the interface —
especially for recurring tasks. Provide an "Import" button that opens a drag-and-drop modal, and
consider a separate "Bulk management" area where users can track import progress (these operations are
often heavier and slower than the user is willing to wait for). Importing can update existing items
(unmatched rows are ignored), add new items (needs a different template), or delete items (needs its
own explicit option and, ideally, its own template) — these are three distinct outcomes and shouldn't
be conflated.

## Limiting selection size

When there's a cap on how many items can be selected at once:

* Once at least one item is selected, show a non-dismissible message stating the limit.
* At 75% of the limit or above, switch that message to a warning, and disable further checkboxes with
  a tooltip explaining why ("Can't select this item because it will go over the selection limit").
narrative.title: Bulk actions

narrative.markdown:
:::note
Merged from the live Cobalt DS's Empty state, Empty value, and Loadings pattern pages. Image-heavy
sections have been condensed to their essential guidance — figures/screenshots referenced by the
source pages were not migrated in this pass.
:::

## Empty state

Empty states are placeholder content for when content can't be shown or is empty — they appear when
there's no data to display and describe what the user can do next. Use them when a page or list
returns no results, whether because it's the user's first time in that section, or because a search or
filter returned zero results.

### Variations

Empty states can show an icon or an illustration, and can be sized for small, medium, or large
viewports.

### When to use

* By default, display an illustration representing the missing content or action.
* If useful, include an action or link to help the user recover and find what to do next.
* Consider every scenario that could cause the empty state.
* The first time someone views an empty board, suggest samples or recommendations to ease getting
  started.
* When a user finishes all their tasks, the tone can be celebratory and inspiring.
* A general "no results" state (e.g. no search results) should stay more neutral, but still motivate
  next steps.

### When not to use

* Don't use an empty state to give feedback about a state/context change during a task — use a message
  or toast instead.
* When multiple sections on a page can be empty, prefer inline notifications over multiple empty
  states.

### Use cases

No results for applied filters, no search results, no bookmarks, no activity, no wrap-up, no
transcription, no connection (when offline, the EmptyState illustration itself can't be shown).

### Behavior

* Layout scales from large to small based on container width.
* Empty states should be vertically and horizontally centered in the content area they replace.
* Don't use illustrations for panels, modals, cards, or other non-full-page empty states.
* If the main header has no actions, follow the empty state with a primary filled button. If the header
  already has primary/secondary buttons, use a primary outlined button instead.
* When combined with a button/link immediately after, snap them together (0px) — the empty state
  already reserves bottom spacing.

### Fallbacks and white-labeling

Instead of an illustration, any Cobalt icon can be used — for tight spaces or white-labeled
applications. White-labeling requires every illustration to fall back to a given icon, so make sure
developers get the fallback icon for every illustration used. This component isn't directly affected by
internationalization.

## Empty value

An empty value indicates a cell or label is empty, equal to zero, or not applicable. Consider three
cases:

| Use case                                            | What to write                                                                                        | Style                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| The value doesn't exist and will never exist        | N/A, Not applicable                                                                                  | color: secondary600, italic             |
| The value doesn't exist but can exist in the future | ∅ (numbers), — (text), or a short written explanation (e.g. "Not answered", "Skipped", "Not scored") | color: secondary600, italic (text only) |
| The value exists and equals zero                    | 0, 0€, 0%, etc.                                                                                      | color: secondary800, regular            |

* **Never / not applicable** — "Not applicable" is preferred over "N/A" where space allows; always use
  a distinct style so it reads as different from real content.
* **Not yet / future** — prefer a short written explanation of what's missing over a bare symbol where
  possible.
* **Zero** — use numerals (0 is the only option) with the appropriate currency/decimal/fraction/percent
  formatting, still styled distinctly from other text.

## Loadings

A loading pattern indicates content is processing, telling the user data is loading and the screen
isn't frozen. This pattern covers full-screen loading, inline loading, skeleton states, and progressive
loading — see also the 3Dots, Spinner, Skeleton, and ProgressBar components individually.

### Full-screen loading — 3Dots

Use when the entire page or application is processing (often after data is submitted/saved). If the
process will take more than a few minutes, include copy and an action telling the user what to do.

Workspace shows 3Dots while an app loads, and no package lets an app show it itself (see
[App loading](/workspace/app-loading/)). Inside your app, load a whole page with a Skeleton.

### Inline loading — Spinner

Use when a single component is processing (e.g. after clicking a button). Only show a spinner if the
expected wait is more than a second. Place it inside the portion of the page being updated.

### Skeleton states

Non-interactive previews of the actual UI structure, communicating that content is loading. Should only
appear for a few seconds, disappearing once content populates. Use when data takes more than 300ms to
load on an average connection.

### ProgressBar

Represents completion of a task or operation as a percentage. Use for file downloads/uploads,
long-running or background processes (e.g. importing data, exporting reports) — to give the user a
sense of context and duration.

### Load more action

Expands a list where only a few options are shown initially, loading data in progressive batches (a
common pattern inside a DropdownItem, for example).

### Choosing between them

|                 | 3Dots                                                                      | Spinner                                                                                                        | Skeleton                                                                                                       | ProgressBar                                                                                     |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What it is      | A progress indicator for a whole journey/page.                             | An animated indicator for a single processing element.                                                         | A non-interactive preview of the UI structure while it loads.                                                  | Continuous progress through a process (e.g. a percentage).                                      |
| When to use     | Loading an entire page or app; a large component; a single modal or panel. | A tiny inline action/feedback where the wait exceeds \~1s; data that can't use skeleton loading (e.g. charts). | Blocks of content loading together, where the page layout is known ahead of time; data taking more than 300ms. | Downloading/uploading a file; a long-running/background process; when duration context matters. |
| When not to use | Small components; inline loading; loading multiple panels/modals.          | An entire page load; multiple spinners on one page; long-running/background processes (use ProgressBar).       | Small components; panels/modals; long-running processes.                                                       | Small components; inline loading; multiple components at once; whole-page feedback.             |

### Combining multiple loadings

Use with caution: a page/app typically starts loading with 3Dots, then its structure loads
progressively with Skeleton. If a page and a Panel/Modal load together, load the Panel/Modal's key
content first with a Spinner, then continue the page's 3Dots loading. Avoid showing multiple loading
components for the same purpose at once (e.g. one Spinner per list item) — prefer a single shared
loading indicator for the group.
narrative.title: Empty States & Loading

Merged from the live Cobalt DS's Forms, Editing, and Errors pattern pages. Image-heavy sections have
been condensed to their essential guidance — figures/screenshots referenced by the source pages were
not migrated in this pass.
:::

## Forms

Forms enable the user to create and edit data. They are also used to collect user data.

Forms can be composed of different input types and other components, such as radio, checkbox, or
toggle. Explore each component's own documentation to understand when and how to use it: Checkbox,
DatePicker, DragAndDrop, Dropdown, Input, InputGroup, Radio, SearchInput, SelectionGroup, Textarea,
Toggle.

### Dimensions

Forms should be single-column and consider:

* width = 50% for large and medium viewports
* width = 100% for small viewports

Forms in panels always have width = 100%. Forms in modals should have width = 50% for large modals,
width = 100% for medium and small modals.

### Spacings

* Inputs should be placed at a distance of 16px from the next.
* Items placed next to inputs, like "delete" buttons, should be placed at a distance of 8px.
* When grouping inputs under the same label, use 12px of spacing between them (including the "add
  more" link/button).
* Inline inputs should be avoided — only use them when two or more inputs are related (e.g. ZIP code +
  City). Composed inputs should be spaced by L:24px / M:16px / S:12px.

### When to use

* Use it to gather short text input.
* Use any of the predefined input sizes.
* Keep labels in close proximity above the input field.

### When not to use

* Avoid using inputs side by side in forms — it can cause usability issues.
* Avoid gathering input from users that isn't absolutely necessary.
* For more extended text input, use a Textarea instead.

Placeholder text should be avoided. Dividers in a form should be spaced according to the viewport:
L:24px / M:16px / S:12px.

### Error inputs

In a form, instead of disabling the submit button until all mandatory inputs are filled, use a default
(enabled) button and, after the user submits the form, provide error feedback with a hint on specific
inputs.

Error input messages should be visible:

* **After the user interacts with the input field.** If the user isn't following the input value
  criteria (e.g. email format), the error message should appear once the user has finished with the
  field and moved to the next one. This excludes a required input the user simply hasn't filled in yet —
  that error should only show after submitting.
* **After the user interacts with the input's action**, when the input has no associated value
  criteria (e.g. an invalid password) — the error should show on submit. In this case, show both an
  error message next to each input with an error, and a summary message at the top of the form
  describing what needs fixing (e.g. "Fix these errors to continue: Phone is required. Email format is
  [example@email.com](mailto:example@email.com).").

## Editing

Editing allows you to edit content on a web page directly, in different ways. Not having a visible Edit
button can increase the probability that users accidentally touch things they don't want to change —
which is annoying while setting up something critical or instant. Edit buttons prevent mistouches and
make the user think before changing things.

### Overlay editing

Brings the editing form just a layer above the page (Modal or Panel), without leaving the page.

* **Use it** when a complex edit doesn't fit into the flow of the page, or when the content being
  edited is important enough to warrant interrupting the flow with a solid editing space.
* **With a Panel** — good when not showing all information at once, or when the user needs to keep the
  page's context visible alongside the edit.
* **With a Modal** — keeps the read-only area condensed and the reading experience neat; best for a few
  inputs and quick editing.

### Section-level editing

Best when users tend to edit sections separately rather than all together. Helps focus attention on one
section and prevents users from mistouching others.

### Page-level editing

Best when users tend to edit several related sections together. A page-level editing trigger (often
fixed to the top) saves repeated edit/save clicks.

A complete page-level form that follows this guidance, as code you can copy:
[Form Page](/layout-templates/form-page/).

### Choosing between them

| Pattern         | What it is                                                                                | When to use                                                                               | When not to use                                                                                       |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Overlay > Panel | Editing form opens in a Panel, with or without overlay.                                   | When not showing all information, or the context needs to stay visible while editing.     | If you have several fields to edit, prefer Panel or Page-level editing instead.                       |
| Overlay > Modal | Editing form opens in a Modal (always with overlay).                                      | For a few inputs, quick editing, giving the edit more highlight.                          | If you have several fields to edit, prefer a Panel or Page-level editing.                             |
| Section-level   | An Edit button on a view-only section opens editing mode on a new page.                   | When users edit sections separately; helps focus and prevents mistouching other sections. | If the user needs to edit multiple sections, prefer Page-level editing.                               |
| Page-level      | An Edit button (often fixed on top) on a view-only page opens editing mode on a new page. | For long or complex editing that needs the user's full attention.                         | If the user only needs to focus on a small block of content, prefer Section-level editing or a Modal. |

## Errors

Errors are unexpected outcomes resulting from user mistakes, technical glitches, or design flaws,
leading to frustration and minimal experiences while interacting with digital products. They should be
communicated promptly and transparently — critical situations, user input errors, system failures,
security/privacy concerns, and form validation all need clear guidance and support.

### Types of errors

Errors are organized by who performs the communication:

* **System errors** — performed by the system, exclusively used by Workspace. Sub-groups: System error
  prevention (destructive/irreversible action validation), System error, Cross-application or global
  system communications.
* **App errors** — performed by the apps. Sub-groups: Input errors (user input errors, file upload
  errors, submission input errors), Errors communication (general, multiple, task error communication),
  No content (existing content, non-existent content), and App error prevention (input errors
  prevention, destructive/irreversible action validation).

### Recommended components per error type

| Error group                       | Sub-group                                  | Component                                                              |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| System error prevention           | Destructive/irreversible action validation | OS pattern                                                             |
| System error                      | —                                          | Workspace system error pattern                                         |
| Cross-application / global system | —                                          | BannerMessage                                                          |
| Input errors                      | User input errors                          | Input with hint                                                        |
| Input errors                      | File upload errors                         | Message                                                                |
| Input errors                      | Submission input errors                    | Input with hint + Message                                              |
| Errors communication              | General                                    | Icon + Tooltip, LabeledIcon + Tooltip, Hint, Tag + Tooltip             |
| Errors communication              | Multiple                                   | Message + General error communication component                        |
| Errors communication              | Task                                       | Toast                                                                  |
| No content                        | Existing content                           | EmptyState (app container), Message (sub-container), Hint (components) |
| No content                        | Non-existent content                       | EmptyState                                                             |
| App errors prevention             | Input errors prevention                    | Icon + Tooltip, LabeledIcon + Tooltip                                  |
| App errors prevention             | Destructive/irreversible action validation | ErrorModal                                                             |

### Example use cases

System errors: the user quits the Talkdesk app; 404/403/500/503; browser not supported; no internet
connection; the user tries to call without mic permissions; a bug rollback; RTM system issues.

App errors: invalid input format; a file too large/wrong type/empty was dragged; too many files
dragged; submitting a form (or a modal/panel form) with errors; a list/table item or property has an
error; a chat message failed to deliver; multiple table items or a flow have errors; an app didn't
open; a download failed; a table/card/section failed to load; no results for applied filters or search;
form inputs that depend on each other's values; destructive-action confirmations (deleting data,
changing permissions, leaving unsaved changes, resetting settings, removing items from a group,
deactivating a property, or any destructive action affecting other products).
narrative.title: Forms & Validation

narrative.markdown:

Sourced from the live Cobalt DS's "Onboarding - Pendo walkthrough" pattern page. Image-heavy sections
have been condensed to their essential guidance — figures/screenshots referenced by the source page
were not migrated in this pass.
:::

Pendo Guide is a 3rd-party platform used to help users through their first experience with our
products.

## Overview

User onboarding is a designed series of interactions and instructions that eases users into a
product's experience — from a simple greeting and explanation to a full series of guided tasks.

## Anatomy

**Welcome/Success message:** Illustration (clarifies or decorates), Title (welcome message subject),
Description (what to expect), Actions (a call to action related to the context).

**Tooltips:** Step numbers (total steps in the walkthrough), Step title (the step's objective), a
Description, and Actions.

### Variations

* **Action buttons** — the first step has only one action; every step after that has two (previous and
  next).
* **Tooltip positions** — top right, top left, side top left, and side top right, depending on where
  the highlighted component sits on screen.

## Usage

The Pendo walkthrough draws the user's attention to areas of interaction, buttons, or locations — most
useful on first access, before the user is aware of the platform's actions and features.

* The welcome message must always be centered.
* Tooltips must be positioned next to the highlighted component, feature, or action.
narrative.title: Onboarding & Wizards

narrative.markdown:
:::note
Merged from the live Cobalt DS's Filtering and Searching pattern pages. Image-heavy sections have been
condensed to their essential guidance — figures/screenshots referenced by the source pages were not
migrated in this pass.
:::

## Filtering

Filtering allows users to hide content that isn't relevant to the task they're performing, keeping
focus on important information. It can be applied to a table, a group of cards, or other kinds of data
collection.

### Multiple filters

Small panels should always be used for multiple filters.

Input default state copy for filtering panels:

| Copy type   | Placeholder default state                                                   | Active default state        |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| When to use | Should never be used — replace empty states with placeholders and guidance. | —                           |
| Examples    | "Select options", "Select a category"                                       | "All agents", "Last 7 days" |

### Single filter

When only one filter can be applied, add a single component to the toolbar to apply it:

* **InputGroup with Dropdown** — when the user can filter by choosing 1 or multiple options from a
  list of several options (e.g. filter by country).
* **Toggle** — when the user can filter by a single boolean option (e.g. show in-progress issues). The
  label goes to the right of the toggle.
* **SelectionGroup** — when the user can choose only one option from up to 6 (e.g. filter by issue
  status: to-do, in progress, done). Avoid on small viewports — replace with InputGroup + Dropdown
  instead.
* **Dropdown** — when the user can choose one or multiple options from a longer list (e.g. filter by
  country). Avoid on small viewports for the same reason.

In small viewports, if the toolbar doesn't have room for the filtering component, replace it with an
icon-only filtering button that opens a popup.

## Searching

The Searching pattern lets users find information quickly and efficiently.

### Character limit

By default, search starts at 1 character. Depending on API limitations or other factors, it can start
at 3 or 5 characters/digits.

### Placement of copy

* **Description** — below the field's name; explains the search field's purpose.
* **Placeholder** — inside the search bar. Active state: shows the first result in alphabetical order.
  Default state: guidance on what to search for (e.g. "Search country").
* **Hint** — below the search bar or inside the popup (at the top), depending on context. Guides the
  expected action and offers search tips.
* **Feedback** — depending on context, can replace the hint. Negative: "No results found." In-between:
  guidance on the search process (disallowed characters, remaining characters needed). Positive: shows
  results.

### Best practices

* Use a hint/feedback inside the popup when space is limited — the popup should appear dynamically
  whenever characters are still missing.
* Prefer the hint/feedback below the search input, appearing as soon as the user clicks the input, even
  before typing.
* Avoid relying on empty states for feedback — the message can be missed.

### Result ordering

* **Numbers** — results can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of the value.
* **Names, emails, articles** — primary results start from the first letter typed; secondary,
  contextually relevant results can follow (e.g. searching "call" surfaces "call" first, "recall"
  secondarily; searching "E" for countries surfaces names starting with E, then contextually relevant
  ones like "España" for Spain).

### Behavior

* **Dynamic search** — starts at 1 character/digit; results appear alphabetically; the popup hint
  updates dynamically as characters are typed; secondary results can appear if contextually relevant.
* **Non-dynamic search** — also starts at 1 character/digit; if multiple items can be searched at once,
  explain how in the hint; clearly communicate any digit/character limitations in the hint.

Avoid using empty states as hints or in-between feedback — reserve them for negative feedback only.
narrative.title: Search, Filtering & Sorting

narrative.markdown:
:::note
This page doesn't map to the spec's Interaction Patterns categories (Forms & Validation, Search/
Filtering/Sorting, Empty States & Loading, System Notifications & Alerts, Onboarding & Wizards, Data
Visualization) — flagged for review. Sourced from the live Cobalt DS's Timezone selector pattern page.
:::

The timezone selector lets the user choose a timezone — used in multiple places in the product when the
user needs to associate a timezone with an object or define a view, like a schedule.

## Anatomy

The selector, a search field, a "recent timezones" group title, the 3 most recently selected
timezones, a divider between recent and all options (only shown when recent timezones are present), a
country name group title, and individual timezone options.

## Behavior

### Opening the selector

Multiple components can trigger the timezone selector — a Dropdown, or a button.

### Search

Given the number of timezones, search is necessary to reduce the effort of finding the right one. It
must support searching by country, city, timezone name, and UTC offset.

### Ordering

1. The 3 most recent timezones (if any), most recent first.
2. Then all options grouped alphabetically by country.
3. Within each country group, options are ordered alphabetically by city.

### Timezone code

Each option shows the abbreviated timezone name and its Universal Time Coordinated (UTC) offset.
narrative.title: Timezone selector

narrative.markdown:
While an app loads, Workspace covers the app's area with its own loader, 3Dots: three dots that jump in turn.
Workspace draws it for every app, and apps can't use it themselves: no Cobalt or Workspace package provides
it. This page describes what Workspace shows while an app and Workspace itself load, and what an app should
use for loading inside its own content.

:::note
Checked against the Workspace source code in October 2026. The [3Dots design](#the-3dots-design) section comes
from the Workspace design guidance. Where the two disagree, this page follows the code and lists the
difference under [Open questions](#open-questions).
:::

## While an app loads

* **Where:** over the app's whole area, centred. Workspace shows it for every app it loads: in the primary
  area, in the secondary area, and in Workspace panels and modals.
* **Look:** three 16px dots in an 80px-wide row, in Primary 9 (`--primary-9`), Primary 7 (`--primary-7`) and
  Primary 4 (`--primary-4`). Each dot jumps up and down every 0.3 seconds, 0.08 seconds after the one before.
* **After an update:** when the app is reloading because a new version was released, a line under the dots
  says "Loading the most recent experience for" and the app's name.
* **After 5 seconds:** if the app still hasn't loaded, Workspace adds "Thanks for your patience…", "Do not run!
  We are working on a better experience." and a **Refresh** button that reloads the app.
* **If the app fails to load,** Workspace replaces the loader with its error screen, and the app's dock
  button gets the "!" badge (see [Dock and drawer](/workspace/dock-and-drawer/#badges)).

All the text is Workspace's own and is translated. An app can't change it.

## While Workspace starts

* **In the browser,** Workspace plays the Talkdesk logo animation (the wordmark and the symbol) while it
  loads. It's on by default, behind a feature flag.
* **In the desktop app,** a small window shows that Workspace is loading. See
  [Desktop app](/workspace/desktop-app/#starting-up-and-going-offline).

## Loading inside your app

Once the app has loaded, loading inside it is the app's job, with Cobalt components:

* **[Skeleton](/components/core/skeleton/)** for a page or a block of content whose layout is known, such as
  the page after the app opens.
* **[Spinner](/components/core/spinner/)** for a single element, such as a button's action, when the wait is
  over a second.
* **[ProgressBar](/components/core/progress-bar/)** for a long or measurable process, such as an upload or an
  export.

See [Empty states and loading](/patterns/empty-states-and-loading/) for how to combine them.

## The 3Dots design

From the Workspace design guidance. The Creative team created the 3Dots animation after Talkdesk's rebrand,
from the brand's concept. It started in video and brand work and was then adopted as the product's main
loader.

### Anatomy

![3dots example — Anatomy](/assets/3dots/anatomy.png)

1. **Dots:** the animated, indeterminate progress indicator.
2. **Label:** text that tells the user what's loading.

### Variants

![3dots example — Variants Sizes: XLarge](/assets/3dots/sizes-xlarge.png)
*Size: XLarge*

![3dots example — Variants Modifiers](/assets/3dots/variants-modifiers.gif)
*Logo symbol animation*

![3dots example — Variants Modifiers](/assets/3dots/variants-modifiers-2.gif)
*Wordmark and symbol animation, used while Workspace starts*

![3dots example — Variants Orientation: Vertical](/assets/3dots/orientation-vertical.png)
*Vertical*

  ![3dots example — Variants Orientation: Horizontal](/assets/3dots/orientation-horizontal.png)
*Horizontal*

### Theming

A theme can change the dots' colours to suit it, for example on a dark background.

![3dots example — Theming](/assets/3dots/theming.gif)
*3Dots for dark backgrounds*

### Guidelines

* **One at a time:** there should be only one 3Dots on screen.
* **Placement:** centred in the area that's loading.
* **Label:** keep it under 80 characters per line, following the
  [W3C guidance on line length](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/page-structure/styling/). For a wait of more
  than a few minutes, tell the user what's happening and what they can do.

![3dots example — Guidelines When to use](/assets/3dots/guidelines-when-to-use.gif)
*A full-screen loading that took longer than expected*

### In Figma

Workspace Library › Apps Loader (3dots):
[3Dots component](https://www.figma.com/file/txlnFgFiMVzav4GpRfjeJ3/Workspace-library?node-id=4%3A91448).

## Open questions

Differences between the code and the Workspace design guidance, for the Workspace team to settle. Until they
do, follow the code.

* **3Dots inside apps.** The guidance recommends 3Dots for loading a whole page, a modal or a panel inside an
  app, but no package provides it: only Workspace draws it, while an app loads. Apps can use Skeleton, Spinner
  and ProgressBar.
* **Reduced motion.** The dots keep jumping when the user has asked for reduced motion.
* **No label while loading normally.** The guidance gives 3Dots a label saying what's loading. Workspace shows
  text only after an update or after 5 seconds.
narrative.title: App loading (3Dots)

name: What an app can ask Workspace for

narrative.markdown:
An app runs in its own iframe and can't draw anything outside it. For everything around it, such as a toast, a
badge on its dock button or a panel over its content, it asks Workspace through the Workspace SDK, and Workspace
draws it. This page lists what an app can ask for, what each request looks like on screen, and what an app
can't ask for.

:::note
Checked against the Workspace source code in October 2026. Where the code and the Workspace documentation
disagree, this page follows the code and lists the difference under [Open questions](#open-questions).
:::

## How requests work

* **Each request needs a capability.** An app lists its capabilities in its Workspace configuration. A call
  for a capability the app doesn't have fails.
* **Some requests need an SDK plugin.** The core `@atlas/sdk` covers toasts, badges, navigation, theme and
  language. Banners, notifications, panels and the secondary area each come in their own package, added with
  `Atlas.with()` before connecting.
* **Every call is asynchronous.** It's a message to Workspace, answered when Workspace has done it.

```js
import Atlas from "@atlas/sdk";
import Messages from "@atlas/sdk-plugin-messages";

Atlas.with(Messages);
await Atlas.connect();
```

## What an app can ask for

| Request                                                    | Capability                                        | Details                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Show a toast                                               | `toast`                                           | [Messages](/workspace/messages/#toasts)                                             |
| Show a banner                                              | `@atlas/messages`                                 | [Messages](/workspace/messages/#banners)                                            |
| Show an operating system notification                      | `@atlas/notification`                             | [Messages](/workspace/messages/#operating-system-notifications)                     |
| Show or hide the "•" badge on its dock button              | `badge`                                           | [Badge](#badge)                                                                     |
| Open a panel or modal holding other apps                   | `@atlas/panels`, `@atlas/menus`, `@atlas/context` | [Panels and modals](#panels-and-modals)                                             |
| Close the secondary area                                   | `@atlas/secondary-area`                           | [Secondary area](/workspace/secondary-area/#building-an-app-for-the-secondary-area) |
| Keep Workspace's address and drawer in step with its pages | `navigation`                                      | [Navigation](#navigation)                                                           |
| Replace its content with Workspace's error screen          | None                                              | [Error screen](#error-screen)                                                       |
| Run in the background and come to the front when needed    | `background`                                      | [Background apps](#background-apps)                                                 |
| Ask another app to do something, or be asked               | `protocol`                                        | [Protocols](#protocols)                                                             |
| Add keyboard shortcuts                                     | `@atlas/shortcuts`                                | [Shortcuts](#shortcuts)                                                             |
| Get the theme and the user's language                      | None                                              | [Overview](/workspace/overview/#theme)                                              |
| Use browser features blocked in the iframe                 | One per feature                                   | [Browser features](#browser-features)                                               |

Other capabilities give an app data or services, such as access tokens, feature flags, storage or logging.
They don't change what the user sees around the app, so they aren't covered here.

## Badge

`Atlas.badge.set(true)` shows a red "•" on the app's dock button; `set(false)` hides it. It shows even while the
app is open. When the app has more than one dock entry, a `path` option picks which one. Use it for something
ongoing that the user should come back to, such as a conversation waiting for an answer.

The "!" badge for an app that failed to load is set by Workspace, not by the app. See
[Dock and drawer](/workspace/dock-and-drawer/#badges).

## Panels and modals

An app can ask Workspace to open a panel or a modal holding one or more other apps, for example a side panel
with details for the record the user is looking at.

* **Where:** over the app that opened it, inside the primary area. It doesn't cover the dock, the drawer or the
  secondary area. Apps in the secondary area can't open one.
* **Panel:** a Cobalt [Panel](/components/core/panel/) on the right, sized for the app's viewport.
* **Modal:** a Cobalt [Modal](/components/core/modal/), sized for the app's viewport, over a backdrop that covers
  only the app's area.
* **Header:** the title the app gives (cut to one line, with the full title in a tooltip), a close button, and
  tabs when it holds more than one app. Built with Cobalt Marketplace [Header](/components/marketplace/header/).
* **Content:** each tab is another app in its own iframe. Which apps it holds is set in a menu definition, the
  same kind that describes dock and drawer entries. The app that opened it passes data to them through a shared
  context.

The app that opened it can show and hide it and is told when its state changes. The user closes it with the
close button.

Use a Workspace panel when its content is another app. For your app's own content, use Cobalt's Panel or Modal
inside your app.

## Navigation

With the `navigation` capability, Workspace and the app keep each other informed about the current page:

* **When the app changes page,** it tells Workspace the new path. Workspace updates the browser's address and
  history, and highlights the matching page in the drawer. Only the app on screen can do this.
* **When the user moves through Workspace,** with the drawer, a link, or the browser's back and forward buttons,
  Workspace tells the app the path to show.

Without it, the drawer and the browser's address don't follow the app's pages.

## Error screen

`Atlas.lifecycle.showError()` replaces the app's content with Workspace's full-area error screen. It accepts
two types:

| Type           | Title           | Message                                                                                    |
| -------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` | Restricted area | The user doesn't have permission and should ask their administrator.                       |
| `NOT_FOUND`    | Page not found  | The page may have moved or doesn't exist; check the address and that the app is installed. |

Any other type is rejected. Workspace shows the same screen when it can't find a page itself. Use it for a whole
page the user can't see; for a part of a page, show the problem inside your app.

## Background apps

An app with the `background` capability starts when Workspace starts, before the user opens it, and keeps
running out of sight. If its configuration allows it, the app can bring itself to the front, for example for an
incoming call, and later return the user to where they were. It can only return them if they haven't moved on
to another app in the meantime.

## Protocols

A protocol is a named action one app offers and others can ask for, such as "open this contact". An app
declares the protocols it handles in its configuration; another app checks that one is available and triggers
it with parameters. Workspace brings the handling app to the front and passes the parameters on. An app can
trigger a protocol only while it's on screen. Toast buttons and notification links use protocols too.

An app can also handle system links, such as `tel:`, the same way.

## Shortcuts

An app declares its shortcuts in its configuration, each with keys, a name and a scope, and then binds a handler
to each one. Workspace lists them, translated, in its shortcuts list.

* **App scope:** the shortcut works while the app is in focus.
* **Global scope:** it works anywhere in Workspace.

Like all Workspace shortcuts, app shortcuts work only while shortcuts are on: they're **behind a feature
flag**, and users can turn them off. The SDK tells the app whether they're on, so it can hide shortcut hints
when they aren't.

## Browser features

The app's iframe blocks some browser features unless the app has the matching capability:

| Feature                                                 | Capability   |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| Submitting a `<form>`                                   | `form`       |
| Opening a popup, new tab or window                      | `popup`      |
| `alert`, `confirm`, `prompt` and `print`                | `modal`      |
| Starting a download                                     | `download`   |
| Going full screen                                       | `fullscreen` |
| Writing to the clipboard                                | `clipboard`  |
| Microphone and speaker, and playing media automatically | `audio`      |
| Camera                                                  | `video`      |
| Security keys and passkeys                              | `webauthn`   |

`alert` and `confirm` draw the browser's own dialog, not Cobalt's. Prefer a Cobalt Modal inside the app.

## What an app can't ask for

* **Opening the secondary area,** or choosing which app it shows. Only the user opens it.
* **Opening, closing or resizing** the drawer, the secondary area or the dock, or making the window bigger.
* **Changing the title bar** or the dock and drawer entries at runtime. Entries come from configuration.
* **Knowing the window's size** or what's open around it. The app sees only its own iframe's width.
* **Adding to the notification center.** See [Messages](/workspace/messages/#notification-center).
* **Drawing outside its iframe.** Cobalt modals, panels, menus and tooltips the app opens itself stay inside
  its own area.

## In a prototype

A prototype runs outside Workspace, so these calls have nowhere to go. The stand-in shell accepts the same
requests and draws what Workspace would: see [Build with AI › In a stand-in shell](/get-started/build-with-ai/#in-a-stand-in-shell), where you can try
them.

## Open questions

Differences between the code and the Workspace documentation, for the Workspace team to settle. Until they do,
follow the code.

* **Minimum viewport.** The SDK documentation describes a `viewport` capability that sets an app's minimum
  viewport, with a warning screen asking the user to resize the window when the app is narrower. The code
  stores the setting, but nothing reads it: no warning screen is shown.
* **Shortcut configuration.** The SDK documentation lists shortcuts as keys and descriptions and says they should
  start with Meta+Shift and are checked against common shortcuts. The code expects a list with an id, keys, a
  name and a scope, and no such check was found.
* **Workspace modals don't trap focus.** Keyboard focus can leave a Workspace modal while it's open.
* **Untranslated label.** The panel and modal close button's "Close" is hard-coded in English.
* **Panels from the secondary area.** Only apps in the primary area can open a Workspace panel or modal.
  Whether apps in the secondary area should isn't documented.
narrative.title: What an app can ask Workspace for

develop another new type of component that impacts the workspace, please feel free to reach out to the Workspace team
so that this need can be captured and understood and follow the instructions to
[request a new feature](https://talkdesk.atlassian.net/l/cp/gobpz09a).

Please, have into consideration that the Workspace components were the subject of an in-depth study and validation

use cases known today.

narrative.markdown:
The Talkdesk desktop app for macOS and Windows runs the same Workspace as the browser, inside its own window.
Apps don't need a separate build for it. What changes is around them: the window's size, floating windows,
links from the operating system, and how the app closes and updates. This page describes those differences
and what they mean for an app.

:::note
Checked against the Workspace and desktop app source code in October 2026. Where the code and the Workspace
design guidance disagree, this page follows the code and lists the difference under
[Open questions](#open-questions).
:::

## How it differs from the browser

|                                                            | Browser                                   | Desktop app                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Window**                                                 | Any size                                  | At least 424 × 540px                                                                     |
| **Title bar**                                              | Workspace's title bar only                | Workspace's title bar, with the operating system's window controls in it                 |
| **Not enough room for a part the user opens**              | A toast asks the user to widen the window | The window widens                                                                        |
| **Floating windows**                                       | Not available                             | Available                                                                                |
| **Links from other programs** (`tel:` and Workspace links) | Not handled                               | Open in Workspace                                                                        |
| **Links that open a new tab**                              | A new browser tab                         | The default browser                                                                      |
| **Closing the window**                                     | Closes Workspace                          | Hides or minimizes it on most setups (see [Closing and quitting](#closing-and-quitting)) |
| **Updates to Workspace**                                   | When the page reloads                     | Downloaded in the background, installed when the user agrees                             |

An app can tell where it's running from `Atlas.environment.getConfig()`, whose `engineType` is `web`,
`desktop` or `pwa` (the installed web app).

## The window

* **Size:** 424 × 540px when it first opens, which is also its minimum. Users can make it bigger but not
  smaller, and it can't go full screen.
* **Position:** it reopens where the user last placed it. If the screens have changed and that place is gone,
  it opens in the top-left corner of the nearest screen.
* **Growing for the shell:** when the user opens the drawer or the secondary area and there isn't room, the
  window widens to fit and keeps its height. See [Space and viewports](/workspace/space-and-viewports/).
* **Title bar:** the operating system's window controls sit inside Workspace's title bar, and the title bar
  drags the window. See [Title bar](/workspace/title-bar/).
* **Zoom:** users can zoom in and out, which leaves fewer CSS pixels for every app.

![The desktop app as a narrow window on a desktop background, measured at 424px wide and 640px tall.](/assets/workspace/overview/desktop-default-size.png)
*First size in the guidance: 424 × 640px*
The code opens the window at 424 × 540px. See Open questions.

  ![The desktop app as a narrow window on a desktop background, measured at 424px wide and 540px tall.](/assets/workspace/overview/desktop-minimum-size.png)
*Minimum size: 424 × 540px*

At its minimum size, an app with sections gets about 356px. Design for it: the Workspace guidance expects over
80% of agents to use the desktop app in a small window next to their CRM.

### Coming to the front

Workspace brings the desktop window to the front when the user clicks one of its operating system
notifications, when a background app asks to come to the front (for example for an incoming call), and when a
link from another program opens in Workspace.

### Staying on top

Users can keep the Workspace window above all other windows with an **always on top** preference. Floating
windows sit above it.

## Floating windows

A floating window is a small, separate window that shows one app and stays on top of every other window,
including Workspace. It's meant for something the user needs to see or act on while working elsewhere, such as
the controls of an ongoing call.

* **Size:** 420 × 74px. It can't be resized, by the user or by the app.
* **Look:** no frame and no title bar: the app draws all of it. The user moves it by dragging.
* **Place:** near the top-right corner of the main screen, 38px from the right edge and 60px from the top.
* **Opened by** an app in the primary area, with the `floating-window` capability. That app launches and closes
  it, and the two apps can send each other messages.
* **Desktop only.** In a browser or the installed web app, the request does nothing and no error is returned.
  Check `engineType` and offer the same controls another way.

Design a floating window as a single row at exactly 420 × 74px: there's no room for a header, scrolling or
wrapping text. Give it a clear way back to the full app, since it has no window controls.

## Links from other programs

The desktop app can open links from other programs, such as a phone number clicked in a web page or a CRM:

* **Phone links** (`tel:`, `td+tel:` and `tel+atlas:`) go to the app that handles phone links, usually to start
  a call.
* **Workspace links** (`td+workspace:/<name>?<parameters>`) go to the app that handles `<name>`. An app handles
  one by registering a `system:<name>` protocol. See [Protocols](/workspace/app-requests/#protocols).

Workspace brings its window to the front and passes the link to the app.

## Links and sign-in

* **Links that would open a new tab** open in the user's default browser instead, apart from a few services
  that need to stay signed in.
* **Signing in with Talkdesk ID** happens in the default browser. While it does, the desktop app shows an "Action required" page
  asking the user to authorize it there.

## Closing and quitting

* **Closing the window on macOS** hides it. Workspace keeps running until the user quits.
* **Closing the window on Windows** quits, unless the account has **minimize to tray** turned on: then it
  minimizes. Minimize to tray is off by default. With it on, a Talkdesk icon in the notification area has
  "Show Window" and "Quit".
* **Quitting** asks first: "Quit Talkdesk app?", "You'll lose any unsaved changes", with Cancel and Quit.

Quitting doesn't wait for apps. If your app holds work the user hasn't saved, save it as a draft as they go.

## Updates

The desktop app downloads updates in the background. When one is ready, Workspace:

* shows an operating system notification, "Update available!", with the new and current versions;
* adds an update entry to the top of the [notification center](/workspace/messages/#notification-center)
  (**behind a feature flag**).

Clicking either opens a dialog, "Update available", with **Not now**, **See release notes** and **Update**.
Update restarts the app on the new version. If a release has to be withdrawn, the same dialog asks the user to
revert to the previous version instead.

## Starting up and going offline

* **While it starts,** a small 240 × 320px window shows that Workspace is loading.
* **With no connection,** a 424 × 540px window says "No internet connection" and asks the user to check it.
* **If Workspace can't load,** the app tries three times, 10 seconds apart, then shows "Error Launching
  Application".

## In a prototype

Pick "Desktop 424 × 540" in the [stand-in shell](/get-started/build-with-ai/#in-a-stand-in-shell)'s bar to see the app at the desktop app's size. The
shell doesn't draw floating windows; if the prototype needs one, show it as a 420 × 74px frame above the
rest.

## Open questions

Differences between the code and the Workspace design guidance, for the Workspace team to settle. Until they do,
follow the code.

* **First size.** The guidance says the desktop app first opens at 424 × 640px. The code opens it at
  424 × 540px, its minimum.
* **Dock width.** The desktop app's code defines a 54px dock width, matching the App Shell Figma component, but
  doesn't use it. Workspace draws the dock at 58px.
* **Where users set "always on top".** Workspace applies and remembers the preference, but no control for it was
  found in Workspace's own screens.
* **Floating windows outside the desktop app.** The request silently does nothing in a browser. Whether it
  should return an error, or fall back to something else, isn't documented.
* **Untranslated text.** The quit and update dialogs, the tray menu, and the loading, offline and launch error
  windows are in English only.
narrative.title: Desktop app

narrative.markdown: This page follows the maintained Atlas chrome adaptation. Read `content/workspace/dock-and-drawer/dock-and-drawer.md` from the bundle root for current geometry, theme and behavior guidance. Imported images retain historical provenance; register business apps/pages through the local scaffold rather than redrawing the shell.
narrative.title: Dock and drawer

narrative.markdown:
Workspace has four ways to tell the user something outside an app's own content: banners across the top of the
content, toasts at the bottom of the window, the notification center in the title bar, and the operating
system's notifications. Workspace draws all four; an app asks for them through the Workspace SDK. This page
describes each one, what an app can control, and when to use which.

:::note
Checked against the Workspace source code in October 2026. Where the code and the Workspace design guidance
disagree, this page follows the code and lists the difference under [Open questions](#open-questions).
:::

## Which one to use

|                     | Banner                                                                                         | Toast                                                                              | Notification center                                                  | Operating system notification                              |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| **For**             | Something that affects Workspace or several apps, and stays true until it's fixed or dismissed | The outcome of a process the user started, when the screen doesn't already show it | Things that happened while the user was elsewhere, kept as a history | Getting the user's attention when Workspace isn't in front |
| **Where**           | Across the top of the primary and secondary areas                                              | Bottom of the window                                                               | Panel from the title bar                                             | The operating system's notification area                   |
| **Stays**           | Until dismissed or removed                                                                     | 3, 5 or 7 seconds, or until dismissed                                              | In the history                                                       | As the operating system decides                            |
| **An app sends it** | Yes, through the SDK                                                                           | Yes, through the SDK                                                               | No: Talkdesk's services do                                           | Yes, through the SDK                                       |

When to use a toast, how to write one and how long it stays are on the
[Toast](/components/core/message/#toast-floating-type) section of Message. This page covers only what Workspace
adds.

For messages about the app's own content, such as a form error or an empty table, use Cobalt components
inside the app, like [Message](/components/core/message/), rather than these.

## Banners

### What they look like

* **Place:** below the title bar, across the primary and secondary areas, starting after the dock and drawer.
  They push the content down; there's no gap between them and the areas.
* **Height:** 48px. In a small window (up to 640px wide) with several banners, 76px.
* **Built with:** Cobalt's [Message](/components/core/message/) as a banner, with a status icon, the text,
  and an optional dismiss button. Side padding is 12px, 16px or 24px, for small, medium and large windows.
* **Variations:** success, warning, info, error and feature. Each has a fixed icon; feature uses a star.
* **Long text** is cut to one line with a "Read more" button, which becomes "Read less" when expanded.
* **Several banners:** the newest shows first, whatever its variation, with Cobalt Marketplace
  [Pagination](/components/marketplace/pagination/) to move between them.
* **Screen readers** announce each banner as an alert.

### Who sends them

* **Apps,** through the SDK.
* **Talkdesk's services,** for example to ask users of an app to refresh Workspace after a release.
* **Workspace itself,** for example when it needs permission to show notifications. That banner has an
  "enable notifications" link in its text.

### What an app controls

An app sets the **text**, the **variation** and whether the banner can be **dismissed**. It can remove its own
banner later. It can't add a title, buttons or an icon of its own.

Without a dismiss button, a banner stays until the app removes it, so remove it as soon as the situation it
describes is over. If a banner reported a problem that then goes away on its own, follow it with a success
banner, unless the fix was trivial. The success banner should name the problem it follows, since a newer
banner may have hidden the first one.

![A yellow warning banner across the top of Workspace saying connectivity issues may affect some features, with a Read less button and a dismiss button.](/assets/workspace/messages/banner-problem.png)
*A warning about a problem*

  ![A green success banner in the same place saying everything is back to normal and no connectivity issues were detected.](/assets/workspace/messages/banner-solved.png)
*The success banner once it's solved*

An app can send a banner only while it's running. An app the user hasn't opened yet, unless it runs in the
background, can't show one at sign-in. A banner goes to every user who has the app open.

### Writing a banner

From the Workspace guidance:

* **Keep it short:** up to 200 characters, most important information first.
* **Help the user solve the issue** when there's a way to.
* **Use sentence case**, with no full stop at the end.
* **End with an ellipsis** for a process that's under way, to show it will be brief.
* **Leave room for translation:** at least 40% more space for wordier languages.
* **Write like a person:** "we" rather than "Talkdesk", and "turn on" rather than "enable".

![A yellow warning banner reading: We need your permission to turn on desktop notifications.](/assets/workspace/messages/banner-do.png)
*Do*
Say “we” and “turn on”, with no full stop.

  ![A yellow warning banner reading: Talkdesk requires your permission to enable desktop notifications, ending with a full stop.](/assets/workspace/messages/banner-dont.png)
*Don't*
Avoid “Talkdesk requires”, “enable” and the full stop.

### When to use each type

Examples from the guidance. Check new banners with the Writing and Workspace teams.

| Type    | Example                                                                                                 |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Error   | The user tries to make a call but hasn't allowed the microphone. Several apps use it, so it's a banner. |
| Warning | The user's network is poor or unstable.                                                                 |
| Info    | The user's role changed, which may change the apps they can use.                                        |
| Success | Talkdesk was unavailable and is back to normal.                                                         |
| Feature | A new version of the desktop app is ready to install. The guidance calls this type Primary.             |

### Several banners, from the guidance

* **Dismissing one:** if it was the only banner, the content moves back up. If it was the first, the user sees
  the next one; otherwise the previous one, to come back to a known place.
* **Expanded banners** collapse again when the user dismisses them or moves to another banner.
* **Alignment:** every part of the banner is aligned to the top. In a small window, the pagination moves to a
  second row to leave room for the text.

## Toasts

### What they look like

* **Place:** in the bottom-right corner of the Workspace window, outside any app's frame, raised enough to clear the call
  bar.
* **Built with:** Cobalt Marketplace [Toaster](/components/marketplace/toaster/), with a status icon, an
  optional title in medium weight, the message and up to two buttons.
* **Types:** success, info, warning, error, primary and secondary. Primary and secondary use a stars icon.

### What an app controls

| Setting          | Options                                                                                | Default   |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| Message          | Required                                                                               | —         |
| Title            | Optional                                                                               | None      |
| Type             | Success, info, warning, error, primary, secondary                                      | Info      |
| Disappears after | Short (3 seconds), medium (5), long (7) or never                                       | **Never** |
| Dismiss button   | On or off                                                                              | On        |
| Buttons          | Up to two, each with a label. A button runs code in the app or opens a Workspace link. | None      |

A toast that never disappears stays until the user dismisses it or the app removes it. Pick the delay from the
[timer rules](/components/core/message/#toast-floating-type): no timer for toasts with actions or that ask the
user to do something, and at least 5 seconds otherwise.

## Notification center

* **Opened from** the notification button in the [title bar](/workspace/title-bar/), which shows the unread
  count. **Behind a feature flag.**
* **The panel** slides in from the right, below the title bar, over a backdrop. It closes on a click outside,
  Esc, or the button again.
* **Each notification** has an optional icon, a title, a description cut at 135 characters, the app it came
  from, when it arrived, and whether it's unread. Notifications are grouped by date, with a button to load
  older ones.
* **Where they come from:** Talkdesk's services create them for a user, and they arrive in real time. Each new
  one also shows as an operating system notification.
* **Clicking one** marks it as read, and opens its link in Workspace when it has one.
* **Kept for 14 days,** then deleted permanently, according to the Workspace guidance.

Keep titles and descriptions short: a title that doesn't fit is cut off, and so is a description over 135
characters.

![The notification center open over a dashboard, listing notifications under Today and Older, each with an icon, a title, a description, the app's name and a blue unread dot.](/assets/workspace/messages/notification-center.png)
*The notification center, from the Workspace design guidance*
The guidance shows it on the left; the code opens it on the right. See Open questions.

Apps can't add to the notification center through the Workspace SDK. The SDK's notification call shows only an
operating system notification, which doesn't appear in the center.

## Operating system notifications

An app can show one through the SDK with a **title**, a **body**, an optional **Workspace link** to open when the
user clicks it, and whether it should **stay until the user acts on it**. Workspace asks the user for permission
the first time, with a banner.

Use them for things the user needs to know while they're in another window, such as an incoming
conversation. Don't use them for feedback on something the user just did in Workspace: use a toast.

## In Figma

The Workspace guidance points to these Figma components:

* **Banners:** Cobalt Design System › Patterns › BannerPattern.
* **Notification center:** Workspace Library › Notification center.

## Open questions

Differences between the code and the Workspace design guidance, for the Workspace team to settle. Until they
do, follow the code.

* **Banner types.** The guidance lists a "Primary" type, whose icon can be changed (for example to a loader).
  The code has "feature" instead, always with a star.
* **Which side the notification center opens on.** The guidance shows it on the left, next to the dock. The
  code opens it on the right.
* **Banner role for screen readers.** The guidance gives errors the alert role and other banners the status
  role, which screen readers announce less urgently. The code makes every banner an alert.
* **Banner actions.** The guidance says banners can't have actions. Workspace's own permission banner has a
  link in its text, but apps still can't add one.
* **Default notification icon.** The guidance says notifications without an icon get a Workspace default. The
  code shows no icon.
* **Apps and the notification center.** The guidance says apps create notifications. Through the Workspace
  SDK, an app can only show an operating system notification; the center is filled by Talkdesk's services.
* **Toast timing.** A toast stays until dismissed unless the app sets a delay. The Toast guidance asks for at
  least 5 seconds, plus 1 second per 10 characters over 50, but the SDK offers only 3, 5 or 7 seconds, or never.
* **Toasts inside the app.** Whether apps should use Workspace toasts or Cobalt's Toaster inside their own
  frame isn't documented. Workspace toasts sit at the bottom of the whole window; a Toaster inside the app is
  limited to the app's area.
* **Untranslated labels.** The banner's "Dismiss", "Read more" and "Read less" are hard-coded in English.
